title: How Do U.S. Multinationals Navigate the Global Minimum Tax?
affiliations: University of Navarra, IESE Business School, , University of Iowa - Henry B. Tippie College of Business and University of Iowa - Henry B. Tippie College of Business

detail.title: How Do U.S. Multinationals Navigate the Global Minimum Tax?
detail.abstract: We examine how U.S. multinationals respond to the introduction of the Global Minimum Tax. Using various data sources, we document strategic responses by firms to mitigate the impact of the Global Minimum Tax. First, corporate disclosures indicate increasing recognition of the Global Minimum Tax but emphasize uncertainty. Second, exploiting historical ownership data and the EU's adoption of Pillar Two, we show that U.S. multinationals are significantly more likely than European multinationals to restructure ownership chains to avoid exposure to the Global Minimum Tax. Further, we show that U.S. multinationals with tax haven exposure do not experience any detectable increase in effective tax rates. Finally, we conduct a survey of U.S. tax directors to gather perceptions of the Global Minimum Tax and provide context for our empirical findings. Overall, our findings highlight how strategic organizational adjustments by U.S. multinationals and tax policy design by low-tax countries substantially attenuate the intended effects of the Global Minimum Tax.

title: Does Management Tone Predict Returns? A Cross-Sectional and Longitudinal Sentiment Analysis of MD&A Disclosures Across Ten NSE-Listed Companies
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Does Management Tone Predict Returns? A Cross-Sectional and Longitudinal Sentiment Analysis of MD&A Disclosures Across Ten NSE-Listed Companies
detail.abstract: This paper applies the Loughran-McDonald (2011) financial sentiment dictionary to the actual, publicly filed Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) sections of ten NSE-listed companies across two consecutive financial years (FY2023-24 and FY2024-25), producing 20 real sentiment observations across the information-technology, banking, and pharmaceutical sectors. The ten companies — TCS, Infosys, LTIMindtree, and Persistent Systems in IT; HDFC Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank in banking; and Sun Pharmaceutical Industries, Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories, Laurus Labs, and Aurobindo Pharma in pharmaceuticals — were chosen to span large-cap and mid-cap tiers within each sector, directly testing the information-asymmetry hypothesis inherited from a companion numerical-screening study. The results are more nuanced than that companion paper would predict. Within IT, Infosys scores net-negative in both years while LTIMindtree shows the sharpest year-onyear improvement in the entire sample (+0.0152), which makes the mid-cap/large-cap IT tone contrast far less tidy than a simple information-asymmetry story. Both banks sit close to tone-neutral, consistent with dense coverage and efficient pricing. In pharmaceuticals, Sun Pharmaceutical is the most positivetoned company in the sample while Aurobindo and Dr. Reddy’s both register net-negative. The yearon-year comparison reveals more movement than the single-year snapshot suggested: seven of the ten companies shifted tone direction between FY24 and FY25, and the size of that shift varies substantially by sector. I present these findings as a genuine, auditable, cross-firm evidence base for the hypothesis that MD&A sentiment carries firm-specific information in the Indian disclosure context, while being explicit that the sample is far too small for statistical inference and that the return-prediction test remains the necessary next step.

publicationDetails.detailsText: SSRN Working Paper Series, June 2026. Independent Researcher. India's Triangular Diplomacy: How New Delhi Navigates Its Relationship with Russia and the United States in the Age of Multipolarity. Alan Joan Amal Raj.

detail.abstract: In an era of accelerating great-power rivalry, India occupies a uniquely paradoxical position: the world's largest democracy, the fourth-largest economy, a founding QUAD member, and simultaneously one of Russia's most steadfast strategic partners. This paper examines how India has engineered and sustained a sophisticated triangular relationship with Russia and the United States-managing deep defence dependencies, growing economic integration, and escalating geopolitical pressure from both poles without formally aligning with either. Employing a structured qualitative comparative method across four analytical dimensions-defence procurement, economic trade, technology partnerships, and crisis diplomacy-and drawing on primary government documents, SIPRI data, bilateral trade statistics, and policy statements from 2020 to 2026, this paper advances an original theoretical argument. It introduces the concept of Asymmetric Balancing-the deliberate compartmentalization of incompatible partnerships into functionally non-competing domains-and demonstrates through systematic case evidence that India's dual-partnership architecture constitutes a calculated grand strategy rather than opportunistic ambiguity. The paper finds that Asymmetric Balancing has enabled India to extract simultaneous strategic value from both partnerships across all four dimensions studied, while managing the principal risks (CAATSA sanctions, supply chain disruption, technology dependency) through sequenced accommodation and principled ambiguity. The framework is tested against three acute crisis episodes (2025 sanctions pressure, 2025 India-Pakistan conflict, 2026 Ukraine peace dynamics) and found to be empirically robust. The paper concludes that Asymmetric Balancing represents a replicable model of middle-power statecraft with implications for IR theory and for states navigating the emerging multipolar order.

title: Aromas in Space: Virtual Reality and Posture Simulated Space Analogues for Evaluating Orthonasal and Retronasal Olfactory Perception
affiliations: RMIT University, IFF, International Flavors and Fragrances (IFF), International Flavors and Fragrances (IFF), Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT University), University of Otago, Independent and

detail.title: Aromas in Space: Virtual Reality and Posture Simulated Space Analogues for Evaluating Orthonasal and Retronasal Olfactory Perception
detail.abstract: The Head-Down Tilt (HDT) is a widely used space analogue for studying food-related chemosensory perception, as it simulates key physiological effects of weightlessness on the human body. However, the integration of this method with Virtual Reality (VR) tools remains underexplored, presenting an opportunity to improve the efficacy of space analogues. A dual study design was used to investigate the combined effect of a -6° HDT and a VR-simulated spacecraft environment on orthonasal (sniffing) and retronasal (in-mouth) odour perception, along with affective responses, and overall experience. In total, 200 participants (orthonasal n=105; retronasal n=95) evaluated three food odours for intensity and liking in one of three randomly assigned contexts: Central Location Test (CLT; non-VR), VR-simulated spacecraft (VR-Space), or a combined VR-simulated spacecraft and -6° HDT condition (VR-HDT). Findings suggest greater almond odour intensity in the VR-Space context compared to the CLT and VR-HDT contexts, but only during retronasal evaluation. In contrast, greater almond liking was found in the VR-HDT context than in the CLT, specifically during orthonasal evaluation. Participant engagement measures captured significantly lower interest (affective value) and focus (active involvement) in the VR-HDT context relative to the CLT and VR-Space. Generally, the VR-HDT experience elicited more negative valence and higher perceived stress compared to both contexts, with moderate levels of loneliness comparable to the VR-Space context. These findings highlight the potential value of integrating digital immersion with altered posture to enhance the ecological validity of space analogues for assessing sensory and affective responses.

title: Digital Transformation Meets Green Lending: Complementary Effects on Bank Competitiveness in India
affiliations: Institute of Management Technology (IMT), Hyderabad, Institute of Management Technology, Ton Duc Thang University and Ho Chi Minh University of Banking

detail.title: Digital Transformation Meets Green Lending: Complementary Effects on Bank Competitiveness in India
detail.abstract: The banking industry is experiencing a dual transformation owing to the development of innovative technology and growing interest in sustainable finance. Whereas investment in FinTech technologies has turned out to be a strategy of choice for many banks striving for competitive advantage, the findings of the previous studies are rather inconclusive concerning its effectiveness and mostly deal with direct effects; in addition, no studies have explored the issue of conditions when digital transformation provides a larger competitive advantage. The present study explores the effect of investment in FinTech technologies on competitiveness of banks and checks whether green credit enhances the importance of digital transformation for competitive advantage. The findings reveal that FinTech investment substantially boosts bank competitiveness, but green credit has a direct negative effect. Banks which are strongly involved in green lending gain more competitive benefits from the digital transformation process. Such synergistic effects are especially strong for public banks and strong banks. This research thus contributes to the literature on banking, FinTech, and sustainable banking by providing evidence that complementarity theory can be used to explain the relationship between the competitive value of the digital transformation and the availability of complementary strategic assets.

title: KYS: Know Your Swarm - A Governance Framework for Multi-agent AI Systems across Autonomous Economies

detail.title: KYS: Know Your Swarm - A Governance Framework for Multi-agent AI Systems across Autonomous Economies
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence governance is entering a new phase. Early frameworks focused primarily on individual models and their data, accuracy, explainability, safety, robustness and fairness. More recent approaches increasingly address AI agents, including their identity, capabilities, permissions, delegated authority and behaviour at runtime. The next governance challenge concerns what emerges when multiple autonomous agents interact, coordinate, delegate, adapt and collectively influence consequential outcomes.

Building directly on Chaudhry (2026a) and Chaudhry (2026b), this paper extends KYS: Know Your Swarm beyond Autonomous Finance and across high-impact sectors and autonomous economies. It retains the five KYS pillars, the Swarm Accountability Gap and the concept of delegation failure developed in the earlier papers, while generalising their application to cross-sector multi-agent systems.

The paper distinguishes the emerging agentic economy, in which AI agents increasingly perform or mediate economic functions, from autonomous economies, in which interactions among autonomous systems become materially consequential to economic, institutional and social outcomes. The agentic economy foregrounds delegated action by individual agents; autonomous economies foreground the wider systems, institutions and collective outcomes that emerge as such activity becomes interconnected.

Drawing on international AI governance instruments, regulatory developments, enterprise agent-governance frameworks and emerging evidence across finance, healthcare, public administration, critical infrastructure, telecommunications, space systems, mobility, physical AI, manufacturing, employment, education, scientific research and gaming, the paper generalises the Swarm Accountability Gap beyond financial services. It argues that local compliance does not guarantee global accountability: every AI agent may be identified, authorised, monitored and technically traceable while the collective outcome remains harmful, discriminatory, difficult to explain or institutionally unowned. It also develops the implications of agent loops, persistent memory, evolving agent harnesses and feedback among agents, all of which may alter deployed behaviour without changing the underlying foundation model.

KYS retains five governance pillars: Agent Identity, Authorized Intent, Interaction Mapping, Human Override and Accountable Redress. The framework does not replace model governance, organisational AI governance, Know Your Agent approaches, deployment authorisation, runtime safeguards, observability, sector regulation or technical assurance. It connects these layers to institutional responsibility for collective outcomes and extends fairness analysis from individual models to system-level effects, including how proxy variables, feedback loops and cumulative decisions may propagate disadvantage across interacting agents.

The paper’s original contribution is to establish the interaction layer as a cross-sector object of governance, distinguish agentic economies from autonomous economies and apply KYS to consequential multi-agent systems beyond finance. Its central claim is that institutions deploying autonomous systems must know every agent, know the authority delegated, understand how AI agents interact, preserve meaningful human override and ensure that an identifiable institution remains accountable when the collective system causes harm.

title: The Inflation-growth Nexus in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Panel Data Investigation with Political Instability as a Moderator

detail.title: The Inflation-growth Nexus in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Panel Data Investigation with Political Instability as a Moderator
detail.abstract: This study investigates the effect of inflation on economic growth across Sub-Saharan African nations, with inflation specified as the primary explanatory variable and economic growth as the dependent variable. Trade openness, population growth, gross capital formation, and political instability are included as control variables. The analysis draws on annual panel data for all 48 Sub-Saharan African countries, as classified by the World Bank, spanning the period 2000-2024 and sourced from the World Development Indicators database. Pooled ordinary least squares and fixed-effects panel estimations are employed to test the study's hypotheses. The findings indicate that inflation exerts a statistically significant negative effect on economic growth throughout the sub-region. Further analysis reveals that political instability moderates this relationship only marginally, exerting a negative but statistically insignificant effect on the magnitude of inflation's impact on growth. Additionally, population growth is found to significantly and adversely affect economic growth in low-income countries within the sub-region, though this effect is not significant among lower-middle-income countries. These findings underscore the importance of monetary policy discipline in fostering sustainable growth and suggest that Sub-Saharan African governments should prioritize inflation-control measures, given the demonstrable growth costs associated with persistently high inflation.

title: When Shelf Life Matters: Multi-period Shelf-space Optimization
affiliations: University of Augsburg, Technische Universität München (TUM) and Technische Universität München (TUM)

detail.title: When Shelf Life Matters: Multi-period Shelf-space Optimization
detail.abstract:
Grocery retailers must continually refine their product offerings to maintain customer attractiveness while safeguarding profitability and reducing food waste, a challenge that is particularly pronounced for perishables. Heterogeneous shelf lives, spoilage risk, customers' expiry-date preferences, and stochastic, period-specific demand create substantial operational complexity because these factors evolve over time and interact across periods. Addressing these characteristics requires a multi-period model that integrates assortment, shelf-space, and inventory decisions. Prevailing approaches, largely based on single-period models, overlook the fact that perishables are sold, replenished, and withdrawn over multiple periods. As a result, inventories contain units with different remaining shelf lives, which directly influence customers' expiry-date-dependent purchasing behavior and subsequent inventory dynamics. 
We develop a novel integrated multi-period model to optimize assortment, shelf space, and inventory for packaged perishables. The model accounts for heterogeneous inventories, product expiration over time, weekly demand patterns, replenishment operations, and customers' expiry-date-dependent withdrawals. To address the resulting NP-hard knapsack problem with stochastic, nonlinear demand and dynamic inventory transitions, we propose a tailored simulationoptimization approach that iteratively updates demands. Using real-world data, we show that explicitly incorporating shelf lives, weekly demand patterns, and customer withdrawal behavior materially changes optimal assortment, shelf-space, and inventory decisions. We generalize the findings with simulated data and demonstrate the substantial potential to increase profitability while simultaneously reducing food waste.

title: How Multi-tier Subscription Shapes Engagement: Direct Effects and Network Spillovers on Digital Platforms
affiliations: , Texas A&M University - Department of Marketing and Renmin University of China

detail.title: How Multi-tier Subscription Shapes Engagement: Direct Effects and Network Spillovers on Digital Platforms
detail.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly adopt multi-tier subscription models, yet it remains unclear whether adding higher tiers creates incremental engagement. The question is especially salient on digital platforms, where visible peer tiers could inspire or discourage engagement through social comparison. We study how multitier subscription programs affect user engagement, both directly through subscribers' own behavior and indirectly through peer spillovers in their social networks, using a unique dataset from a languagelearning platform that introduced a higher premium tier (SVIP) alongside its standard premium tier (VIP). We employ a stacked difference-indifferences design with generalized propensity scores for multivalued treatments under network interference to identify direct and spillover effects separately. We find that higher-tier subscriptions generate substantially greater participation and faster learning progression than the standard tier. Although both tiers produce an initial post-subscription spike attributable to the payment itself, the standard tier's effect decays quickly, whereas the higher tier's persists when its feature value meets subscribers' needs. Spillovers from peer tiers depend systematically on the distance between users' own tiers and their peers': nearby higher-tier peers motivate engagement, whereas more distant higher-tier peers discourage it. These findings have important implications for the design of subscription programs and social networks on digital platforms.

title: SBIR: Reauthorization And Reform
affiliations: George Washington University - Law School

detail.title: SBIR: Reauthorization And Reform
detail.abstract:
After months of contentious delay, Congress appears poised to reauthorize the Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) program and its close relative, the Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) program.  These programs-known as "America's seed fund"-are important sources of non-dilutive federal funding available to help American small businesses research, develop, and ultimately commercialize innovative new technologies. 

This REPORT last addressed the SBIR program in September 2025, highlighting a bid protest decision from the Government Accountability Office that demonstrated the potential value of SBIR contracts in the mergers and acquisitions market. The closing sentence read: "We are cautiously optimistic that Congress will, once again, renew the SBIR program. 
In retrospect, perhaps we should have been more pessimistic. On September 30, 2025—the same day that appropriated
funding expired across the Federal Government—statutory authorization for the SBIR and STTR programs lapsed as well.
While the “shutdown” was largely resolved with stop-gap continuation funding by mid-November, the SBIR and STTR
programs have been stalled in a legislative logjam that effectively paused new Phase I and Phase II awards for the last six months.

Finally, on March 3, 2026, the Senate seemed to reach a viable compromise, dubbed the Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act (S.3971). The House passed the bill on March 17, leaving only the President’s signature before it becomes law. The compromise legislation, if enacted, would bring several reforms.

title: Recursive Leadership Theory: How Leader Interior Development and Organizational Renewal Form a Single Recursive Loop

detail.title: Recursive Leadership Theory: How Leader Interior Development and Organizational Renewal Form a Single Recursive Loop

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and chief executive of ThriveAxis (CLP Ventures, LLC) and has a commercial interest in the People-Forward Leadership™ framework, which this paper provides a theoretical structure for. The field observation in Section 7 is drawn from a paid consulting engagement, an anonymized practice account with no participant research. The theory's evidentiary standing rests on the falsifiable prediction specified in the paper rather than on the author's practice.

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes Recursive Leadership Theory (RLT). Its central thesis is a unification. The interior development of a leader and the renewal of an organizational system, long theorized in separate literatures, are two arcs of a single mutually recursive loop, joined at the leadership team. Renewal originates in a leader's reconstitution of identity, transmits through the senior team as a proving layer that validates change at the micro scale, reaches the wider system, and returns to the leader as the input to the next cycle. A review of the open systems, organizational learning, strategic renewal, leader development, team, and succession literatures shows that each addresses one component of this loop, yet none specifies the whole. Renewal theory leaves the locus of renewal's drivers unresolved, interior development theory stops at the individual boundary, and succession research documents disruption without a developmental mechanism. RLT fills that void with a specified structure, and it generates a falsifiable signature prediction that no existing theory shares. Renewal is sustained or lost at leadership succession, depending on whether the incoming leader enters the loop, independent of team strength. The theory is differentiated from complexity leadership theory, the direction-alignment-commitment ontology, shared and distributed leadership, trickle-down models, and the cybernetic tradition, and is illustrated through a three-year field observation of a public-sector organization. Implications are developed for succession planning, senior team development, and organizational adaptation under artificial intelligence, where recent evidence on expertise atrophy makes the theory's negentropic function urgent and human development the scarce input to renewal.

Recursive Leadership Theory, the People-Forward Leadership™ framework it formalizes, and the field observation reported in Section 7 originate with the author. The author used Claude (Anthropic) to assist with literature research and drafting, and Grammarly to proofread for grammatical errors. All theoretical content, claims, and final text were reviewed, verified, and approved by the author.

title: Federal Contracts At The Supreme Court: Three Recent Opinions Reshape Expectations Around Third-Party Claims Against Contractors
affiliations: George Washington University - Law School

detail.title: Federal Contracts At The Supreme Court: Three Recent Opinions Reshape Expectations Around Third-Party Claims Against Contractors
detail.abstract: The federal contracting community learned a lot from the U.S. Supreme Court over the last few months. Across three opinions, the Supreme Court reshaped and clarified the legal landscape governing federal contractor liability to third parties. And activity on the Court's docket in May 2026 suggests a fourth opinion may be coming to further clarify the extent to which states can regulate federal contractor operations. A primary takeaway from the opinions is that private contractors do not enjoy the full spectrum of privileges and immunities that protect the Federal Government from third-party claims and state regulations. That imbalance incentivizes third-party claimants and state regulators to target federal contractors-as defendants, regulated entities, or both. To be sure, contractors may find protection from a patchwork of judicial doctrines that (1) limit or preempt contractor liability arising from compliance with lawful Federal Government direction, (2) permit contractors to remove cases from state to federal court, and even (3) provide contractors immunity from state regulations. But this tapestry provides only partial protection, and the Supreme Court appears unwilling to mend the seams. To the extent third-party claims and state regulation are undermining the Government's ability to procure goods and services-Congress will need to act. Until then, as always in this industry-seller beware.

title: Reframing the Modern Welfare Paradigm: From the Trust Assumption to Technological Governance and Long-Term Equity

detail.title: Reframing the Modern Welfare Paradigm: From the Trust Assumption to Technological Governance and Long-Term Equity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This research is independent and was not funded by any organization that could influence its conclusions.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a policy analysis paper based on public reports, case studies, and institutional review. One illustrative example in the manuscript is drawn from the author's personal experience as a citizen interacting with a federal agency (Social Security Administration field office). This example is used solely to illustrate the importance of person-job matching in public administration—ensuring staff are assigned to roles aligned with essential job functions. It is not intended to question the employment of individuals with disabilities, which is both legally required and morally appropriate. Reasonable accommodations should be provided; for instance, visually impaired staff can be effectively placed in suitable roles such as telephone-based customer service or positions supported by assistive technology.
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
Traditional public welfare and administrative procedures in the United States are predicated on a high-trust “honor system” of self-declaration. This institutional design, rooted in assumptions of cultural homogeneity and strong informal social controls, has become structurally obsolete amid demographic diversification, social atomization, transnational mobility, and sophisticated digital fraud. The result is massive benefit leakages, erosion of taxpayer confidence, and a growing trust deficit that undermines the legitimacy of the welfare state.

Drawing on GAO estimates showing 11–15 percent fraud rates ($100–135 billion) in pandemic-era unemployment insurance programs, this paper demonstrates that static cost-benefit analyses systematically undervalue the long-term “governance capital” created by credible verification systems. Empirical evidence from states using third-party digital identity platforms (e.g., ID.me in Arizona) shows dramatic reductions in fraudulent claims—a 68.3 percent drop in ongoing claims within one week—without bureaucratic expansion.

The analysis employs the “reverse-cannikin law” (bucket theory) to argue that equity does not require lowering verification standards. Instead, governments should maintain rigid, uniform eligibility criteria while providing targeted external assistance for vulnerable populations. Sustainable reform requires a dual strategy: external procurement of technology for frictionless back-end auditing, paired with internal civil service optimization that emphasizes merit-based performance and eliminates ideological redundancies that degrade core capacity.

Anchored in sociological jurisprudence and core constitutional principles (general Welfare, due process, equal protection, and legislative authority), the paper proposes a systematic three-tier policy audit—Repeal, Amend, Legislate—to update obsolete administrative frameworks. Only by migrating from testing human nature to competence-driven technological governance can modern institutions achieve fiscal integrity, administrative competence, and genuine long-term social equity.

title: Flux-corrected Diagonal Frog: Second Order and Positivity at All Time Steps
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - NYU Tandon School of Engineering

detail.title: Flux-corrected Diagonal Frog: Second Order and Positivity at All Time Steps

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the authors.
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received.

detail.abstract: By Godunov's theorem, linear second-order finite-difference schemes for the Fokker-Planck equation cannot preserve positivity. The Diagonal Frog (DF) framework previously bypassed this barrier using eventual positivity, but required a strict minimum time step. This paper resolves the small-step limitation using a nonlinear extension of the DF solvers. We split the second-order directional operator into a monotone M-matrix core and an antidiffusive flux correction. A Zalesak-type limiter is then applied iteratively within the implicit banded solve. The resulting Flux-Corrected DF (FCDF) schemes (variants A and B) are unconditionally positive across all time steps. Because the limiter acts on fluxes rather than point values, these schemes conserve discrete mass exactly and maintain second-order accuracy. Crucially, the limiter activates only within unresolved layers. This ensures the global L 1 convergence remains second-order uniformly in the cell Péclet number, avoiding the first-order degradation seen in the Chang-Cooper scheme. The method's Picard iteration is contractive under a purely convective step restriction. To support arbitrary step sizes, we develop an active-set reformulation. This solves the system using a semismooth Newton iteration, where computational cost scales only with the number of nodes where positivity binds. Finally, we introduce a defect-corrected time stepping approach that restores second-order time accuracy. Numerical experiments on Ornstein-Uhlenbeck and advection-dominated benchmarks confirm our claims.

title: Postscript Iv: Federal Circuit Addresses Cica Override Litigation
affiliations: George Washington University - Law School

detail.title: Postscript Iv: Federal Circuit Addresses Cica Override Litigation

keywords: Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit

detail.abstract: We are overdue for an update on "CICA override" litigation-that is, derivative bid protest litigation challenging an agency's decision to override the automatic stay that is typically triggered when a protester files a timely protest under the Competition in Contracting Act. In the last several years, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit has issued three decisions addressing some of the unique procedural issues that arise in CICA override litigation: Life Science Logistics LLC v. U.S., 172 F.4th 1357 (Fed. Cir. 2026), NIKA Technologies, Inc. v. U.S., 987 F.3d 1025 (Fed. Cir. 2021), 63 GC ¶ 49, and Safeguard Base Operations, LLC v. U.S., 792 F. App’x 945 (Fed. Cir. 2019). All three of these appeals required the Federal Circuit to grapple with mootness, which is not surprising given how long the appellate process takes in relation to the 100-day statutory limit on CICA-based protest actions at the Government Accountability Office. The most recent decision, Life Science, addresses the role of traditional injunction factors once a Court of Federal Claims judge deems an agency’s override to be unjustified. Among the three opinions, the most impactful appears to be dicta from the non-precedential Safeguard opinion, which correctly confirms that neither agencies nor COFC judges are bound to follow the four-factor test for grading agency override decisions set forth in Reilly’s Wholesale Produce v. U.S., 73 Fed. Cl. 705 (2006).

title: A Functional Approach to Fixed-income P&L Attribution
affiliations: World Bank

detail.title: A Functional Approach to Fixed-income P&L Attribution

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is employed by the World Bank. This article represents the author's personal views and does not represent the views of the World Bank Group. No other conflicts of interest to declare.

detail.abstract: Standard fixed-income P&L attribution produces systematic residuals that undermine financial reporting and trigger capital surcharges under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) P&L Attribution test. We propose the Functional P&L Attribution (FPLA) framework, built on the Exact Smooth Term Structure Estimation (ESTE), to reduce these residuals. Using the smooth, exact-fitting curve that ESTE provides, we derive closed-form first-and second-order sensitivity formulas requiring no numerical bumping. The resulting P&L identity decomposes realized gains into carry, roll-down, delta, and a second-order covariance term that arises because the curve construction itself depends on the prevailing quoted rates-a term structurally absent from key-rate methods and non-zero even for deterministic cash-flow portfolios. In the absence of model inconsistency and numerical error, the decomposition yields an exact discrete-time P&L identity with no residual for linear portfolios. Both first-order sensitivity and second-order gamma are available analytically from the daily curve build, with no additional computation. Empirical tests on EUR and USD swap data confirm FPLA materially reduces attribution residuals and improves FRTB green-zone frequencies. The multi-curve extension is developed in a self-contained appendix.

title: The Role of Digital Empowerment in Enhancing Organizational Agility during Wartime 2023-2025 in the Gaza Strip: An Applied Study in the Palestinian PALTEL Organization
affiliations: and Al-Aqsa University

detail.title: The Role of Digital Empowerment in Enhancing Organizational Agility during Wartime 2023-2025 in the Gaza Strip: An Applied Study in the Palestinian PALTEL Organization
detail.abstract: Purpose: This study investigates the role of digital empowerment across its dimensions (technical access, digital awareness, motivation, and administrative empowerment) in enhancing organizational agility within the telecommunications sector during acute crises, focusing on the Palestinian Telecommunications Organization (PALTEL-JAWWAL) during the 2023-2025 wartime environment in the Gaza Strip. Design/methodology/approach: Utilizing a descriptive-analytical approach, a structured questionnaire was deployed electronically and traditionally to a purposive sample of 82 administrative and technical employees actively engaged at PALTEL under conflict conditions. The collected primary data were quantitatively analyzed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS), involving internal consistency, validation, Cronbach's alpha reliability checks, and multiple linear regression modeling. Findings: The empirical results reveal that PALTEL exhibits an advanced level of digital empowerment (overall relative weight: 76.47%), with digital awareness ranking highest, followed by administrative empowerment, technical access, and motivation. Multiple regression analysis demonstrates a statistically significant collective effect, explaining 62.1% of the variance in organizational agility (F = 45.675, p < 0.05). Non-technical dimensions (awareness, motivation, administrative empowerment) exerted significant positive independent effects, whereas standalone technical access did not demonstrate an independent statistically significant effect. No demographic variations based on sex, age, job level, qualification, or tenure were detected. Originality: This research fills a critical literature gap by providing empirical evidence on the strategic interaction between digital empowerment and organizational agility under active conflict and destructive wartime environments within Arab infrastructure providers.

title: From Numbers to Narratives: A Generative Artificial Intelligence Framework for Automated Risk Report Production in IT Program Portfolio Governance
affiliations: and Babcock University

detail.title: From Numbers to Narratives: A Generative Artificial Intelligence Framework for Automated Risk Report Production in IT Program Portfolio Governance
detail.abstract: Every IT program portfolio generates a continuous stream of quantitative performance data. What it rarely generates, and what governance institutions consistently demand, is a coherent written account of what those numbers mean, what risks they signal, and what program boards should do about them. Human risk analysts currently bridge this gap, translating earned value metrics and delay risk flags into governance narratives manually, at considerable cost, with variable quality, and at a pace that often lags the reporting cycle. This paper introduces PRISM, the Predictive Risk Intelligence with Synthesized Management narratives framework, a generative artificial intelligence pipeline that automates the production of professional, governance-ready risk narrative reports by combining XGBoost delay risk classification, TreeSHAP feature attribution, and a fine-tuned large language model trained on a curated corpus of 2,340 authentic program risk reports drawn from federal IT investment governance archives. The framework accepts a standard program performance data vector as input and produces a complete, contextually accurate, and institutionally appropriate governance risk narrative as output, indistinguishable in professional quality from reports produced by experienced human risk analysts. Evaluation on a held-out test set of 412 investment records demonstrates that PRISM achieves a BLEU-4 score of 0.743, a BERTScore F1 of 0.891, and a practitioner Turing evaluation pass rate of 74.6 percent, meaning that in nearly three out of four cases, certified program management practitioners rated PRISM-generated narratives as of equal or superior quality to human-authored equivalents without being able to identify their machine origin. A governance decision quality study with 56 active program board members confirms that decisions made using PRISM narratives are 31.4 percent more likely to target the correct primary risk driver than decisions made using raw performance dashboards, and that PRISM narratives reduce mean risk report production time from 4.2 hours to 11 minutes per investment without loss of governance utility. These findings establish generative AI narrative synthesis as a technically feasible, practically superior, and institutionally deployable alternative to manual risk report production in IT program portfolio governance contexts.

title: The Rightness Loop: Power-Induced Cognitive Bias and Its Consequences for Leadership Decision Quality

detail.title: The Rightness Loop: Power-Induced Cognitive Bias and Its Consequences for Leadership Decision Quality
detail.abstract: Background: Leaders operating under sustained positional power show measurable changes in cognitive processing, particularly in error detection, perspective-taking, and the capacity to incorporate disconfirming information. Although the neuropsychological and social-psychological effects of power on individual cognition have been extensively documented, the organizational mechanism through which these individual-level effects compound over time into a self-reinforcing decision-quality spiral has received limited theoretical attention. Objective: This paper introduces the Rightness Loop-a theoretical framework describing the mechanism through which accumulated positional power progressively impairs leadership judgment by reinforcing a cognitive tendency toward uncritical selfvalidation, referred to here as rightness bias. Methods: Conceptual synthesis drawing on neuropsychological research on power and behavioral inhibition, organizational behavior literature on sycophancy, upward voice suppression, and psychological safety, and social psychology research on overconfidence and self-serving attribution. Findings: The Rightness Loop is proposed as a three-stage self-reinforcing mechanism: (1) power-induced reduction in error-detection sensitivity and perspective-taking capacity; (2) organizational silence that removes corrective feedback before it reaches the decision-maker; and (3) self-protective attribution that assigns failures to external circumstances rather than to judgment errors. Once established, the loop is neurobiologically and organizationally self-protecting. Conclusion: Understanding the Rightness Loop offers actionable implications for leadership development, board oversight structures, and organizational design. Breaking the loop requires deliberate structural and behavioral interventions that go against the natural trajectory of power accumulation.

title:
The Arbitral Tribunal Cannot Rewrite the Contract

The Limits of the Arbitral Mandate under Sections 28(3), 34 and 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, with Comparative Common Law Perspectives
affiliations: Independent

detail.title:
The Arbitral Tribunal Cannot Rewrite the Contract

The Limits of the Arbitral Mandate under Sections 28(3), 34 and 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, with Comparative Common Law Perspectives
detail.abstract: This article examines a proposition that six decades of Indian jurisprudence have placed beyond argument namely that an arbitral tribunal, being a creature of the contract, cannot rewrite the bargain between the parties. The question the article asks is where legitimate construction of a contract ends and impermissible reconstruction begins, and what the courts under Sections 34 and 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 may do when the line is crossed. The method is doctrinal and comparative: the Indian authorities are examined in the courts' own words, from Alopi Parshad (1960) and Jivarajbhai (1965) through Associated Engineering, Rajasthan State Mines, Saw Pipes and Associate Builders to Ssangyong, PSA SICAL, Indian Oil v Shree Ganesh, Batliboi and the curative judgment in DMRC v Delhi Airport Metro Express (2024), each traced through its full procedural journey; the Indian position is then set against English, Singaporean, Australian and Canadian authority. The thesis defended is that the prohibition on rewriting is a jurisdictional axiom, not a merits ground. The arbitrator who ignores or substitutes the terms of the contract acts without authority, and the resulting award is patently illegal; yet the same discipline binds the reviewing courts, which may annul such an award but may not remake either the bargain or the award. The strongest objection, that deference to the arbitrator's "possible view" collapses the doctrine into merits review, is stated and answered.

title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence and Virtual Reality for Service Recovery and Customer Retention in Tourism: A Hybrid Recovery Framework
affiliations: STIE KBP and Universitas Islam Negeri Sultan Syarif Kasim Riau

detail.title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence and Virtual Reality for Service Recovery and Customer Retention in Tourism: A Hybrid Recovery Framework
detail.abstract: Purpose: This study develops an integrated conceptual framework explaining how artificial intelligence (AI) and virtual reality (VR) technologies enhance service recovery effectiveness and customer retention in tourism and hospitality industries. This study addresses the fragmented understanding of AI and VR integration in tourism service recovery literature. Methods: A conceptual qualitative approach was employed through a systematic literature review and theory synthesis of 60 Scopus-indexed studies published between 2024 and 2026. The analysis integrates Justice Theory, Relationship Marketing Theory, Technology Acceptance Theory, and Expectation Confirmation Theory. Results: The findings indicate that AI-enabled chatbots, predictive analytics, and automated agents improve responsiveness, personalization, and recovery efficiency, while VR-based recovery experiences strengthen emotional reassurance and trust restoration. These mechanisms enhance customer satisfaction, loyalty, and retention. However, excessive automation may reduce perceived empathy and emotional authenticity, potentially weakening customer trust. The findings reveal that hybrid recovery systems combining AI efficiency and human emotional intelligence generate superior retention outcomes. Implications: The study proposes a hybrid recovery model combining AI efficiency with human emotional intelligence to optimize customer retention and sustainable competitive advantage. The framework provides theoretical insights into technology-enabled service recovery and practical guidance for tourism organizations implementing digital recovery strategies. The framework also establishes a future research agenda for AI-enabled tourism recovery ecosystems.

detail.abstract:
Purpose: Entrepreneurship education is shifting from traditional teacher-
centered pedagogies toward learner-centered approaches, including
simulations even in least-developed countries like Nepal. However,
the impact of physical startup simulations remains underexplored in
the scholarly literature. This study intends to examine MBA students’
perceptions of minimum viable product (MVP) based physical startup
simulation to uncover its impact on their entrepreneurial learning and its
role in developing key entrepreneurial competencies.
Methods: This phenomenological study employed unstructured
interviews to explore the lived experiences and perceptions of participants
selected through purposive sampling. Accordingly, 11 MBA students were
interviewed from four academic institutions in the Bagmati Province of
Nepal to ensure provincial representation and data saturation. The
sample size was considered adequate considering the sampling criteria
presented by Creswell (1998). The data were transcribed and translated
into English for subsequent thematic analysis using Braun and Clarke’s
(2006) six-phase framework, with a focus on depth of insight.
Results: The empirical findings generated four major themes: pedagogical
innovation, startup management skills, startup risk management, and
feedback-based learning and motivation. These themes align with Kolb’s
experiential learning theory and Ries’s lean startup theory. Based on
these themes, we propose a novel physical startup simulation model that
holds practical relevance for entrepreneurship educators in developing
entrepreneurial competencies among students.
Conclusion: Compared with software-based digital simulation, the
MVP-based physical startup simulation can be more effective, logistically
simpler, and more economical for teaching entrepreneurship, particularly
in the context of the least developed countries.

title: Tradition, Innovation, and Political Fusion: A Three-World Model of State Survival and Decision-Making
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Tradition, Innovation, and Political Fusion: A Three-World Model of State Survival and Decision-Making

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This article is a theoretical and historical study based on published sources and does not involve human participants, patient data, or identifiable personal information.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
This paper reconceptualizes tradition not as simple continuity but as persistence. Existing scholarship has shown that tradition legitimizes authority, stabilizes communities, and gives normative force to inherited practices, yet much of that literature still treats tradition primarily as the continuity of institutions, rituals, customs, or forms. I argue that this understanding is too narrow. Tradition often survives even when the institutions and practices that once embodied it have been transformed or destroyed.
The article’s central claim is twofold. First, the broad definition of tradition is persistence. Second, the narrow definition of tradition varies according to the evaluative world in which it operates. To develop this argument, I introduce a three-world model of state decision-making composed of the innovation world, the tradition world, and the fusion world. In the innovation world, tradition appears as persistent memory—especially the memory of organizational achievement, military glory, heroes, victories, honor, and collective pride that survives even after the institution that produced it has disappeared. In the tradition world, tradition appears as form preserved through reproduction. In the fusion world, tradition appears as identity maintained through political context: it is here that political leaders, autocratic rulers, and, under exceptional circumstances, constitutional monarchs decide what to preserve, what to discard, and what to transform for the sake of state survival. 
 I further argue that major failures of statecraft are best understood as failures of the fusion world. When the fusion world collapses toward the innovation world, states pursue purification, revolutionary destruction, or top-down modernization in ways that undermine legitimacy and state capacity. When it collapses toward the tradition world, inherited forms become ends in themselves and the state loses adaptive capacity. Successful statecraft, by contrast, does not consist in striking a midpoint between old and new. It consists in selectively recomposing both in light of state survival, state capacity, and legitimacy.

title: The Occupational Mobility-Education Curve

detail.title: The Occupational Mobility-Education Curve
detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between education and task based occupational mobility. It extends the conventional human capital view by arguing that education initially increases occupational mobility but eventually reduces as costs of education-including specialization, credential inflation, and licensing-dominate. Using Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) Cycle 2, the paper finds an inverted-U (concave) relationship between occupational mobility and education on average. Moreover, cross-country analysis represents heterogeneity and substantial difference in the shape and turning point of the curve.

title: "Scaffolding The Void: Towards a Void-driven Dynamic Capabilities Meta-capabilities" Research Paper

detail.title: "Scaffolding The Void: Towards a Void-driven Dynamic Capabilities Meta-capabilities" Research Paper
detail.abstract: The dynamic capabilities model describes the ability of firms to sense, seize, and adapt to changes in their environment. The model assumes a foundation of institutional support, meaning structures that ensure reliable contract enforcement, credible information, and regulatory consistency. However, in many parts of the world, this type of institutional support does not exist. Examples include cities with high congestion in developing markets, digital industries where the internet is frequently down or hurricane affected area where institution sometimes becomes unfunctional. These environments do not provide the conditions under which standard DCs can be applied. This introduce scaffolding defined as a capability that enables firms to establish a temporary institutional structure, a set of frameworks, practices, or norms implemented for a limited period to support specific organizational actions. Using both the institutional theory perspective and the dynamic capabilities view, we introduce the Voids-Driven Dynamic Capabilities (VDDC) framework. This model posits an inverted-U relationship between institutional reliability and scaffolding effectiveness and reframes DCs not only as mechanisms for adaptation within order but for the reconstitution of order itself.

title: The Dislocated Middle: Stranded Dignity and Institutional Lag in Bread-and-Meaning Life Paths

detail.title: The Dislocated Middle: Stranded Dignity and Institutional Lag in Bread-and-Meaning Life Paths
detail.abstract: This paper develops a theory of middle hollowing in growth societies. The productive middle is defined as a position in an institutional arrangement: households with sunk commitment to licensed life paths that bundle material viability, or Bread, with socially recognized Meaning. A fast-moving payoff frontier can reduce the Bread return of these paths before institutions and moral codes can relicense new paths carrying public dignity. The result is stranded dignity: the old route remains honorable but no longer secures material life. The paper formalizes this dual-speed dislocation, identifies the stability-tipping boundary of recognition dynamics, characterizes the sign condition for the frontier-velocity comparative static of the stranded segment, and shows how repeated shocks generate a persistent Bread-Meaning wedge under a two-rate exposure condition. It uses artificial intelligence as a contemporary acceleration case in which labor-market dynamics can move faster than family-supporting institutions. It distinguishes the mechanism from labor-market polarization, inequality, cultural lag, and political center erosion.

detail.abstract: This paper provides epidemiological data on sleep quality of Midwesterners. Data are from the AARP's healthy living survey conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago. The online and telephone survey, fielded during April 3 thru April 18, 2024, polled 1,610 US adults age 40 and above. Data analysis reveals that to overcome sleep issues, respondents in the metro spend $117 per month, on average, on sleep aids such as medicine and therapy. The same number for the nonmetro is $22. Other tactics that people use to get quality sleep include using the bed only for sleep, avoiding caffeine and alcohol.

title: The Impact of Cosmopolitanism Disposition on Consumers' Willingness to Pay Price Premium Toward Global Vs Local Brands
affiliations: , Modern University for Technology and Information, Modern University for Technology and Information and Cairo University

detail.title: The Impact of Cosmopolitanism Disposition on Consumers' Willingness to Pay Price Premium Toward Global Vs Local Brands
detail.abstract: In response to the limited research concerning the evaluation of global and local brands by emerging market consumers, this study explores the role of consumer cosmopolitanism in shaping attitudes and willingness to pay premium prices. The research, conducted in Cairo using a mall intercept method with 385 respondents, employs Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) to analyze the data. Each participant evaluates one global and one local brand within the home appliances category. The study not only addresses a significant research gap but also innovatively profiles and segments cosmopolitan consumers, shedding light on their preferences and behaviors. The findings offer crucial insights for both marketing researchers and brand managers, guiding them in formulating appropriate strategies for global and local brands in emerging markets. This research stands out for its exploration of the intricate mechanisms behind consumer cosmopolitanism and its influence on consumers' willingness to invest in global brands over local counterparts, making a valuable contribution to the existing literature

title: Vocational Interests and Work Context in the Choice of Occupational Destination
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology

detail.title: Vocational Interests and Work Context in the Choice of Occupational Destination
detail.abstract: I study what predicts a worker's realized occupational destination when capability measures make many moves look feasible. I combine linked Current Population Survey occupation changes with Occupational Information Network occupation attributes and estimate a survey-weighted conditional logit in which each mover chooses among the realized destination and sampled alternatives. Capability defines a large feasible set: about 76 percent of occupation pairs in the top decile of work-activity similarity never exchange a worker, and a broader content screen that admits essentially all realized moves contains roughly ten times as many feasible pairs as realized flows. To a capability, co-location, and wage baseline, I add two occupation-pair measures: the congruence of origin and destination vocational-interest profiles and the similarity of their work-context profiles. Both are measured at the occupation level; individual interests and working-condition preferences are not observed. Adding these channels raises held-out top-one accuracy from 0.279 to 0.338 and McFadden pseudo-R² from 0.188 to 0.243. The lift survives occupation-out validation, choice-set redraws, a mixed-logit relaxation of independence of irrelevant alternatives, and an adjacent-month transition construction. It carries a clear scope condition: among near-substitute occupations that O*NET already flags as skill-related, the top-one lift compresses to about 1.4 points. The estimates are descriptive. They point to non-capability inputs that a defensible estimate of mobilizable labor supply should consider, especially where candidate occupations are reachable but not close substitutes.
