title: Effective Strategies for Sustainable Funding and Resource Mobilization in Local NGOs in the MENA Region

detail.title: Effective Strategies for Sustainable Funding and Resource Mobilization in Local NGOs in the MENA Region

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing personal or financial interests that could have influenced this thesis.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The thesis involved NGO-sector interviews and survey inputs. The thesis states that ethics approval was obtained, informed consent was used, and confidentiality and privacy were maintained for participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This MBA thesis was prepared as part of the author's MBA study at ILC Mena and did not receive specific external funding.

detail.abstract: This MBA thesis examines sustainable funding and resource mobilization strategies for local non-governmental organizations in the MENA region. It focuses on the financial, operational, governance, and partnership challenges that affect local NGO sustainability in humanitarian and development contexts. Drawing on literature review, stakeholder insight, and practice-oriented analysis, the thesis identifies strategies for diversifying funding sources, improving financial management capacity, strengthening local ownership, building partnerships, promoting transparency and accountability, and improving resilience in crisis-affected environments. The study offers recommendations for local NGOs, donors, international organizations, and other stakeholders seeking to support more sustainable, locally grounded humanitarian and development responses in the MENA region.

title: The Neural Microstructure Technique: A Framework for Recovering Heterogeneous Information from Customer Order Flow in FX Markets

detail.title: The Neural Microstructure Technique: A Framework for Recovering Heterogeneous Information from Customer Order Flow in FX Markets
detail.abstract: This note introduces the Neural Microstructure Technique (NMT): a forecasting framework combining disaggregated customer order flow with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) recurrent neural networks to measure how much of each customer segment's predictive content in FX markets is orthogonal to publicly observable macroeconomic information. The technique is motivated by the sequential, path-dependent nature of orderflow accumulation by informed institutional traders-a temporal structure that standard linear and cross-sectional non-linear models cannot represent. Applied to weekly UBS G10 order flow data disaggregated into asset managers, hedge funds, corporates, and private clients (November 2001-November 2007), the NMT reveals that asset manager order flow is only 16.1% explained by standard macro benchmarks, against 39.4% for corporates, consistent with informed-trading theory. Asset managers generate an annualised Sharpe ratio of 0.71 against 0.24 for the random walk; aggregate order flow is indistinguishable from the benchmark (SR = 0.22). The NMT was developed in the author's doctoral dissertation (Galeazzi, 2023) and is described in full in the companion working paper (Galeazzi, 2025).

title: Shifting Paradigms in Cross-Border Service Exports: Legal Compliance and GST Registration Thresholds for Independent Consultants in India

detail.title: Shifting Paradigms in Cross-Border Service Exports: Legal Compliance and GST Registration Thresholds for Independent Consultants in India
detail.abstract: This policy brief examines the evolving Goods and Services Tax (GST) framework governing cross-border service exports in India. With the rise of independent consultants engaging foreign clients, maintaining compliance regarding the Reverse Charge Mechanism (RCM), Letter of Undertaking (LUT) renewals, and precise place-of-supply determinations is critical. This paper provides a practical roadmap for freelancers to preserve zero-rated export status, optimize their presumptive taxation models, and navigate currency realization requirements without incurring unnecessary compliance costs.

title: What is Left for Us? Second Scholarship Against the Degradation of Research by AI
affiliations: Yale University - Digital Ethics Center and Yale University - Digital Ethics Center

detail.title: What is Left for Us? Second Scholarship Against the Degradation of Research by AI
detail.abstract: We argue that generative AI can degrade research by eroding the very practices through which scholarly judgement is formed and academic trust is built. As constitutive conditions for the production and validation of knowledge, these practices cannot be reduced to the final outputs of research, which is what AI so effectively simulate. Accordingly, when researchers delegate central tasks of inquiry to systems like Large Language Models (LLMs), they may stop enacting these practices and, with them, lose access to the formation they provide. An individual research output generated by AI may even appear improved but the researcher behind it fails to develop. Against this risk, merely keeping humans "in the loop" as prompters or quality-checkers of AI outputs is insufficient to preserve research as a site of intellectual formation. What is needed instead is a renewed commitment to research as a lived practice in which judgement is formed gradually, often through frictions, and participation in a scholarly community. We defend it because it rests on four sources and warrants of research that cannot be automated: tacit knowledge, personal commitment, socialisation, and deep reading. This practice enacts what we call 'second scholarship', by which we understand the re-appropriation of scholarly craft, chosen out of a critical experience of what generative AI can and cannot do. What cannot and should not be delegated becomes what research communities must value and answer for. This is what is left for us.

title: Batam, Bintan and the Singapore-Indonesia Investment Nexus: Foreign Capital in the Riau Islands Free Trade Zone

detail.title: Batam, Bintan and the Singapore-Indonesia Investment Nexus: Foreign Capital in the Riau Islands Free Trade Zone
detail.abstract:
We document that the foreign investment of Indonesia's Riau Islands is, to a first approximation, one city's account with one neighbour. Singapore supplied 69% of Batam's foreign direct investment in the first half of 2025 (IDR 7.9 trillion; S$617.3 million), and in the first quarter of 2024 its US$240.1 million was 65% of the top-five source-country inflow and more than three times the next source, China (US$72.2 million). Batam itself accounted for 79.2% of Riau Islands FDI in 2022, 83.6% in the first half of 2023 and 73.5% in early 2026, so the province's foreign capital is largely Batam's, and Batam's is largely Singapore's. The relationship is old: the Singapore-Johor-Riau growth triangle was announced in December 1989, and Batamindo Industrial Park began construction in 1990 as an offshore floor for Singapore electronics. What is new is scale and composition. Batam's total realized investment reached IDR 25.46 trillion in 2024 (+63% year on year) and IDR 33.66 trillion in the first nine months of 2025 alone, but foreign investment's share of that total fell from 77% in early 2024 to about 51% in early 2026 as domestic capital surged (+147.85% in the nine months to September 2025). We read Batam as a proximity nexus that is deepening its Singapore link in absolute terms while broadening its investor base beyond it.
We document that the foreign investment of Indonesia’s Riau Islands is, to a first approximation, one city’s account with one neighbour. The province’s foreign capital is largely Batam’s, and Batam’s is largely Singapore’s. Singapore supplied 69% of Batam’s foreign direct investment in the first half of 2025, and its dominance is not a one-quarter artefact; the city has been Batam’s top foreign investor since 2023 (Singapore EDB, 2025). The relationship is also old. It was designed into the map in December 1989, when the Singapore-Johor-Riau growth triangle was announced, and it has run more or less the same way since. What has changed recently is the size of the flow and the arrival of domestic capital beside it, and those two shifts are worth separating from the Singapore story that still anchors the whole.

title: What Drives Poor Financial Decisions? The Role of Payoff Structure
affiliations: , University College London and University College London

detail.title: What Drives Poor Financial Decisions? The Role of Payoff Structure

declarations.ethicsApproval: The study is approved by the UCL Research Ethics Committee (Ref: EP/2023/012).
declarations.funderStatement: This study is supported by the Experimental Psychology Society Small Grant Scheme.

detail.abstract: Financial decisions such as those involved in stock trading should, at least partly, be based on similar features to detecting trends in time-series data. When presented as a purely perceptual task, people's accuracy in detecting trends is generally considered good, but real-world individual investors underperform the market globally. In a series of controlled experiments, we isolated the framing and the payoff structure, instructing participants to make decisions based on real-time evolving time series. Our results show that participants' decisions were not affected by trend direction in a classic perceptual decision-making scenario, whilst in a classic trading scenario they performed worse in both speed and accuracy during downward compared to upward trends. In a final experiment where we carefully controlled the reward structure of both scenarios and the only relevant differentiating factor was the labels of the decisions, we did not find evidence for this difference in trend sensitivity between scenarios, but participants made overall slower decisions in the trading scenario. Taken together, these results imply that sensitivity to trend direction is likely driven by the reward structure of the classic trading scenario, where downward trends imply penalties regardless of the correctness of decisions. Computational modelling indicates an underlying impairment of information processing during downward trends. The difference in overall response speed between the trading and perceptual conditions in the final experiment implies a further difference between trading and perception which extends beyond the payoff structure.

title: The Shape of Things to Come: Managing Trade and Supply Chain Threats and Disruption under Globalization V3

detail.title: The Shape of Things to Come: Managing Trade and Supply Chain Threats and Disruption under Globalization V3
detail.abstract: The disruption of the rules-based trade order (the "rupture") is widely characterized as a policy choice, premised on a diagnosis that trade policy had led the industrialized west into deindustrialization and loss of good jobs. Given this diagnosis, the solution is to reverse the trade liberalization that had created Globalization V2 in order to recapture industrial activity and create good industrial sector jobs. A logical necessity is that the economies that had bought into the global division of labour must now write off the investments predicated on that framework and cede the jobs back to the industrialized west. This includes not only China, at whose doorstep much of the blame for the ills attributed to globalization is laid, but also the vast majority of small open economies that had carved out niches in the global division of labour. This paper argues that this diagnosis is fundamentally wrong. Globalization V2 was about production, not trade-it emerged from the enablement of the "global factory" by technological development, not by trade policy, which followed rather than drove developments. Moreover, the factor content of output-whether goods are produced with labour or capital-is not determined by trade but by domestic factor market conditions. There is accordingly no theoretical basis for a "China Shock" to jobs when there was no "China Shock" to output. Tariffs cannot undo past technological progress and so cannot achieve the proximate goals of the policies driving the rupture, which points to continued improvision and associated uncertainty. Meanwhile, the continued rapid evolution of technology, which has ushered in the age of data and artificial intelligence (AI), has steepened the rise in economic rents and concentrated their capture, cocking the trigger for commercial conflict. That conflict arrived on cue and is driving a post-rupture realignment of countries into a Global North seeking to reassert data and AI sovereignty, a Global South seeking to monetize its supply-chain assets in the capital-expenditure-heavy AI build-out, and two "Middle Kingdoms" pulling apart but still linked by stretched supply chains. The basic logic of the global factory, and the rulesbased operating system built for it, remains intact; trading firms must however manage new-found trade and supply-chain risk in this emerging Globalization V3.

title: Why do Southeast Asia's largest companies list in New York instead of at home?

detail.title: Why do Southeast Asia's largest companies list in New York instead of at home?
detail.abstract:
We document that the largest Southeast Asian equity listings of the past decade were raised offshore rather than on the region's own exchanges, and that among the marquee US listings the mode of going public predicted the outcome more reliably than the venue did. The three SPAC listings debuted near a combined $65 billion and gave most of it back; the one conventional IPO, Sea Limited, listed at about $4.9 billion in 2017 and traded near $59 billion in mid-2026. Grab's single 2021 raise of about $4.5 billion exceeded the roughly $3.0 billion that all 122 Southeast Asian exchange IPOs raised in 2024, the same year SGX lost a net sixteen companies.
We document that the visible peak of Southeast Asian equity capital-raising over the past decade was reached offshore rather than on the region’s own exchanges, and that among the marquee US listings the mode of going public predicted the outcome more reliably than the New York address did. Three of the four best-known Southeast Asian names on US markets, namely Grab, VinFast and PropertyGuru, went public through SPAC mergers at a combined debut value near $65 billion and have since surrendered most of it. The one that submitted to a conventional order book, Sea Limited, listed at about $4.9 billion in 2017 and traded near $59 billion in mid-2026. A separate magnitude fixes the scale. Grab’s single 2021 raise of roughly $4.5 billion exceeded the approximately $3.0 billion that all 122 Southeast Asian exchange IPOs together raised in 2024.

title: Economic Viability of Food Rescue Under Enhanced Tax Deductions: A General Threshold Formula, Failure Conditions, and Urban Simulation
affiliations: Stevens Institute of Technology

detail.title: Economic Viability of Food Rescue Under Enhanced Tax Deductions: A General Threshold Formula, Failure Conditions, and Urban Simulation
detail.abstract: Tax savings from food donations can offset the cost of a pickup trip, but no closed-form framework has existed for determining when they do or by how much. We derive the donor's expected net benefit per trip, Π(w) = t • E[h(C, P)] • w-E[Costs], and the minimum viable donation weight, w * = E[Costs]/(t • E[h(C, P)]), where w is pounds donated, t is the donor's marginal tax rate, C is cost per pound, P ∼ N (αC, σ 2) is stochastic profit per pound with markup α, and h(C, P) is the per-pound tax deduction under any deduction structure. The net benefit formula gives donors a trip-level profit calculation, food rescue organizations a dispatch screening rule, and policymakers a tool for evaluating how deduction design affects which donors and food categories are economically reachable. We embed the U.S. PATH Act deduction in a two-parameter family h β,κ (C, P) = min(κC, C + βP) and derive four closed-form failure conditions in donation weight, trip distance, tax rate, and profit multiplier that map the full non-viable region. Under a 21% corporate tax rate and a 2-mile trip, w * ranges from 1.6 lbs for prepared meals ($6.00/lb) to 15 lbs for fresh produce ($1.00/lb), a tenfold difference driven entirely by cost per pound. Above α = 2 the PATH Act deduction cap makes additional margin irrelevant, so high-margin and moderate-margin donors face identical incentives. We illustrate the formula on 466 real donor locations and 41 verified recipient nonprofits across three urban areas using surplus weights calibrated to ReFED (2024) sector estimates, finding viability rates of 89-93% in dense urban cores and lower rates for fresh produce and beverage donors at longer distances, consistent with the distance failure condition.

title: When Values Meet Incentives: Moral Wiggle Room and Rational-Agent Recommendations Across Generations
affiliations: University of Economics in Bratislava, Slovak Academy of Sciences and Slovak Academy of Sciences

detail.title: When Values Meet Incentives: Moral Wiggle Room and Rational-Agent Recommendations Across Generations
detail.abstract: We investigate whether self-interested behavior becomes more prevalent when choice architecture explicitly encourages payoff maximization. In a crossgenerational laboratory experiment, we compare Generation Z (Zoomers) and Baby Boomers across three decision-making contexts involving a conflict between values and monetary incentives: charitable giving, performance self-reporting, and a social (Prisoner's) dilemma. We induce moral wiggle room by providing treated participants with rational-agent recommendations identifying the choice that maximizes their own monetary payoff, thereby endorsing selfishness and dishonesty. Baseline results show that Boomers are more generous and more honest than Zoomers, while cooperation is similar across generations. Rational-agent recommendations reduce charitable giving among Zoomers and increase expectations that opponents will defect, which is accompanied by lower rates of cooperation, particularly among Boomers. In contrast, recommendations to behave dishonestly do not significantly increase cheating in either generation. Our findings suggest that moral wiggle room may facilitate self-interested choices at the margin, but that internalized values remain powerful constraints on opportunistic behavior.

title: The Qatari 747 Bridge Aircraft Requirements Trades, Mission Risk, and Oversight Questions in a Rapid Presidential-Aircraft Retrofit
affiliations: Independent Scholar

detail.title: The Qatari 747 Bridge Aircraft Requirements Trades, Mission Risk, and Oversight Questions in a Rapid Presidential-Aircraft Retrofit

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Self funded

detail.abstract: This paper examines the Qatari Boeing 747-8i bridge aircraft introduced into the presidential airlift mission as an interim capability pending delivery of the delayed Boeing VC-25B replacement aircraft. The paper does not allege that the bridge aircraft is unsafe, nor does it rely on classified information. Instead, it applies publicly available facts to standard aircraft-systems, mission-integration, certification, electromagnetic interference/electromagnetic compatibility (EMI/EMC), software-assurance, cybersecurity, and acquisition-oversight principles. The central question is whether a foreign-origin, rapidly modified bridge aircraft has been publicly treated as equivalent to Air Force One without disclosure of the requirements trades, waivers, test evidence, operational restrictions, full taxpayer cost, and post-service disposition terms necessary for meaningful oversight. Public statements indicate that the bridge aircraft was delivered on a compressed schedule and that "mission trades" were made compared with the long-term VC-25B program. Public reporting and Air Force materials also indicate a broader mixed-fleet and 747-8 transition posture, including continued VC-25A and C-32 availability and separate 747-8 aircraft for training and sustainment. The paper argues that these facts justify congressional, Government Accountability Office, Department of Defense Inspector General, and classified test-and-evaluation review. It concludes with structured oversight questions regarding mission equivalence, defensive systems, EMI/EMC validation, software and cyber assurance, cleared workforce controls, cost accounting, and disposition of taxpayer-funded upgrades.

title: Regime-conditional Distributional Comparison of Trading Strategies: A GAMLSS/ZAGA Framework Applied to the S&P 500
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Regime-conditional Distributional Comparison of Trading Strategies: A GAMLSS/ZAGA Framework Applied to the S&P 500
detail.abstract: Conventional comparisons of algorithmic trading strategies reduce each performance metric to a single number over the full backtest horizon, thereby discarding information about how performance varies with market conditions. This paper proposes a distributional framework that addresses this shortcoming. A walk-forward backtest of 146 out-of-sample folds on the S&P 500 (2002-2025) is used to compute the Adjusted Information Ratio (IR*) for a polynomial Support Vector Machine strategy (SVMP) and a buy-and-hold benchmark (BH) in each fold. The resulting IR* sequences are modelled jointly via a Generalised Additive Model for Location, Scale and Shape (GAMLSS) with a Zero-Adjusted Gamma (ZAGA) response, with distributional parameters conditioned on market regime covariates: realised volatility and cumulative market momentum. Strategy comparison is conducted through (i) regime-specific differences in expected IR* (ΔE) and its variance (ΔVar), derived analytically from the fitted ZAGA parameters, and (ii) parametric bootstrap tests of three null hypotheses concerning E(IR*), Var(IR*), and their ratio, evaluated at six representative market regimes. The results demonstrate that the dominance relationship between SVMP and BH is conditional on market regime. The proposed GAMLSS/ZAGA framework constitutes a methodologically rigorous and practically interpretable alternative to conventional strategy evaluation.

title: Forecasting Bitcoin Implied Volatility: On-Chain Signals, Belief Formation, and Limits to Arbitrage

detail.title: Forecasting Bitcoin Implied Volatility: On-Chain Signals, Belief Formation, and Limits to Arbitrage

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study used only publicly available, anonymized secondary data from financial markets and publicly accessible databases. No human participants, personal data, or identifiable information were involved. Accordingly, ethics committee approval and informed consent were not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was conducted independently as part of the requirements for the MBA (Finance) dissertation at Arun Jaitley National Institute of Financial Management.

detail.abstract: Implied volatility summarises what market participants believe about future risk, and it is traded through instruments with nonlinear, Vega-dependent payoffs. As a result, conclusions about whether volatility is predictable depend not only on statistical accuracy, but on how signals are mapped into economically meaningful payoffs. This dissertation studies day-ahead changes in Bitcoin implied volatility, as measured by the Deribit Volatility Index (DVOL), and uses crypto options markets as a high-frequency laboratory to examine how informational signals interact with payoff structure and market frictions. Using publicly observable state variables including on-chain profit measures (SOPR, NUPL), short-horizon price dynamics, macroeconomic momentum indicators, and sentiment data, I document modest but robust out-of-sample predictability in one-day-ahead changes in DVOL. A tree-based ensemble model (XGBoost) achieves an out-of-sample R-squared of 0.0527 over a held-out test sample of approximately ten months, while an AR(1)–GARCH(1,1) benchmark estimated on identical data produces a negative Rsquared, indicating it cannot beat a constant-mean forecast at the daily horizon. Statistical predictability does not, however, translate into economic profitability when the predicted signals are mapped into a spot-normalised PnL with realistic transaction costs. The simulated strategy delivers a slightly negative total return and a strongly negative Sharpe ratio, while a passive Buy & Hold Bitcoin benchmark generates a tripledigit annualised return over the same window. I argue that this divergence reflects two distinct frictions rather than model failure: limits to arbitrage in a market with thin option liquidity and meaningful execution costs, and a deliberate payoff mis-specification embedded in the linear, spot-normalised PnL itself. Volatility payoffs are inherently convex and scale with option Vega, so linear normalisation by spot mechanically suppresses returns relative to costs and conceals economically meaningful belief dynamics. Machine learning is used here as a diagnostic tool to uncover nonlinear state-dependence in the data, not as a substitute for economic structure. Feature attribution via gain and SHAP values shows that short-term price changes, on-chain profitability measures such as SOPR, and Federal Funds Rate momentum carry the largest influence on next-day DVOL adjustments, consistent with a view of implied volatility as a belief-driven object shaped by macro conditions, on-chain positioning, and price dynamics. The dissertation contributes in three ways. First, it documents short-horizon predictability in Bitcoin implied volatility using publicly observable state variables that proxy belief formation and balance-sheet stress. Second, it shows that conventional spotnormalised PnL evaluations can be misleading when applied to volatility signals. Third, it offers empirical evidence consistent with limits-to-arbitrage interpretations in cryptovolatility markets and outlines a path toward payoff-consistent evaluation frameworks for future work.

title: Patriarchal Family Order in Abrahamic Religions: Women's Dignity, Gender Roles, and the Ethics of Family Leadership

detail.title: Patriarchal Family Order in Abrahamic Religions: Women's Dignity, Gender Roles, and the Ethics of Family Leadership
detail.abstract: This article explores patriarchy in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam through a comparative reading of sacred texts on marriage, women's spiritual status, and their rights within religious society. It argues that, although the Abrahamic traditions are rooted in patriarchal structures, patriarchy in its original religious form cannot be reduced solely to the oppression of women.

title: The Price of the Floor: Quantifying the Cost of Ample Reserves in U.S. Monetary Policy Implementation
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School and Columbia University

detail.title: The Price of the Floor: Quantifying the Cost of Ample Reserves in U.S. Monetary Policy Implementation
detail.abstract:
This paper reassesses the Federal Reserve's current monetary policy implementation regime, known as the ample reserves framework. Every system of monetary policy implementation brings benefits and costs, and while the benefits of today's regime have been extensively studied, less attention has been paid to its costs. Building on a detailed historical narrative, we develop a counterfactual consolidated balance sheet analysis to highlight two distinct benefits to the commercial banking sector: (i) the incremental deposit franchise value created by interest-bearing reserves funded by deposits yielding substantially less than the risk-free rate, and (ii) the uncompensated maturity transformation benefit that results when the System Open Market Account (SOMA) warehouses mark-to-market risk that would otherwise reside on private sector balance sheets. Quantitatively, the deposit-franchise value peaked at about $200 billion (or 1% of banking assets) in 2023.

Our findings complicate the prevailing view that ample reserves are distributionally neutral. The regime delivers
enhanced control of short-term interest rates, but it also likely generates significant and new revenue for commer-
cial banks. Understanding the scale of these effects is a prerequisite to judging whether the benefits of the cur-
rent framework outweigh its drawbacks. We conclude by outlining alternative architectures—a return to a corridor
system, a lean-ample system, and a tiered remuneration system—that could preserve policy agility while curbing
implicit transfers.

title: Explicit Methods for Portfolio Optimization with Realistic Costs and Constraints
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences

detail.title: Explicit Methods for Portfolio Optimization with Realistic Costs and Constraints
detail.abstract: We present algorithms for mean-variance optimization with realistic costs, including borrow costs, bid-offer spread cost, and market impact according to the well-known square root law. The algorithm performs coordinate updates, each of which reduces to a univariate subproblem with a closed-form algebraic solution. The technique extends to problems with box constraints, and to certain kinds of multi-horizon objectives. We demonstrate an improvement in the computational complexity when the covariance matrix has a factor structure.

title: The Subscription Life: A Globally Distributed, Data-driven Examination of the Shift from Ownership to Access

detail.title: The Subscription Life: A Globally Distributed, Data-driven Examination of the Shift from Ownership to Access
detail.abstract: Across nearly every region with reliable data, three trends have run in parallel for the past two decades: housing has become significantly less affordable for new entrants relative to income, recurring-payment business models have grown several times faster than the broader economy, and wealth has concentrated by age (toward older cohorts) and within each cohort (the top decile holds a larger share than it used to). This paper begins by examining what the post-WWII Western ownership regime materially provided to the households that lived under it. It then documents the phenomenon globally, presents the case in favor of the access-over-ownership shift on its own merits, and examines its costs across financial, psychological, and demographic dimensions. It closes by reporting what different actors have tried in response — distinguishing between approaches that aim to restore ownership directly, approaches that aim to make non-ownership less harmful, and approaches that have not produced their stated results — and what the empirical record says about each.

title: Mechanism Design for Permissioned Distributed Ledgers: Lessons from the Brazilian DREX Pilot

detail.title: Mechanism Design for Permissioned Distributed Ledgers: Lessons from the Brazilian DREX Pilot
detail.abstract:
In late 2025 the Central Bank of Brazil (BCB) discontinued the Hyperledger Besu pilot platform of its DREX permissioned-CBDC programme and signalled a redesign of the next phase, while the broader DREX initiative remained under development. Throughout the documented pilot, consensus authority stayed within six BCB-operated nodes running QBFT, while the sixteen institutional participants operated non-validating nodes. We therefore approach the DREX experience not as a failed governance experiment by institutional validators but as a motivating case for a broader question: under what conditions could institutional participants of heterogeneous type be safely promoted to validators in a future distributed phase of a permissioned CBDC? 

     We develop an action-incentive-compatibility condition for the permissioned-CBDC setting under parametric type heterogeneity (BAIC): an incentive condition stated on validators' actions rather than on reported types, designed against the regulator's distributional knowledge of validator types. (We retain the Bayesian label for the design-against-distribution object; under the present calibration the expectation over other validators' types is degenerate, a point we make explicit in Section 5.3.) A four-archetype typology of candidate validators systemic banks, mid-tier banks and cooperatives, authorised ntechs, and registry institutions characterises the heterogeneity any future distributed phase would need to discipline. Privacy law enters as a lower bound on the false-positive rate of any admissible monitoring signal, generating a privacysustainability frontier we characterise analytically. A Quadruple Alignment result gives sucient conditions for systemic integrity on four levels consensus protocol, individual BAIC, validator-list composition, and regulatory feasibility of the required monitoring with explicit hypotheses for necessity. The composition condition is stated in a synchronised form consistent with the timing of the coalitional game: a coalition of eective per-member gain at most G max is deterred for archetype k when G max ≤ D k , where D k is the discounted per-member deterrence threshold that accounts for both detection and the honest path's own false-positive exposure. 

     Under a parametrisation disciplined by institutional facts, only systemic banks satisfy the synchronised composition certicate; mid-tier banks fail it by a non-trivial margin under pilot monitoring, and are not jointly admissible with systemic banks at the legal privacy oor; ntechs and registry institutions exhibit a decit that persists under any isolated reduction in the false-positive rate within the maintained parameterisation it is not closed by better monitoring alone. The reported centralised reorientation of DREX, which the model represents as a counterfactual low-false-positive benchmark for a distributed network, leaves the ntech and registry decit untouched, because it lies in the archetypes' utility fundamentals rather than in monitoring precision; closing it would require changing those fundamentals (mandate, reputational stake, accessible gains, or voting rights), not merely the signal.

title: Which Data should be Publicly Accessible? Dispatches from Public Managers
affiliations: , Arizona State University (ASU), University of Illinois at Chicago - Department of Public Administration and Arizona State University

detail.title: Which Data should be Publicly Accessible? Dispatches from Public Managers
detail.abstract: Open government data (OGD) seeks to promote transparency and accountability by enabling public access to government data. While public managers are increasingly supportive of OGD initiatives worldwide, researchers note that they also carefully select which data to release to balance openness with traditional values of professionalism and secrecy as well as concerns about cyber incidents and privacy. Understanding the factors that influence this micro-level choice is important to make valuable types of data publicly accessible. Using 2018 survey data from a nationally representative sample of 2,500 department heads in 500 small and medium-sized US cities, we look at variation in public managers' level of comfort with making different types of government data open-from criminal records to government employee salary data. We find that managerial comfort reflects historic practices of public accessibility and privacy concerns with individual data. Managers who believe OGD creates positive outcomes for society are more comfortable with publicly disclosing all types of data. We also find variation across department types, suggesting fragmented views towards OGD within public organizations.

title: Inequality of Opportunity in Central Mexico: How Circumstances Shape Earnings across States and Age Cohorts

detail.title: Inequality of Opportunity in Central Mexico: How Circumstances Shape Earnings across States and Age Cohorts

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I hereby declare that there are no financial, personal, or professional conflicts of interest that could influence the results, interpretations, or conclusions presented in this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, animal subjects, or any vulnerable populations requiring informed consent or institutional review board approval. No primary data were collected from or about individuals. Therefore, formal ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. All costs associated with the preparation and submission of this work were borne solely by the author.

detail.abstract: This study examines inequality of opportunity (IOp) in earnings across Mexico's central region, comprising six states (Mexico City, Estado de México, Hidalgo, Morelos, Puebla, and Tlaxcala), following the Bourguignon-Ferreira-Menéndez (2005) framework and extending Cortés Cisneros (2025). Using data from the 2010 National Census of Population and Housing, we decompose earnings inequality into components attributable to circumstances (gender, indigenous identity, and region of birth) and effort (years of education and internal migration), estimating direct and indirect effects at regional, state, and age-cohort levels. Our findings reveal that IOp accumulates strongly over the life cycle, growing from 1.8% among the youngest cohort to 17.5% among the oldest regional cohort, indicating that labor market trajectories diverge systematically based on predetermined characteristics. The direct effectoperating through discrimination, network biases, and structural barriers-consistently outweighs the indirect effect channeled through education and migration, particularly among older workers. We uncover substantial state-level heterogeneity: while most states exhibit positive total effects ranging from 0.6% to 5.9% of observed inequality, Puebla presents a unique compensatory pattern where the indirect effect acts as an equalizer, and Tlaxcala displays the most dramatic age-related increase in IOp. These findings argue against one-size-fits-all policies, calling instead for age-differentiated, state-specific interventions targeting the direct channels of discrimination and structural exclusion that persist even when education and migration are accounted for.

title: Cybersecurity Threats in Local Government: A Sociotechnical Perspective
affiliations: Independent and

detail.title: Cybersecurity Threats in Local Government: A Sociotechnical Perspective
detail.abstract: The use of information and communication technologies (ICTs) by local governments is widespread and meant to improve managerial effectiveness and public engagement. ICTs are commonly used by governments to collaborate and communicate with stakeholders. Yet, the use of ICTs increases local governments exposure to cyberthreats. Cyberthreats are increasing and local governments are often under-resourced and underprepared for them. While many organizations combat cyberthreats with technological solutions, it is well known that social aspects-including manager vigilance and buy-in-are critical in reducing cyber incidents. Thus, governments require both social and technical solutions to cyberthreats. This research takes a sociotechnical perspective to examine the relationships between social (e.g., values and perceptions) and technical factors (e.g., design and capacity) and cyber incidents in local government. We use data from a 2018 national survey of public managers in 500 U.S. cities, data from city government websites, and the U.S. Census. The results indicate that manager buy-in and perceptions interact with technical aspects to explain reported cyber incidents in government. The findings expand our understanding of how social and technical factors are associated with cyberthreats in government, particularly manager behavior and organizational technical capacity.

title: Oversharing: The Downside of Data Sharing in Local Government
affiliations: Arizona State University (ASU) - School of Public Affairs, Arizona State University (ASU) and

detail.title: Oversharing: The Downside of Data Sharing in Local Government

declarations.ethicsApproval: The Human Research Ethics committees at Arizona State University (Study # 00003818), approved the questionnaires.

detail.abstract: Health crises, climate change, and technological hazards pose serious managerial and equity challenges for local governments. To effectively navigate the uncertainties and complexity, municipalities are increasingly collaborating with one another and sharing data and information to improve decision-making. While data sharing fosters effectiveness in responding to threats, it also entails risks. One major concern is that local government managers often lack the knowledge and technical skills required for safe and effective data sharing, exposing municipalities to cyberthreats. Drawing on data sharing and cybersecurity scholarship, we investigate whether increased data sharing among local governments makes cities more or less vulnerable to cyberincidents. We test our hypotheses using data from two national surveys of U.S. local government managers conducted in 2016 and 2018. Our findings contribute to the literature on technology and risk in government by informing both public managers and researchers about the potential threats associated with data sharing.

title: Beyond Automation: AI and the Human Value of Sell-Side Analysts
affiliations: and University of California, Irvine - Paul Merage School of Business

detail.title: Beyond Automation: AI and the Human Value of Sell-Side Analysts
detail.abstract: We examine how analysts’ information acquisition and processing differ when analysts have access to AI resources, focusing on investment banks’ AI investments. We propose and test a two-step framework, which is informed by in-depth interviews with analysts. First, consistent with AI facilitating automation-assisted public information processing, we show that AI investments are associated with more timely earnings forecasts following 10-K filings, particularly after the implementation of iXBRL, which increases the machine readability of filings. Second, we show that analysts reallocate the time and capacity freed by automation toward acquiring and incorporating private information, supported by several sets of evidence: AI investments (1) are associated with higher quality and bolder earnings forecasts, particularly when private information is more important and accessible to analysts; (2) are associated with an expansion of analyst coverage to new firms and industries; and (3) are associated with higher information seeking efforts, particularly greater participation in earnings conference calls. Additionally, exploiting the launch of AskResearchGPT at Morgan Stanley, an in-house generative AI designed for research, we find results consistent with our main analyses. Overall, our study provides insights into the potential for AI to reshape the human value of sell-side analysts.

title: Germany's Rural Physician Admission Quota and Regional Inequality in General Practitioner Supply: A Microsimulation Study to 2040
affiliations: Leibniz Universität Hannover, Leibniz  Universität Hannover, Leibniz  Universität Hannover - Institute of Economics and Leibniz Universität Hannover

detail.title: Germany's Rural Physician Admission Quota and Regional Inequality in General Practitioner Supply: A Microsimulation Study to 2040

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval was not required because this study did not involve human participants or animals. All analyses were conducted using existing anonymised data that do not permit the identification of individuals.
declarations.funderStatement: Association of Statutory Health Insurance Physicians in Lower Saxony.

detail.abstract:
Background: Germany’s rural physician admission quota (Landarztquote, RPAQ) reserves medical school places for applicants who commit to ten years of general practice in underserved areas. We examine how alternative allocation models shape its impact on regional inequality in GP supply.

Methods: In this ex-ante microsimulation study, we project GP supply across the 105 GP planning areas of Lower Saxony, Germany, to 2040, drawing on complete individual-level physician-register data, official population data, and statutory needs-planning parameters. The RPAQ (60 students annually; first graduates practising from 2035) is modelled as redistribution of a fixed number of future entrants. We compare four allocation models with the baseline projection. We report the numbers of planning areas and the population below the 75% and 90% thresholds and assess regional inequality using the population-weighted Gini coefficient as the main outcome, alongside the Theil-L and Atkinson indices.

Findings: Without the RPAQ, underprovision spreads: areas below the 75% threshold increase from 2 to 16 and the Gini rises from 0·068 (2025) to 0·104 (2040). All allocation models eliminate underprovision below 75% by 2040. However, inequality gains involve trade-offs: under the water-level model, more areas cluster just below 90% (52) than under fill-up (36) or baseline (43). On aggregate inequality, the water-level model performs best (Gini 0·055), followed by historical (0·078), fill-up (0·080), and equal distribution (0·087).

Interpretation: The inequality impact of the RPAQ depends decisively on the allocation model. Physician admission quotas should therefore include explicit allocation mechanisms.

title: Occupational Variation in the Impact of Retirement on Functional Independence: Evidence from SHARE
affiliations: Flinders University - College of Business Government and Law and Flinders University

detail.title: Occupational Variation in the Impact of Retirement on Functional Independence: Evidence from SHARE

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No known Interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: No need for Approval
declarations.funderStatement: No Fund for this reseach

detail.abstract: This paper examines the causal impact of retirement and retirement duration on functional independence across occupations. Using panel data from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), we estimate the causal effect of retirement on functional independence using a fixed-effects instrumental-variables (FE-IV) approach that exploits statutory retirement eligibility ages as instruments, and a fuzzy regression-discontinuity design (RDD) around retirement age thresholds. We find that retirement worsens functional independence among both white-collar and blue-collar workers, with the blue-collar effect approximately five times larger in magnitude. Functional consequences concentrate at the retirement transition rather than accumulating with retirement duration for either occupational group. Gender-specific analyses reveal that retirement significantly worsens functional independence for both men and women among blue-collar workers, with men experiencing larger point estimates, while effects among white-collar workers are small and statistically insignificant for both genders.

title: When Enforcement Letters Reach Their Limits: Accumulated Debt and Property Tax Compliance Working

detail.title: When Enforcement Letters Reach Their Limits: Accumulated Debt and Property Tax Compliance Working

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses anonymized administrative records. The field experiment was designed and implemented by the Ministry of Finance of Mexico City in 2014 as part of its regular tax administration activities. The author analyzed de-identified secondary data and had no contact with individual taxpayers. The data are owned by the Ministry of Finance of Mexico City and cannot be redistributed by the author.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Letters to taxpayers are the most widely used behavioral tool for raising tax compliance, yet the evidence centers on their average effects. I study a field experiment covering roughly 90,000 delinquent property taxpayers in Mexico City, paired with a model that combines deterrence and liquidity constraints. Accumulated debt turns out to be the main driver of treatment-effect heterogeneity: the effect of all eight letter variants weakens as debt rises, and neither the signatory nor the taxpayer's socioeconomic status accounts for this decline. The likelihood of payment falls monotonically with debt. The number of overdue bimesters paid traces an inverted U that peaks near 16 bimesters, a profile shared by treated and control groups. Under chronic delinquency, deterrence messages remain effective while public-goods messages converge to the control group. Enforcement letters, then, are best paired with debt-management tools.

title: "Megadeal" Subsidies, Local Spillovers and Corporate Innovation
affiliations: California State University, Long Beach, Singapore Management University - School of Accountancy and

detail.title: "Megadeal" Subsidies, Local Spillovers and Corporate Innovation
detail.abstract: We examine whether the largest place-based, firm-specific corporate subsidies (“Megadeals”) awarded by state and local governments affect local firms’ innovation. First, we document that 1) subsidy firms innovate in the subsidized county and 2) subsidy firms bring inventors from other counties into the subsidized county, consistent with subsidy firms generating new knowledge locally. In our main test, we use a stacked cohort design with stringent fixed effects to document that local firms increase patenting following a Megadeal. Cross-sectionally, effects are increasing 1) in subsidy firm innovativeness, 2) in the technological closeness of subsidy firms and local firms, 3) when subsidy and local firms share an industry and 4) when the subsidized location has a heavy college presence. Additionally, we document that following a Megadeal, local firms increasingly make citations to subsidy firm patents and that the patent similarity of local and subsidy firms increases. We document that subsidy firm inventors are more likely to move to local firms following a Megadeal. We also find that subsidies for labs, headquarters and high-tech manufacturing plants drive our main results. These results are consistent with knowledge spillovers being one channel through which we observe an increase in local firm patenting following Megadeals.

title: When Transparency Backfires: Real-Time Trading Disclosure and Price Efficiency
affiliations: University of International Business and Economics, University of International Business and Economics (UIBE) - School of International Trade and Economics and University of International Business and Economics (UIBE) - University of International Business and Economics (UIBE), Students

detail.title: When Transparency Backfires: Real-Time Trading Disclosure and Price Efficiency
detail.abstract: Can more transparency make prices less efficient? This study investigates this question using China's May 2024 Stock Connect reform, which ended real-time disclosure of Northbound trading while leaving foreign trading access unchanged. In a difference-indifferences design, we find that removing disclosure improves price efficiency. The evidence is consistent with reduced herding, whereby real-time disclosure of Northbound flows encourages excessive reliance on common trading signals, amplifies noise, and impedes information aggregation. The disclosure termination has real effects, improving investment efficiency and reducing financing costs. These findings suggest that enhanced trading disclosure can impair price discovery, highlighting the importance of disclosure design.

title: Watering with Salt Water: Active Need Frustration in Virtual Higher Education
affiliations: Shahid Beheshti University, Shahid Beheshti University, Shahid Beheshti University and Trinity College Dublin

detail.title: Watering with Salt Water: Active Need Frustration in Virtual Higher Education
detail.abstract: Higher education faces an anthropological fracture: the erosion of physical campus life and a rising undergraduate rebellion against technology-mediated instruction. While institutional discourse prioritizes technical utility, 43% of students report acute digital burnout. Adopting a relativist ontology and a Big Qual phenomenological framework, this study analyzed open-ended narratives from 1,157 undergraduates at Shahid Beheshti University to capture the existential and psychosomatic drivers of this aversion. Our findings map an ontological protest against the digital void, structured across five distinct thematic domains: (i) The Ghost of the Polis (relational erosion and social anonymity); (ii) The Biology of the Box (somatic pathology and technostress); (iii) The Domestic Prison (spatial cannibalization of the academic zone); (iv) The Existential Theft (developmental arrest and meritocratic devaluation); and (v) The Pedagogical Betrayal (assessment hostility). Synthesized through Self-Determination Theory (SDT), the results demonstrate that the digital medium acts as an active "thwarting agent" rather than a neutral delivery system. The analysis reveals a "salt water" effect: a lack of campus life causes low need satisfaction, while the structural constraints of the "digital cage" induce active need frustration. Ultimately, undergraduate aversion is a defensive reaction to the perceived theft of a transformative rite of passage. The study advocates for a "Need-Supportive Digital Design" framework prioritizing embodied social presence over digital convenience, offering administrators a roadmap for addressing global retention crises.

title: IS BANK SUPERVISION FIT FOR PURPOSE?
affiliations: Harvard Law School

detail.title: IS BANK SUPERVISION FIT FOR PURPOSE?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA

detail.abstract: The 2023 failures of Silicon Valley, Signature, and First Republic Banks provoked widespread criticism of bank supervision – a distinctive administrative function that goes beyond rule enforcement to identify, and seek correction of, practices that threaten bank safety and soundness.  But the effectiveness of supervision cannot be evaluated without specifying more precisely the role it is supposed to play in today’s bank regulatory system, which rests on an extensive body of statutory and regulatory rules that reflect policymakers’ views of the best balance between credit creation and financial stability.  This article first proposes that the contemporary purpose of supervision should not be an open-ended effort to make banks safer than required by regulation, but one to ensure that regulations are not undermined by regulatory arbitrage, imperfect risk measurement, or poor risk management by banks.  The article then examines whether the current supervisory function is capable of performing this role. Using the 2023 bank failures as a starting point, the article proceeds with a broader institutional analysis, concluding that recurring supervisory shortcomings reflect structural rather than idiosyncratic problems. Political pressures, resource and expertise constraints, the opacity of supervisory activity, and organizational incentives that favor compliance with centrally prescribed priorities over independent judgment all undermine supervisory effectiveness. While supervision remains essential in a rule-based regulatory system, it will not be fit for purpose unless these structural impediments are addressed with a reform program that goes beyond the incremental steps that have been offered in the wake of the 2023 failures.

title: Implementation of RPwD Act, 2016 in Elementary Schools in Mizoram: Challenges Faced by Teachers ​
affiliations: Mizoram University and Mizoram University

detail.title: Implementation of RPwD Act, 2016 in Elementary Schools in Mizoram: Challenges Faced by Teachers ​
detail.abstract: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016, mandates inclusive education for children with disabilities in India. However, significant implementation gaps persist, particularly in under-resourced regions. This study examined the challenges faced by elementary school teachers in implementing the RPwD Act, 2016 across five districts of Mizoram. A descriptive cross-sectional survey design was employed, involving 250 teachers selected through purposive and stratified random sampling from 25 elementary schools (5 per district), achieving a 97% response rate (n=242). Data were collected using a structured questionnaire assessing teacher awareness, implementation challenges, and resource adequacy, along with an observation checklist for infrastructure assessment. Descriptive statistics (frequencies, percentages, means) and inferential statistics (chi-square tests) were used for analysis. Findings revealed critical gaps: only 24.5% of teachers had read the Act's provisions, merely 10.5% were familiar with the 21 recognized disability categories, and 98% lacked knowledge in identifying specific learning disabilities. Infrastructure assessment showed that while 87% of schools had ramps, 0% had accessible classrooms or suitable furniture for children with mobility impairments. All teachers (100%) reported absence of special educators, lack of teaching-learning materials, and large class sizes as major barriers. The study concludes that significant gaps exist between policy mandates and ground-level implementation. Recommendations include comprehensive teacher training programs, infrastructure upgrades, deployment of special educators, and strengthened monitoring mechanisms to realize the Act's objectives in Mizoram's elementary schools.

title: The Impact of Urbanization on Unemployment: Empirical Evidence from Provincial Panel Data in Vietnam
affiliations: Academy of Finance

detail.title: The Impact of Urbanization on Unemployment: Empirical Evidence from Provincial Panel Data in Vietnam
detail.abstract: Urbanization is a key driver of economic restructuring, but its effects on unemployment may vary across localities and stages of development. This article examines the impact of urbanization on unemployment in Vietnam using a balanced panel dataset of 63 provinces and centrally governed cities for the period 2018-2024, yielding 441 observations. After comparing alternative panel-data models and correcting for heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation, and cross-sectional dependence using Driscoll-Kraay standard errors, the results show that urbanization can contribute to labour-market improvement when accompanied by economic growth, higher human-resource quality, and broader human development. On this basis, the study proposes policy implications for promoting sustainable urbanization in association with job creation, improved human-resource quality, and stronger labour supply-demand linkages.

title: Another Sputnik Moment? Evaluating Potential Market Repricing and Margin Compression from the Kimi K3 AI Release
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: Another Sputnik Moment? Evaluating Potential Market Repricing and Margin Compression from the Kimi K3 AI Release
detail.abstract: The arrival of Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, a 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight multimodal mixture-of-experts model featuring a 1-million-token context window, represents a Sputnik moment for artificial intelligence capability and market expectations. Unlike the 2025 DeepSeek efficiency shock, which transmitted primarily as a capital expenditure and training-cost deflation event, Kimi K3 acts as a scale-driven pricing power and margin compression shock. By delivering near-frontier reasoning and long-horizon agentic capabilities via open weights, K3 challenges proprietary enterprise software moats and high-multiple application wrappers. This study evaluates the equity risk and intrinsic value vulnerability of an eight-stock technology basket across three distinct tiers: Hyperscalers, Semiconductors, and Enterprise Software. Utilizing a Capital Asset Pricing Model and an inverted Gordon Growth Free Cash Flow to Equity framework with a 3.85% risk-free rate, the analysis demonstrates that high-multiple software entities experience severe valuation contractions, exceeding 75% under a 3-percentagepoint long-term growth reduction. Conversely, cyclical memory providers and buffered hyperscalers exhibit asymmetric downside resilience.

title: The Reaction-Function Ratchet Wage Suppression as a Monetary Externality, and Its Correction

detail.title: The Reaction-Function Ratchet Wage Suppression as a Monetary Externality, and Its Correction
detail.abstract: For four decades, monetary policy has treated rising wages as the leading edge of inflation and rising profits as a residual not worth a sentence in a statement. Over the same four decades the labor share of American income fell by roughly six percentage points, the institutions that once transmitted wages into price spirals were dismantled, and the inflation that finally arrived was led by margins, not paychecks. This monograph argues that these facts are one fact. The stabilization regime is asymmetric: it polices the income of the factor that cannot exit and accommodates the income of the factor that can. Each tightening cycle cuts labor’s share; no expansion is allowed to run long enough to restore it. The result is a one-way ratchet whose downstream costs, chronic demand weakness, falling neutral rates, debt-financed consumption, and a politics of grievance, now return to the regime as the one form of inflation it cannot fight: tariffs, restriction, and fiscal dominance. The regime is manufacturing its own enemy. The monograph proposes a repair: a tolerance rule under which the central bank permits bounded inflation while wages catch up within a productivity corridor, the labor share sits below its historical norm, and elevated margins do the absorbing; a fiscal pair, payroll relief financed by taxation of margins above trend, that prices the externalities the market cannot; and the institutional coordination that solves what neither can. The design is stress-tested against its own failure modes, including the incentive of concentrated firms to attack the rule’s trigger, and its unresolved weaknesses are stated plainly.

title: Socioeconomic Differences in Food Item Accessibility through Online Delivery in the Netherlands: A Cross-Sectional Study
affiliations: Wageningen University & Research, Wageningen University & Research, Wageningen University & Research, Wageningen University & Research and Wageningen University

detail.title: Socioeconomic Differences in Food Item Accessibility through Online Delivery in the Netherlands: A Cross-Sectional Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract:
Background: Online meal delivery platforms (OMDP) have become an important part of food environments, yet evidence has largely focused on socioeconomic differences in online food outlet accessibility rather than the food items consumers can order. We examined whether accessibility to food items across food categories on the largest Dutch OMDP varied by area-level socioeconomic status (SES) and whether differences persisted after accounting for food outlet number and population size.

Methods: In this cross-sectional study, we collected OMDP data using automated web scraping. Dutch postcode districts were linked to area-level SES and categorized into low-, middle-, and high-SES tertiles. Food outlets and food items were linked to districts by served postcodes. We classified over 1·5 million food items into 20 categories using a keyword-based approach. Negative binomial generalized estimating equation models estimated socioeconomic differences before and after adjustment for food outlet number and population.

Findings: Non-alcoholic drinks (9·6%), sandwiches (6·0%), and meat dishes (6·0%) were the most accessible food categories, whereas soups (0·4%), breads (0·5%), and noodles (0·6%) were the least accessible. Accessibility was consistently highest in low-SES areas across all categories. Compared with high-SES areas, low-SES areas had greater accessibility to non-alcoholic drinks (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 1·9, 95% CI: 1·7–2·2), sandwiches (IRR 1·9, 1·8–2·2), and meat dishes (IRR 1·8, 1·7–2·0). Socioeconomic differences were consistent across food categories. Adjustment for food outlet number largely eliminated socioeconomic differences, whereas population adjustment did not alter the overall pattern.

Interpretation: Lower-SES areas in the Netherlands had greater access to food items via OMDPs than higher-SES areas. However, these differences reflected overall access to food items rather than specific food categories and were largely explained by the number of food outlets serving each area. Discretionary foods dominated across all areas, underscoring the need for policies and provision that promote healthier, more equitable online food environments.

title: Do Macroeconomic Fundamentals Forecast Exchange Rates?
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Do Macroeconomic Fundamentals Forecast Exchange Rates?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare that we have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: We reexamine Meese-Rogoff (1983) puzzle by applying the long-horizon regression framework of Mark (1995) to monthly GBP/USD and CAD/USD data spanning January 1971 to March 2025. The model regresses multi-step-ahead exchange rate changes on the current purchasing power parity (PPP) misalignment between the spot rate and its fundamental value. All inference is conducted using Newey-West heteroskedasticity-and-autocorrelation-consistent (HAC) standard errors, which are essential given the overlapping observations generated by long-horizon forecasting. For GBP/USD, the PPP coefficient βk is statistically significant at short-to-medium horizons under the full sample but deteriorates markedly in the post-1998 period, suggesting a structural weakening of the PPP signal in the modern era. For CAD/USD, the relationship is weaker at one month but surprisingly robust and persistent at medium-to-long horizons, holding across both sub-samples. Volatility regime analysis reveals that PPP predictability is concentrated in high-volatility periods for both currencies, consistent with an arbitrage-cost interpretation. We conclude that PPP fundamentals contain genuine predictive information but that its magnitude, persistence, and statistical robustness are highly currency-and period-specific.

title: Sequentially Valid Uncertainty: A Bound on Coverage Degradation for Dropout-Informed Conformal Prediction under Regime Shift
affiliations: University of Oxford

detail.title: Sequentially Valid Uncertainty: A Bound on Coverage Degradation for Dropout-Informed Conformal Prediction under Regime Shift

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval was not required for this case study. Written informed consent was obtained from the participant(s) for the collection and publication of relevant data.

detail.abstract: Monte Carlo (MC) dropout turned an existing regularization trick into a cheap way to get predictive uncertainty from any dropout-trained network, but its uncertainty estimates carry no coverage guarantee and are known to be systematically miscalibrated, particularly under distribution shift. Conformal prediction supplies the missing guarantee, but the classical guarantee requires exchangeable data-an assumption time series violate by construction. Recent work (MC-CP, EPICSCORE, DCP) has begun fusing dropout-derived uncertainty with conformal calibration for sequential data, but treats the fusion as an algorithmic design choice, targeting approximate marginal coverage empirically without a provable account of how the coverage gap scales with the severity of the exchangeability violation. We provide that account. We studentize the conformal nonconformity score by the MC-dropout predictive standard deviation, wrap it in an ACI-style online quantile tracker (DS-ACP), and prove three results: the resulting long-run coverage guarantee is scoreagnostic-inherited from ACI itself rather than a new property of studentization (Lemma 1); an explicit, non-fitted worst-case bound on the finite-time coverage gap via a local exchangeability-violation coefficient δ t (Proposition 1), confirmed in a controlled synthetic experiment where the measured gap correlates with δ t at r = 0.98 (R 2 = 0.96); and a generalization of that bound to arbitrary (not just piecewise-constant) dropout bias via a triangle-inequality argument over pairwise rescaling distances, requiring no linearization and verified numerically in 30/30 randomized configurations (Proposition 2). The paper's distinctive contribution is this diagnostic account of why and by how much dropout-informed conformal scores can fail-not a claim that studentization reliably improves interval efficiency in practice, which we test directly and do not find: on a real trained network, naive MC-dropout variance initially made DS-ACP worse than a raw-residual baseline, traced to a missing aleatoric-variance term and fixed with a held-out variance-floor estimate; but on real electricity and M4 hourly benchmarks (15 series each, two datasets unrelated in domain and scale), an apparent width-efficiency advantage that replicated across seeds for one client did not survive extension to more series, and the same null result replicated independently on the second dataset. We report this retraction directly rather than let the earlier, more favorable result stand. We further run the official code of a real competing system (EPICSCORE) as a baseline; an initial comparison was confounded by a mismatched point predictor, and correcting for it substantially narrows the apparent gap while a smaller, real effect remains. Code, data-access instructions, and full experimental logs for every reported result are released in the supplementary material. Preprint. Under review.

title: Policy Legibility and the Limits of Democratic Accountability: Evidence from Voter beliefs
affiliations: and

detail.title: Policy Legibility and the Limits of Democratic Accountability: Evidence from Voter beliefs
detail.abstract: Democratic accountability depends on voters' ability to infer how public policies affect their welfare. We study this ability using surveys conducted around the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, the 2020 presidential election, and the 2021 American Rescue Plan. Across 11,303 respondents, we compare stated beliefs with respondentspecific statutory benchmarks and common-truth policy facts. We supplement these surveys with candidate-placement and factual-belief measures from the American National Election Studies. We find that welfare-relevant policy consequences are substantially less legible to voters than candidate positions. Beliefs about policy consequences are weakly organized by party, highly dispersed within party, and, for several items, dispersed on a scale comparable to the policy consequence itself. The contrast persists among politically attentive, sophisticated, and affectively engaged voters. An empirically calibrated spatial model maps dispersion of the observed magnitude into electoral incentives and shows that lower legibility substantially flattens the vote-share return to policy moderation. Policy legibility therefore places an important constraint on welfare-based democratic accountability.

title: Drinking Water, Sanitation, and Health in India: Policy Framework, Challenges and Opportunities

detail.title: Drinking Water, Sanitation, and Health in India: Policy Framework, Challenges and Opportunities

publicationDetails.detailsText: The Routledge Handbook of the Indian Economy, edited by Debashis Chakraborty and Anirban Biswas - Forthcoming

detail.abstract: Drinking water and sanitation has received significant attention over the last four decades at the global and national level. Yet, millions of people in India do not have access to safe drinking water and proper sanitation facilities. The served and unserved population is dependent on multiple modes and models of water provisioning to meet their basic requirements. There is great variation in terms of access to water sources, amount and quality of water consumed, and access to sanitation facilities. All these factors critically influence the human health. This chapter does a comprehensive analysis of these challenges and chart out the impact of these issues on Indian economy. In addition, it examines major government policies promulgated in recent years to address these issues and explore the future challenges for the Indian economy.

title:
Human Progress and the Rat Roads of Britain 
The Operator View of Infrastructure
affiliations: University of Birmingham

detail.title:
Human Progress and the Rat Roads of Britain 
The Operator View of Infrastructure
detail.abstract: Britain's motorways entered an old road-field. Long before the Preston Bypass opened and the M1 followed, Britain already moved through Roman lines, parish roads, village lanes, turnpikes, farm access, market routes and small roads shaped by settlement, land, water, animals, property and memory. These inherited roads-called here 'rat roads'-are often treated as awkward remnants of a pre-motorway age. This paper treats them as a serious human system. They shape conduct, force attention to place, expose movement to pedestrians, cyclists, hedges, bends, villages, animals and weather, and preserve a close knowledge that modern speed can weaken. The motorway is therefore a new speed form entering a human ecosystem, not simply a faster line. The central question is how motorways can emerge inside an inherited road-field without reducing the integrity of the world they enter. The paper argues for motorway design as melding: the disciplined insertion of speed into an old field so that range expands while local conduct, ecological continuity, social respect and close knowledge survive. Human progress is then judged by knowing and respect, not movement alone. Civilisation is not proved by speed. It is proved by the capacity to introduce speed without losing the world.

title:
Scoring Point-Cloud Distributional Submissions 

The Nearest-the-Pin Parimutuel, Jittered Outcomes, and the Heat Ladder

detail.title:
Scoring Point-Cloud Distributional Submissions 

The Nearest-the-Pin Parimutuel, Jittered Outcomes, and the Heat Ladder

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Intech Investments funded the early phase of the Microprediction platform that motivates theoretical issues addressed in this paper.

detail.abstract: Point-cloud forecasts are often evaluated by smoothing the submitted samples into a kernel density estimate and scoring that density at the realised outcome. This apparently natural procedure is not proper: under logarithmic scoring at the raw outcome, a forecaster is generally rewarded for submitting samples from a deconvolution of their belief by the smoothing kernel, rather than from the belief itself. For Gaussian beliefs and Gaussian kernels this incentive has the simple form "shave ℎ 2 from the covariance." We show that the defect is repaired by adding outcome noise from the same kernel used to smooth the submission. More generally, composing a proper score with a fixed Markov kernel preserves propriety, and strict propriety for the original report is recovered exactly when the induced channel is injective; for convolution kernels this is equivalent to the set where the characteristic function is nonzero being dense. For Gaussian kernels, repeating the repaired score over a ladder of smoothing scales decomposes log-score regret, via the relative de Bruijn identity, into Fisher-divergence bands plus a coarse-scale KL term. We also describe a high-dimensional alternative based on random one-dimensional projections, whose average CRPS is, up to an explicit dimension constant, the multivariate energy score. The results are population-level: finite clouds, endogenous bandwidths, and finite-player equilibria are left open.

title: The Magnum Opus: The Detektor-Safe Harness - A Computational Protocol for Non-Collusive Autonomous Orchestration and ASI Alignment in Perishable Inventory Markets

detail.title: The Magnum Opus: The Detektor-Safe Harness - A Computational Protocol for Non-Collusive Autonomous Orchestration and ASI Alignment in Perishable Inventory Markets
