detail.abstract: The Principle of Reasonableness identifies illegal benefit as a criterion for calculating administrative fines, but does not define its limits. This article proposes three criteria to delimit it: direct causal connection with the infringed obligation, the cessation of capitalization upon extinction of the obligation or loss of ownership by the infringer, and the requirement of adequate reasoning in determining the compliance scenario. A correction is also included regarding the erroneous citation of the author's thesis in OEFA pronouncements on detection probability.

title: Bayesian Distillation: A RateDistortion Theory of Model Compression and the Inverse of Scaling Laws
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and George Mason University

detail.title: Bayesian Distillation: A RateDistortion Theory of Model Compression and the Inverse of Scaling Laws
detail.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a large teacher model into a small student that retains most of the teacher's predictive quality at a fraction of the cost. Empirically this yields a striking bargain on the order of 95% of the teacher's capability at 10% of its size that is the mirror image of neural scaling laws, in which quality improves only as a slow power law of scale. We give a Bayesian account that explains this asymmetry. We identify the ideal teacher with the posterior predictive distribution and cast distillation as a forward KullbackLeibler (KL) information projection of that predictive onto a low-capacity student family; the classical soft-target cross-entropy of Hinton et al. (2015) is recovered exactly as the population objective, and temperature scaling is recovered as tempering of the predictive, i.e. a power posterior. Our central object is a ratedistortion function for distillation, D(R), that measures the smallest attainable predictive KL at student rate (description length) R. We show that the 95% at 10% phenomenon is exactly the statement that D(R) has steep early curvature, governed by the spectral decay of the teacher's predictive operator, and we prove this contrasts with scaling laws because distillation represents an already-discovered function rather than discovering it. We make the theory concrete through a provable instance sparse variational Gaussian process distillation, whose distortion is controlled by tail eigenvalues and we give a PAC-Bayes generalization bound in which the teacher predictive plays the role of a data-dependent prior, together with a globallocal shrinkage account of the student's eective rate. Controlled experiments conrm a steep ratedistortion elbow, recovering roughly 95% of the reducible distortion at about one-eighth of the teacher's size, while a scaling-law learner would require two orders of magnitude more resource for the same delity.

title: The Insurability of Skill: Vocational Specificity, Structural Change, and Mobility over the Life Course

detail.title: The Insurability of Skill: Vocational Specificity, Structural Change, and Mobility over the Life Course
detail.abstract: Vocational education systems trade a faster school-to-work transition against diminished employment late in working life, a pattern strongest in apprenticeship countries. The standard human-capital reading treats this trade-off as a portfolio choice under known risk. This paper recasts it as an insurance problem. Occupation-specific skills are an illiquid, non-diversifiable household asset whose acquisition is viable only because employment, unemployment, and wage protection-together with the training system's certification infrastructure and employer co-investment-constitute an implicit insurance arrangement covering occupational income risk. Applying standard insurability criteria shows the arrangement is sound while occupational decline is idiosyncratic, and fails when structural change is directed at task content shared across occupations: correlated shocks place a floor under pooled risk that no pool size overcomes, the implicit contract is repriced ex post, and the uninsured residual falls on latecareer workers. The late-career vocational penalty is therefore regime-dependent rather than structural, which reconciles divergent findings across countries and periods. The paper derives four testable predictions, outlines a research design on linked employer-employee administrative data, and draws policy implications: portability by design, explicitly priced cover in place of implicit promises, and a public backstop for the correlated tail.

title: Knight's Identity, Quantile Regression, and the Polson-Scott Algorithm
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Knight's Identity, Quantile Regression, and the Polson-Scott Algorithm
detail.abstract: The quantile check loss is convex but non-smooth, and two devices have grown up around its single kink. Knight's identity expands the loss into a subgradient score and a non-negative remainder, and is the engine of M-estimation asymptotics. The asymmetric-Laplace data augmentation, read through the mixture/envelope hierarchical duality of Polson and Scott (2016), represents the loss by a latent scale and drives Bayesian and MM computation. These are usually treated as unrelated tricks; we argue they are two faces of one convex object. Knight's identity is the profiling (Fenchel-Moreau) reading; the normal variance-mean mixture is the marginalization (Bernstein-Widder) reading; and the two classical missing-data identities are the bridge between them. Fisher's identity returns Knight's score as the marginalized augmented score, exactly and elementarily, and Louis's identity returns Knight's curvature as the observed information, which, we show, vanishes pointwise and lives entirely at the kink, re-emerging only after the data average. Seven experiments make the correspondence quantitative: the mixture reproduces the asymmetric Laplace to the last constant, the score identity holds to machine precision, the Louis cancellation is confirmed, and the linear-programming, MM, and Gibbs estimators agree to  in the coefficient. The two readings part company only in their conditioning: at extreme τ the profiling iteration slows sharply while the marginalization sampler degrades gracefully, a contrast the duality predicts and the experiments trace.

title: The Sovereign Conglomerate: A Structural-Functionalist Model of Institutional Stabilization, Capital Concentration, and Political Market Segmentation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Sovereign Conglomerate: A Structural-Functionalist Model of Institutional Stabilization, Capital Concentration, and Political Market Segmentation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known financial, commercial, institutional, or personal conflicts of interest that could have influenced this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a theoretical and conceptual research framework. It did not involve human participants, patient data, surveys, interviews, experiments, or identifiable personal information. Accordingly, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

keywords: Theoretical Framework and Research Design Macro-Political Economy / Structural Sociology / Systems Theory Submission Status

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes a conceptual model of how modern institutional society may function under conditions of extreme technological, financial, and informational integration. Rather than treating rising inequality, institutional distrust, and political polarization as independent democratic failures or unintended distortions within liberal-capitalist systems, this study advances an alternative systems-theoretical interpretation: the Sovereign Conglomerate Model. The framework reconceptualizes advanced institutional society not primarily as an ideologically governed democratic republic, but as a vertically integrated macro-organizational system oriented toward systemic continuity, infrastructural stabilization, capital preservation, and adaptive equilibrium management.

Under this perspective, phenomena commonly treated as democratic dysfunctions—including wealth concentration, institutional interdependence, sovereign debt expansion, and hyper-polarization—are analyzed as interconnected outputs emerging from recursive institutional incentive structures operating within technologically integrated financial and informational systems.

The model identifies three interacting institutional tiers:

  1. Executive Directorate: Concentrated asset-holding and infrastructural ownership systems.
  2. Institutional Interlock: Corporate, bureaucratic, technological, financial, regulatory, and media coordination networks.
  3. Segmented Mass Base: Labor populations functioning simultaneously as labor infrastructure, consumer markets, legitimacy substrates, and behavioral-data reservoirs.

The analysis further proposes that political fragmentation functions not as an engineered teleological design, but as an emergent structural coupling that redirects social energy horizontally across segmented identity formations, thereby under certain conditions lowering the probability of vertically unified opposition against concentrated institutional power. The model rejects conspiratorial intentionality and instead emphasizes emergent convergence generated through overlapping incentives, systemic risk minimization, financial interdependence, adaptive institutional selection, and recursive informational dynamics operating within complex systems environments.

title: Bayesian Decision-Theoretic Variable Selection: Costs, Ridge Hyperparameters, and Explainable AI
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, George Mason University and

detail.title: Bayesian Decision-Theoretic Variable Selection: Costs, Ridge Hyperparameters, and Explainable AI
detail.abstract: We revisit Lindley (1968)'s decision-theoretic framework for variable selection and establish four new results. First, Lindley's prediction paradox : under a flat prior the full-model OLS predictor is optimal-variable selection only improves prediction when a sparsity prior or complexity cost is imposed, so every standard criterion (R 2 , AIC, BIC, LASSO) is implicitly Bayesian with a specific cost structure. Second, Lindley's variable-specific costs in the control problem are precisely per-variable ridge hyperparameters; BIC corresponds to  σ ^2 log(n)/2 and AIC. Third, the Single Best Replacement (SBR) algorithm of Polson and Sun (2019) satisfies a formal oracle property-model-selection consistency and minimax rate under the sparse Riesz condition-that LASSO lacks under the irrepresentable condition. Fourth, we develop Decision-Theoretic Explainable AI (DT-XAI): posterior inclusion probabilities are the natural feature attributions, costs encode privacy and acquisition constraints, and the Bayesian Model Averaged (BMA) predictor propagates model uncertainty-including the between-model variance absent from SHAP and LIME-through to explanations. Minimum Description Length (MDL) costs provide a Shtarkov-optimal cost specification connecting Lindley's framework to Kolmogorov complexity. We illustrate on the Hald cement data (Hald, 1952), confirming that the prediction and control optimal active sets differ.

title: Efficiency Bounds for GBC Quantile Prediction: Local Kernels versus Global Neural Networks
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and George Mason University

detail.title: Efficiency Bounds for GBC Quantile Prediction: Local Kernels versus Global Neural Networks
detail.abstract: We study the statistical efficiency of estimating a one-step-ahead predictive distribution directly through its conditional quantile function, without specifying a likelihood, a parametric model, or a set of latent parameters. Casting the predictive problem inside the generativequantile framework of Schmidt-Hieber and Zamolodtchikov (2024)  we compare two estimators of the conditional quantile map. A local kernel estimator attains the minimax rate m-2β /(2β +d) in the ambient history dimension d; a global sparse ReLU network estimator-the architecture underlying the generative Bayesian prediction method of Polson and Sokolov (2023); Nareklishvili et al. (2025)-attains m-2β /(2β +k+1) in an effective compositional dimension k ≪ d. The neural estimator thereby escapes the curse of dimensionality whenever the quantile map factors through a low-dimensional summary of the history. We prove a minimax lower bound of m-2β /(2β +k) for the summary problem; a single shared network is nearoptimal, falling one effective dimension short because it resolves all quantile levels through one function, and we show that a level-adaptive architecture-a fixed basis in τ with network capacity allocated across levels in proportion to coefficient size-closes this gap for k ≥ 2, attaining the minimax rate exactly under a mild mixed-smoothness condition and up to an arbitrarily small exponent loss under Hölder smoothness alone. We give the full risk decompositions, extend the analysis to multivariate targets through the Knothe-Rosenblatt transport, and show that the same rates certify Generative Bayesian Computation (GBC) for posterior simulation under Y → θ , X → y. A simulation study on a heteroskedastic autoregression confirms the predicted exponent.

title: Selected Evidence, Omitted Information, and Belief Updating in Large Language Model Decision Support
affiliations: Nanyang Technological University (NTU) and

detail.title: Selected Evidence, Omitted Information, and Belief Updating in Large Language Model Decision Support
detail.abstract: AI advisors often receive selected rather than complete evidence. A prompt may include the favorable parts of a hiring file, the regulatory checks in a due-diligence screen, or a procurement dashboard that omits conflict-of-interest information. We test whether large language models use the selection process to infer what the prompt leaves out. The design adapts Enke's WYSIATI task: an initial signal induces a High/Low assessment, later evidence is selected conditional on that assessment, and final estimates are compared with Bayesian and visible-sample benchmarks. Study 1 provides the diagnostic benchmark and reanalyzes Enke's human microdata. Humans and several models move toward visible-sample updating, while GPT-5.5 largely corrects the numeric contrast. Rationale outputs provide diagnostic evidence rather than hidden chain-of-thought traces: many responses echo the selection rule, but Bayesian correction is more closely associated with explicit hidden-expectation reasoning. Study 2 embeds the same structure in domain-framed numerical tasks for financial due diligence, hiring, and procurement. Selected is compared with a posterior-equivalent coarse-placeholder Control that shows the same selected ratings and makes the omitted-side midpoint explicit. The contrast remains after Full-arm arithmetic checks. A later visible-only instruction moves estimates further toward the displayed sample. The results identify a specific failure in numerical updating from selected evidence.

title: How Does Digital Literacy Shape Farmers’ Income Inequality and Welfare Gaps?
affiliations: Beijing Forestry University, Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics, Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics and Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: How Does Digital Literacy Shape Farmers’ Income Inequality and Welfare Gaps?
detail.abstract: In the context of rapid development of the digital economy, digital literacy has become a crucial variable influencing farmers' welfare and social equity. Based on 2,921 micro-samples from the 2020 China Rural Revitalization Survey (CRRS), this paper constructs a multi-dimensional welfare index system encompassing economic, health, living conditions, and subjective well-being to systematically analyze the impact of digital literacy on farmers' welfare inequality and its underlying mechanisms. The results show that improved digital literacy significantly suppresses farmers' welfare inequality, a conclusion consistent across different model specifications and robustness tests. Mechanism analysis reveals that digital literacy indirectly alleviates welfare inequality by narrowing the income gap, with the mediating effect accounting for approximately 15% of the total effect. Heterogeneity analysis shows that digital literacy exerts a more pronounced role in improving the welfare of middle-aged and elderly farmers and low-income farmers, demonstrating a clear "compensation effect." These findings not only enrich the theoretical research on the relationship between digital literacy and welfare inequality but also provide policy implications for advancing digital inclusion and the rural revitalization strategy.

title: The Intertemporal-Clearinghouse Theorem: A Universal Mechanism to Purge Moral Hazard from Banking Infrastructure

detail.title: The Intertemporal-Clearinghouse Theorem: A Universal Mechanism to Purge Moral Hazard from Banking Infrastructure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: Abided by all ethical standards.
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Intertemporal-Clearinghouse Theorem, a regulatory mechanism that eliminates the incentives for private firms to exploit hidden information, forcing them to align their operations with systemic stability. We first mathematically prove that Intertemporal-Clearinghouse is a universal property governing risk-bearing networks afflicted by hidden behavior. Leveraging this proof, we construct an active regulatory policy lever that utilizes an intertemporal tracking filter to continuously predict and capture true underlying risk. We demonstrate the practical utility and scalability of this theorem by applying it to banking infrastructure, establishing an operational framework for capital adequacy that brings about a permanent, deterministic reduction in systemic risk. Subsequently, we juxtapose these findings against an annual-tracking implementation of the Intertemporal-Clearinghouse framework within a regulated insurance network to demonstrate the mechanism’s structural autonomy across different institutional and temporal horizons. This approach fundamentally departs from prevailing macroprudential literature, shifting the focus away from describing or measuring the distortions of asymmetric information and toward deploying a self-executing mechanism that actively resolves them.

title: Overlap and the Reach of a Regression Discontinuity: A Double Machine Learning Diagnostic
affiliations: and National Taiwan University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Overlap and the Reach of a Regression Discontinuity: A Double Machine Learning Diagnostic
detail.abstract: A regression discontinuity design (RDD) has strong internal validity but identifies a treatment effect only at a threshold. Gulen et al. (2026) use a causal forest to extend such an estimate into conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) across the population, trading internal for external validity. We show that their causal forest shares its first stage with Double Machine Learning (DML): its "centering" step is the Neyman-orthogonal orthogonalization that the doubly-robust learner, the R-learner, and automatic debiasing all use, so the forest is one member of that family, differing in the final-stage learner rather than in the identifying moment. Our contribution is a diagnostic rather than a new estimator, and rests on a stated selection-onobservables assumption rather than on the design. The extension itself is done by the finalstage learner, but the first-stage propensity measures how far a local effect can travel, because covariate-based extrapolation is bounded by conditional overlap. Two designs that differ in overlap make the point. Where overlap is ample, in the covenant-default study of corporate investment, the DML estimators reproduce the original findings. Where the covariates predict treatment almost perfectly and overlap collapses, in a close-election study of Islamic rule and female education, the naive average effect extrapolates into regions without treated units and flips the sign of the local estimate, which only overlap-respecting estimators recover. A knowntruth simulation shows that no member of the DML family dominates, and that automatic debiasing degrades gracefully where inverse-propensity weighting fails. Reading the DML first stage tells you whether, and how far, an RDD estimate generalizes.

title: AI-guided Priority Clarification Before Health Insurance Plan Selection: A Randomized Pilot Study
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: AI-guided Priority Clarification Before Health Insurance Plan Selection: A Randomized Pilot Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of PlanVoyager, a free health plan comparison platform, and has a commercial interest in consumer health insurance decision tools. The pilot used fictional plans and did not recommend, rank, or promote any insurance product.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study was conducted as a minimal-risk product-development usability pilot and was not reviewed by an institutional review board. Participants provided informed electronic consent before any survey data were collected. Sessions without recorded consent collected no survey data and are reported only in the participant flow. The study used fictional health insurance plans; no medical, protected health, or personally identifying information was collected for analysis; no plan recommendations were made; and findings are reported only in aggregate.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently by the author through PlanVoyager. No external grants, institutional funding, insurance-carrier funding, or commercial sponsorship supported the study.

detail.abstract: Choosing a health insurance plan is among the most consequential recurring financial decisions U.S. households make, and a large literature documents that consumers systematically struggle with it, frequently selecting dominated plans and misunderstanding basic cost-sharing concepts. Decision-support tools typically address the comparison stage of this problem. This pilot study examines an earlier stage: whether consumers can articulate what they want from a plan before comparing options. We report a randomized pilot (30 initiated sessions; 9 completers) testing the feasibility of a brief, eight-question interview conducted by a large language model that elicits and summarizes a participant's coverage priorities before an otherwise identical comparison of six fictional ACA-style plans. The interview clarified priorities without recommending plans. Descriptively, interviewarm completers reported higher priority clarity (mean 9.2 vs. 7.0 on a 10-point scale), larger stress reduction (-2.2 vs.-0.75 points), higher post-experience understanding (9.2 vs. 8.0), and markedly higher willingness to reuse the experience (80% vs. 25%). Substantial baseline imbalance in confidence and probable ceiling effects preclude any efficacy conclusion, and the sample is far too small for statistical inference. We present these results as feasibility and usability findings, describe the bilingual (English/Spanish) implementation, and outline the design of a larger preregistered trial.

title: Pay Now, Regret Later?
affiliations: Bank of Israel

detail.title: Pay Now, Regret Later?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: non
declarations.ethicsApproval: the research has ethic approval and was pre- registred

detail.abstract: Risk disclosures are widely used in credit markets, yet their effectiveness remains unclear. We study this where all spending is already deferred, so installment splitting adds a further layer of deferral on everyday purchases. In a preregistered experiment (N = 1,000), a risk prompt does not significantly reduce take-up. Yet it leaves a welfare trace: installment users told that a prompt had once been required and was now removed report lower satisfaction, consistent with disclosure-induced regret. Those most likely to split are already financially stretched-precisely the group the prompt fails to reach. Effective protection may require tailoring disclosure to borrower characteristics.

title: From Horizontal to Vertical Differentiation: Global Markov Equilibria and Regime Transitions
affiliations: Aix-Marseille University

detail.title: From Horizontal to Vertical Differentiation: Global Markov Equilibria and Regime Transitions
detail.abstract: We study a dynamic model of quality competition in which two firms continuously invest in product quality while competing in prices. Depending on the magnitude of the quality differential relative to transportation costs, competition may be predominantly horizontal, predominantly vertical, or intermediate. We derive the corresponding Markov-perfect equilibrium conditions and show that the dynamic problem can be represented by a unified system of differential equations whose coefficients depend on the prevailing competition regime. Our main contribution is to characterize the global equilibrium dynamics generated by endogenous transitions across these regimes. We show that local equilibrium trajectories must satisfy smooth-pasting and transversality conditions in order to define globally admissible equilibria. The equilibrium selection problem is therefore one of global continuation rather than local stability. The analysis reveals a rich dynamic structure. For low transportation costs, a globally admissible equilibrium continuation originates from a vertical steady state and connects smoothly the vertical, intermediate, and horizontal regimes. As transportation costs increase, this continuation disappears before the vertical steady state itself ceases to exist. Beyond a critical threshold, a new steady state emerges within the intermediate regime. For a non-empty range of parameter values, this intermediate steady state becomes globally attractive and generates an admissible equilibrium continuation connecting the three regions of the state space. These results highlight how endogenous quality investment can induce transitions between fundamentally different forms of competition and show that the intermediate regime, usually viewed as a transient configuration in static models of product differentiation, may instead become the long-run equilibrium outcome.

title: Do Monetary and Macroprudential Policies Interact Differently in a Digital Economy? Evidence from Arab Countries
affiliations: Arab Monetary Fund

detail.title: Do Monetary and Macroprudential Policies Interact Differently in a Digital Economy? Evidence from Arab Countries
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether digital financial development moderates the interaction between monetary and macroprudential policies in Arab economies. Digital financial development is defined as the degree to which financial services are transformed and delivered through digital technologies, typically capturing the expansion of digital infrastructure, digital payments, and the adoption of fintech-related services within the financial system. Using an unbalanced panel of 12 countries over the period 2010-2024, we estimate dynamic panel models employing System GMM and LSDVC estimators. The empirical analysis adopts a dual-outcome framework, considering both economic growth (GDP growth) and financial stability (Financial Stability Index) as dependent variables, in order to capture the real and financial dimensions of macro-financial policy transmission. The results indicate that monetary and macroprudential policies are complementary, as their interaction term is positive and statistically significant across specifications. Moreover, digital financial development strengthens this complementarity, although the magnitude of the effect remains modest in economic terms. The interaction effect is more pronounced for financial stability than for GDP growth, suggesting that policy transmission operates more strongly through the financial channel than through the real economy channel. Heterogeneity analysis further shows that the complementarity between monetary and macroprudential policies is more pronounced in economies with higher levels of digital financial development. Overall, the findings suggest that digitalization enhances macro-financial policy transmission mechanisms without fundamentally altering the underlying structural relationship between monetary and macroprudential policies.

title: Chinese Import Competition and Labor Compensation: Evidence from India
affiliations: Indian Institute of Management Bangalore

detail.title: Chinese Import Competition and Labor Compensation: Evidence from India
detail.abstract: This paper examines how increased Chinese import competition affects the composition and distribution of labor compensation within Indian manufacturing firms. Leveraging firm-level panel data and exploiting variation in industry-level import penetration, we document several important findings. First, greater import competition leads to an increase in overall labor compensation as a share of total firm expenditure, driven primarily by increased salaries for managerial and skilled employees. In contrast, firms do not adjust statutory components such as provident fund contributions but instead reduce discretionary, non-statutory benefits like welfare expenditures. These compositional shifts are more pronounced among larger firms, multi-product firms, and firms located in states with pro-worker labor regulations. Additionally, large domestic and exporting firms exhibit stronger increases in salary payments compared to small domestic firms, highlighting heterogeneous firm-level responses to trade shocks.

title: Quality of Decentralised Extension Services and Farmers’ Willingness to Pay: Evidence From Northeast India
affiliations: Sikkim University, Sri Sathya Sai Institute of Higher Learning and Sikkim University

detail.title: Quality of Decentralised Extension Services and Farmers’ Willingness to Pay: Evidence From Northeast India
detail.abstract: This study attempts to understand the farmers' perception of the quality of extension services and their willingness to pay for quality extension services. It also identifies the major determinants that influence the farmers’ willingness to pay for extension services in Northeast India. Primary data for this study was collected from 160 rice-growing farmers from the Golaghat district of Assam, India. The study used descriptive statistics to understand the socio-economic status of the farmers. The Likert Scale was used to understand the farmers' satisfaction with the extension services on four dimensions of quality including timeliness, accuracy, relevance and ease of understanding. The Contingent Valuation Method was used to measure the farmers' willingness to pay and the binary logistic regression was used to identify the factors that influence the farmers’ willingness to pay. The results show that the majority of the farmers were satisfied with the extension services and were willing to pay for them. In terms of amount, the farmers were willing to pay an average of Rs 190. The results of the logistic regression showed that age, education, experience and total production were statistically significant determinants of willingness to pay. The findings from this study can be helpful for policymakers, extension workers and institutions associated with extension services in the proper planning and implementation of extension services.

title: From System Defence to Dependency Governance: Delegated Trust, Non-Human Identity, and Secure AI-by-Design

detail.title: From System Defence to Dependency Governance: Delegated Trust, Non-Human Identity, and Secure AI-by-Design

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests related to this working paper. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent any employer, client, vendor, or affiliated organization.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: Not applicable

detail.abstract:
Enterprise cyber incidents are often described as breaches, outages, vendor failures, or operational disruptions. These labels are useful, but they do not always explain why the impact spreads so widely. Some recent incidents suggest that important failures are no longer happening only at the edge of individual systems. They are also showing up in the relationships between systems, vendors, identities, APIs, and business processes. This working paper examines several 2024-2025 incidents, including the Salesloft Drift OAuth-token compromise affecting Salesforce customers, the UNC6040 vishing campaign, Change Healthcare, the CrowdStrike outage, Marks & Spencer, Jaguar Land Rover, and emerging deepfake-related risks. Although these incidents differ by sector and mechanism, they can point to a common governance problem: organizations are granting authority to systems, vendors, integrations, and identities faster than they can reliably monitor or withdraw it. 

The paper extends this analysis to enterprise artificial intelligence deployment. Many generative and agentic AI systems are entering that same environment. They are connected to data, given access to tools, and placed inside workflows before governance has fully caught up. The same concerns reappear in AI deployment: non-human identity, API authority, retrieval systems, unsafe tool use, monitoring gaps, and revocation that has not been tested. Drawing on NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, and OWASP LLM and Agentic Security guidance, the paper derives governance implications for secure AI deployment from the incident patterns analyzed. It focuses on inventory, ownership, authority-based risk classification, architectural containment, pre-deployment assurance, monitoring, and revocation. The paper concludes with practical oversight questions for boards, CISOs, and risk committees seeking to manage AI as a controlled enterprise dependency rather than another layer of unexamined delegated trust.

title: Investment, Debt and Taxes
affiliations: , Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, Washington University in St. Louis - Olin Business School and San Diego State University

detail.title: Investment, Debt and Taxes
detail.abstract: The extant evidence is mixed on whether companies respond to tax incentives when making capital structure decisions. We argue that it is important to examine capital structure choices in the context of external financing needs, such as when funding corporate investment. We examine 99 years of panel data for US public companies and also study, for the first time, the two largest tax hikes of the last century (one in the 1940s, one in the 1950s). Consistent with tax incentives, we find that firms use more debt to fund investment when they face higher corporate income tax rates. As a result, leverage responses to tax rate increases are highly dependent on firms' needs for investment funding, with leverage increasing significantly more for higher growth firms. A battery of tests shows that these results are unlikely to be driven by changes in economic conditions or investment opportunities.

title: Protected by History, Expanded by PracticeFederal Reserve Independence, Functional Inheritance, and the Constitutional Triangle after Trump v. Cook

detail.title: Protected by History, Expanded by PracticeFederal Reserve Independence, Functional Inheritance, and the Constitutional Triangle after Trump v. Cook
detail.abstract: In June 2026 the Supreme Court decided the constitutional status of independent agencies twice in a single week. In Trump v. Slaughter, it placed the Federal Trade Commission within a presidential hierarchy that leaves little room for the independent agency model of Humphrey's Executor. In Trump v. Cook, a 5-4 majority denied the Government's application to stay the injunction keeping Governor Lisa Cook in office while litigation continues, and concluded that Congress may constitutionally protect Federal Reserve Governors from removal without cause. The Court grounded that exception not in the Federal Reserve Acts of 1913 and 1935 but in a tradition reaching back to the Bank of North America, while Footnote 6 reserved the status of additional regulatory powers attenuated from monetary policy. Roberts includes Andrew Jackson in that tradition only to disqualify the Jacksonian countertradition as a source of constitutional authority. This paper reads Cook as institutional grandfathering combined with prospective functional scrutiny, an analytical characterisation rather than an established doctrinal label. The institutional centre is protected; the functional perimeter remains open. The decision brings three genealogies into conflict: a constitutional genealogy that supplies the Court's historical principle, a statutory genealogy that produced the modern Federal Reserve through legislation and congressional reconstruction, and an operational genealogy that expanded the institution through dealer finance, emergency lending, Treasury market support, and international swap lines. The paper's contribution is to distinguish institutional protection from functional inheritance. Cook protects the Federal Reserve as an institution; it does not decide which later developed functions inherit that protection. A function by function test, organised around necessity, access, loss, reconstruction, and separability, is applied to three cases. Treasury market support receives strong inheritance at the monetary core and contested inheritance at the perimeter. Section 13(3) emergency lending receives conditional inheritance because Congress reconstructed the function after 2008. Swap lines and FIMA receive partial and contested inheritance, with access as the central weakness. The pattern is the paper's principal finding: functional inheritance is not a constant property of the institution but varies with legislative reconstruction. The constitutional consequence follows. The President cannot reconstruct the Federal Reserve by removal. Congress can reconstruct it by statute, though major reconstruction has occurred only in rare windows of crisis and political alignment, and where Congress does not act, the perimeter will be drawn through litigation. Because the dollar system extends beyond the American polity, even completed reconstruction remains globally incomplete: the constitutional foundations of dollar governance are domestic, while its consequences are not.

title: Flood Shocks, Trade Networks, and Import Exposure Risk: Evidence from a Global Food Panel, 2000–2021
affiliations: University of Delaware

detail.title: Flood Shocks, Trade Networks, and Import Exposure Risk: Evidence from a Global Food Panel, 2000–2021

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing personal, financial, or professional interests that could have influenced the research, analysis, interpretation, or presentation of this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, animal subjects, patient data, or personally identifiable information. Therefore, ethics approval was not required.

detail.abstract: Trade is widely treated as a buffer when floods hit major food exporters: importing countries may draw on alternative suppliers or adjust through stocks and domestic supply, and aggregate food availability tends to remain stable. Substitution does not guarantee diversification. Importers may source from suppliers that share the same flood exposure as the original shock, deepening structural vulnerability while caloric availability stays stable. We are not aware of prior global panel evidence linking exporter flood exposure to an importer-level measure of flood risk embedded in staple sourcing networks. We construct Flood Trade Exposure (FTE), trade-weighted flooded cropland in an importer's supplier network, for 159 countries over 2000-2021, and estimate import composition associations using satellite flood data, shift-share, and instrumentalvariable designs. We find no statistically detectable annual decline in national per-capita calorie availability as exporter flood exposure rises. Each importer's flood-exposed staple portfolio share rises with exporter flood severity (β = 0.047, p < 0.001). The Sub-Saharan Africa point estimate is 4.9 times the global estimate. Climate projections show rising import exposure risk for low-income countries under SSP3-7.0. FTE monitoring can sit alongside caloric indicators and signal when portfolio exposure is rising.

title: Quantifying International Technology Transfer Dynamics: A Stochastic Pipeline and Input-Output Modeling Approach

detail.title: Quantifying International Technology Transfer Dynamics: A Stochastic Pipeline and Input-Output Modeling Approach

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is a graduate student researcher at the Harvard Graduate School of Education, and the Executive Director of TECH Tokyo.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Written consent has been provided for the case studies.

detail.abstract: This study establishes a multi-dimensional macroeconomic framework to quantify the regional and international economic impacts of university-to-industry technology transfer initiatives (Leontief 1986; Roessner et al. 2013). Utilizing Wassily Leontief's Input-Output (I/O) formulations alongside a forward-looking stochastic pipeline model, we estimate the cumulative gross domestic product (GDP) contributions, employment generation, and productivity spillovers resulting from cross-border intellectual property (IP) licensing (AUTM 2024; BIO 2022). Applying this methodology to the active technology portfolios of corporate members within TECH Tokyo's Innovation Exchange, the empirical model projects 37.00 expected agreement executions from a dataset of 252 active candidate technologies (TECH Tokyo 2026). Results indicate a cumulative Japanese GDP contribution of $364.08 million (¥54.61 billion) and direct spillover output of $102.90 million across originating economies (USA, UK, and EU). Enterprise-level microeconomic assessments further reveal substantial transaction cost savings when licensing directly from academic institutions relative to inter-firm asset acquisitions (Williamson 1981).

title:
Strategic Asset Allocation and Downside Risk Management for a Small Defined Benefit Pension Fund:
A Liability-Aware Multi-Asset Portfolio Approach

detail.title:
Strategic Asset Allocation and Downside Risk Management for a Small Defined Benefit Pension Fund:
A Liability-Aware Multi-Asset Portfolio Approach

The views expressed in this paper are solely those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of Arizona State University, the W. P. Carey School of Business, Bloomberg Finance L.P., GeminiSoft Solutions Inc., Edward Jones, or any current or prior employer.

The analysis is based on a hypothetical pension fund case, publicly traded securities, and aggregated Bloomberg-derived portfolio analytics.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external financial funding. The paper was developed independently from graduate-level applied portfolio work. Academic resources, including Bloomberg Terminal access, were available through the W. P. Carey School of Business at Arizona State University during the original case-development process. No organization, employer, or data provider funded, or sponsored the conclusions of this paper.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a practical strategic asset allocation framework for a small defined benefit pension fund with near-term benefit payments, ongoing employee contributions, and a need to balance capital preservation with long-term growth. Using a case portfolio constructed for a hypothetical commercial and residential cleaning company with 1,000 employees, the study evaluates a diversified allocation across high-quality fixed income securities, defensive equities, commodity ETFs, currency exposures, money market instruments, and equity option overlays. The objective is not to maximize return in isolation, but to design a portfolio that can support recurring pension obligations while limiting downside risk in stressed market conditions. The proposed allocation places meaningful weight on U.S. Treasury and investment-grade corporate bonds, complemented by defensive equity sectors, gold and silver exposure, short-term liquidity, and covered call and protective put strategies on selected equity holdings. Back-tested portfolio statistics indicate a total return of 35.92% over the evaluation period compared with 17.85% for the benchmark, a Sharpe ratio of 0.7286 compared with 0.1652 for the benchmark, lower annualized downside risk, and a portfolio beta below one. Scenario results suggest that the portfolio underperforms in sharp equity rebounds but provides meaningful protection during crisis periods such as the Lehman default and broader financial stress. The findings support a liability-aware, multi-asset approach for smaller pension funds that require stable income, liquidity discipline, and controlled exposure to equity-market drawdowns.

title: What the Data Can See: Sheet-Specific Information Signatures of the Strategic-Inattention Fold

detail.title: What the Data Can See: Sheet-Specific Information Signatures of the Strategic-Inattention Fold
detail.abstract: The strategic-inattention trap studied by a companion regime-space analysis presents, as a stakes parameter is varied, a fold with three distinct sheets: a boundary collision at which the trap configuration is born — the recovery boundary, below which a trapped unit returns to engagement — a Maxwell sheet at which the engaged and trap configurations carry equal payoff, and an interior saddle-node at which the engaged configuration is destroyed. This paper asks what that fold looks like from data, and shows that the three sheets carry three distinct information signatures whose visibility is governed by the observation window. Short-window, branch-conditional data — the regime into which finite audit samples fall, because the trap is an absorbing state with exponentially long escape times — carry identifying power that diverges at the interior saddle-node. Long-run ensemble statistics, including a rising variance, peak instead at the Maxwell sheet. The boundary collision is the recovery boundary — the stakes level below which the trap ceases to be a rest point and a trapped unit can return — and it is informationally silent: on the trap branch the observed action does not respond to the stakes, so branch-conditional Fisher information about the parameters that set the recovery boundary is exactly zero. The fall itself is not the hidden event. A unit tracking the engaged optimum departs adiabatically at the interior saddle-node, where branch-conditional identification diverges, and the classical critical-slowing-down variance of its fluctuations diverges there too; shock-driven falls, which can occur anywhere in the band, register in the ensemble weight. What no monitoring statistic reveals is recovery: whether a trapped unit could be brought back is decided by the very parameters its silent data cannot identify. The early-warning reading must also be qualified, because a rising variance is ambiguous between two observables on two sheets — the between-basin ensemble variance, which peaks at the Maxwell sheet, and the within-well fluctuation variance, which grows toward the saddle-node — so that reporting a rising variance without saying which mislocates the transition. The upshot is a reversal of the naive worry: the fall is visible, and it is recovery that is not. The signature locations are shown to be robust across the detection sensitivity and the production value and across two distinct short-window observation models, while their exponents and magnitudes are calibration-dependent; the finite-noise correction to the ensemble signature is not merely bounded but predicted by a two-well prefactor law. A remark notes that the penalty scale —the parameter policy sets most directly — is the flattest direction of the model manifold, and hence the one monitoring data least identify.

detail.abstract: This field practicum report presents the experiences, learning outcomes, and professional development gained during a sixty-day placement at Friends in Village Development Bangladesh (FIVDB), undertaken as a partial fulfillment of the Bachelor of Social Science (BSS) degree in Social Work at Shahjalal University of Science and Technology. The practicum was conducted under the Young People Building Urban Resilience in Bangladesh project of FIVDB funded by UNDEF, which aims to strengthen climate resilience and disaster preparedness among vulnerable urban communities in Sylhet City Corporation through youth engagement and community participation. The report describes the organizational profile of FIVDB, the project's objectives, implementation strategies, and the responsibilities assigned during the placement. It highlights practical involvement in community meetings, baseline surveys, awareness campaigns, Youth Action Group activities, vulnerability mapping, and community mobilization. The report also demonstrates the application of social work knowledge, values, methods, and skills through casework, group work, community organization, and research activities. Furthermore, it reflects on the challenges encountered, professional competencies developed, and the significance of integrating classroom learning with field-based practice. Overall, the practicum enhanced the author's understanding of community development, climate change adaptation, participatory approaches, and ethical social work practice, contributing substantially to professional growth and preparedness for a future career in social work.

title: Do Published Equity Anomalies Survive Clean Data? * Nine US-Equity Papers Replicated on Survivorship-Free Data by an AI Research Agent
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Quantpedia

detail.title: Do Published Equity Anomalies Survive Clean Data? * Nine US-Equity Papers Replicated on Survivorship-Free Data by an AI Research Agent

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Vladimir Rodeski is the founder of PolyQuant AI, a commercial quantitative-research operation, and conducted this study using its AI research pipeline. Radovan Vojtko is CEO and Head of Research of Quantpedia, a commercial provider of quantitative trading-strategy research, which published a companion summary of this work. The authors received no external funding for the study and hold no financial position that benefits from its findings, which are predominantly null and negative on the strategies evaluated.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses only historical financial-market data
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external or grant funding. It was conducted internally by the authors.

detail.abstract: We replicate nine published US-equity anomaly papers on survivorship-free, point-in-time data covering roughly 61,000 active and delisted tickers from 1998 to 2025, using an AI research agent (Claude Opus 4.7 and 4.8, Anthropic). The in-sample window is 2000-22; the out-of-sample window 2023-25 is fixed and pre-registered before any result is read. Each paper runs through a two-pass fidelity review: a code-fidelity pass checks the generated backtest against the extracted paper specification; an execution-fidelity pass reads the trade log against the paper's stated behaviour. We apply the Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016) t > 3 multiple-testing hurdle on full-sample alphas, value-weighting and a micro-cap screen following Hou, Xue and Zhang (2020), and realistic turnoveraware cost stressing. Three of nine papers show a statistically significant full-sample alpha; only Bali, Cakici and Whitelaw (2011) clears t > 3; on paper-faithful builds, none survives out-of-sample. The study's lone apparent survivor, Zhu, Sun and Stivers (2021) at OOS Sharpe 1.95 on our first build, was a construction artifact the authors caught once the gated source was obtained: built from notes while the paper was paywalled, it diverged from the paper's design (a corner-sort rather than the specified reversal-within-quintile), and on a faithful rebuild it inverts to-0.95. A parallel look-ahead demonstration shows that sorting on retroactively split-adjusted rather than as-traded prices manufactures approximately 3.5 Sharpe points of illusory out-of-sample edge from a single price field. The fidelity discipline is the methodology result; the null on anomalies on clean data is the empirical result.

title: Digital Transformation, Industrial Agglomerations, and Innovation: A Review of Analytical Patterns and Structural Gaps

detail.title: Digital Transformation, Industrial Agglomerations, and Innovation: A Review of Analytical Patterns and Structural Gaps

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests and no relevant non-financial interests to disclose.
declarations.funderStatement: This publication has emanated from research jointly funded by Taighde Éireann – Research Ireland under Grant number 13/RC/2094_2, the European Union’s Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions under grant number 101126578 and was supported in part by University of Galway.

detail.abstract: Place-based digital industrial policy for innovation rests on a research base whose analytical foundations remain poorly understood. This paper presents a systematic review of 219 studies (2015-2025) on digital transformation in industrial agglomerations, using a CIMO-inspired analytical framework as an organising reference, with innovation as the central outcome lens. The synthesis uncovers three systematic structural patterns: conceptual fragmentation across four incompatible framings of digital transformation; methodological retrospection, where the most integrative empirical work relies on static ex-post designs while dynamic modelling remains peripheral; and geographic concentration, with China and Russia dominating while the Global South remains absent. An integrative synthesis demonstrates that these patterns compound each other, producing an innovation evidence base more limited than its volume suggests, one that systematically underweights the skills, sustainability, and governance outcomes central to contemporary digital transition agendas, smart specialisation strategies and place-based digital industrial policy. This review provides a diagnostic map for regional scientists and policymakers, establishing the boundary conditions of current theory and outlining a multi-level, process-oriented research agenda to inform territorially differentiated industrial policy.

title: Analyzing An Early-Phase Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial Using Generative AI
affiliations: Case Western Reserve University, Case Western Reserve University and Case Western Reserve University

detail.title: Analyzing An Early-Phase Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial Using Generative AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval:
The parent trial was approved by the University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center Institutional Review Board.
The parent clinical trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04019197) was approved by the University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center Institutional Review Board. The current study is a secondary methodological analysis that exclusively utilized completely de-identified subject-level data from this parent trial. Because the data were entirely de-identified, this secondary analysis did not require additional, separate ethical approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This study was supported by the Clinical and Translational Science Collaborative of Northern Ohio (NCATS/NIH grant UM1TR004528). The parent trial was funded by R01DK121619.
declarations.clinicalTrialRegistration: The parent trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04019197).

detail.abstract:
Background: Randomized controlled trials require reproducible data-cleaning and statistical-analysis workflows, but these workflows are often resource-intensive and dependent on specialized expertise. We evaluated whether contemporary large language models could assist with core analytic tasks in a phase 2b trial setting.

Methods: Using de-identified subject-level data, a data dictionary, and protocol-driven rules from a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of once-weekly semaglutide for HIV-associated lipohypertrophy, we assessed Gemini 2∙5 Pro and GPT-5 Pro across supervised analytic tasks. Tasks included protocol-driven data validation, generation of reproducible preprocessing code, statistical model recommendation, guided model execution, and comparison with prespecified reference analyses.

Findings: Both models generated useful, auditable code for deterministic preprocessing tasks and identified key data-quality signals, including time-invariant field inconsistencies and selected missingness patterns. For standard longitudinal models, LLM-generated estimates were broadly concordant with reference analyses under guided workflows. Performance was less reliable for non-standard or skewed-outcome analyses, particularly model selection and standard-error reproduction for quantile-regression outputs, and several tasks required expert prompting or schema clarification.

Interpretation: LLMs may be useful as supervised co-analysts for deterministic, code-expressible components of early-phase RCT analysis, especially when outputs are rerunnable and reviewed by human analysts. Their role in statistical model selection and non-standard inferential workflows remains conditional on expert oversight, explicit data dictionaries, controlled execution environments, and further validation.

title: Safety Framework Cards: A Standardized Specification for Documenting Frontier AI Safety Commitments

detail.title: Safety Framework Cards: A Standardized Specification for Documenting Frontier AI Safety Commitments
detail.abstract:
Look at any major frontier AI lab today and you'll find a public safety framework. Anthropic published its Responsible Scaling Policy in September 2023, then revised it four times, most recently to v3.1 in April 2026. OpenAI shipped the Preparedness Framework and moved it to v2.0 in April 2025. DeepMind followed with the Frontier Safety Framework, now at v3.0 (September 2025). Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Cohere, and xAI have their own. Every document is a wall of prose. Every one is structured differently. That's the problem.

Regulators keep asking whether these things are actually comparable to each other. Insurers ask it too. So does the Frontier Model Forum. Nobody has a good answer right now, because answering means reading every framework end-to-end.

The answer should be yes, and this paper argues that the way to get there is a shared machine-readable format. I call it a Safety Framework Card. Six structural dimensions: risk ontology, capability thresholds, evaluation methodology, mitigation commitments, governance triggers, revision protocol. The spec itself is a JSON schema. I retrofit eight published frameworks into cards, and a ninth card documents Mistral's non-publication, which is itself a finding worth reporting. An open-source validator and an HTML renderer ship alongside the paper.

Across the nine cards, the audit surfaces three convergences, four divergences, and one universal disclosure gap. Design-wise, the paper copies the Model Cards (Mitchell et al., 2019) and Datasheets for Datasets (Gebru et al., 2021) playbook. Propose a standardized artifact. Ship a reference implementation. Let adoption follow.

title: Money without Borders: The History of International Currencies

detail.title: Money without Borders: The History of International Currencies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: I gratefully acknowledge financial support from the Sven Svensson Foundation for Numismatics, the Gunnar Ekström Foundation, and the Sven and Dagmar Salén Foundation.

detail.abstract:
This chapter traces the historical emergence and competition of international currencies from antiquity to the present. It introduces a theoretical framework for understanding the conditions required for a currency to become internationally dominant: large volume, stable value, liquidity and low transaction costs, political and military strength of the issuing state, and institutional trust and transparency. Building on network-effects theory, the analysis highlights how the use of a dominant currency tends to reinforce itself: as more agents adopt it for trade, finance, and reserves, its value and convenience increase, creating a self-reinforcing monetary hierarchy. In addition, complementary financial innovations—such as deposit banking, clearing mechanisms, and bills of exchange—have often supported a currency’s rise to international prominence.

These criteria are tested through case studies of major currencies from antiquity to the present: the Athenian tetradrachm, the Roman denarius and aureus, the Byzantine solidus, the Islamic dinar, the Italian florin and ducat, the Spanish dollar, the Dutch guilder, the British pound sterling, and the US dollar. Each case illustrates how the necessary conditions were fulfilled—and in some instances, why they ultimately failed. Despite the diversity of contexts and monetary systems over time, the analysis reveals striking continuity in the foundations of international currency status. The same fundamental principles apply to all
dominant currencies—whether they were based on commodity money, representative money, or fiat currency. Volume, stability, liquidity, trust and institutional credibility, financialinfrastructure, and some form of political, economic, or diplomatic backing have remained essential. The chapter concludes by reflecting on contemporary challenges to the US dollar and what history suggests about the possibility—and limits—of monetary change in the
twenty-first century.

title: Substitutive Popular Urbanism: Toward a Theory of Resident-Driven Infrastructure in the Governance Void

detail.title: Substitutive Popular Urbanism: Toward a Theory of Resident-Driven Infrastructure in the Governance Void
detail.abstract: The preceding contributions to this theoretical architecture have examined the dependent peripheral city from above: as a node positioned within a metropolitan hierarchy (the Vulnerable Buffer City model), as a territory internally disarticulated across spatial, social, and environmental dimensions (Socio-Ecological Urban Disarticulation), as a trajectory of widening inequality over time (Cumulative Territorial Fractures), as a system of structurally imbalanced material flows (Disrupted Peripheral Urban Metabolism), and as an institutional field diffused across uncoordinated authorities (the Governance Fragmentation Trap). Each of these frameworks, for all its explanatory power, shares an underlying vantage point: the resident of the peripheral neighborhood appears chiefly as an object of dysfunction, a recipient of deficits imposed from above. This article inverts that vantage point. It asks what residents themselves do in the space opened by institutional absence, and proposes that the answer is neither passivity nor simple suffering, but sustained, competent, and largely unrecognized infrastructural production. Drawing on Asef Bayat's account of the quiet encroachment of the ordinary, Ananya Roy's reconceptualization of informality as a mode of urbanization rather than its failure, AbdouMaliq Simone's notion of people as infrastructure, and James Holston's theory of insurgent citizenship, this article develops the concept of Substitutive Popular Urbanism (SPU): the proposition that, under conditions of governance fragmentation and metabolic disruption, residents of marginalized neighborhoods systematically construct parallel, non-codified infrastructural systems-private wells, informally wired electricity networks, unofficial waste collection, undocumented land transactions-that substitute for absent institutional provision and, in so doing, actively reshape urban space according to a logic the state neither authors nor fully controls. Three testable hypotheses are advanced, together with a methodology for mapping the density, function, and legitimacy of substitutive infrastructure in Témara. The article closes by arguing that SPU does not merely complete the five-theory architecture developed across companion contributions; it complicates it, by raising the open question of whether resident-driven substitution ultimately mitigates the imbalances those theories describe, or quietly entrenches them by relieving the state of the pressure to resolve them.

title: Territorial Stigmatization and Symbolic Disinvestment: Toward a Theory of the Reputational Constraint on Peripheral Urban Development

detail.title: Territorial Stigmatization and Symbolic Disinvestment: Toward a Theory of the Reputational Constraint on Peripheral Urban Development
detail.abstract: The theoretical architecture developed across the preceding six contributions to this research programme has proceeded almost entirely along a materialist register: demographic pressure absorbed without adequate resources, internal disarticulation between spatial and environmental development, cumulative widening of territorial gaps, structurally imbalanced flows of water and waste, institutional fragmentation across uncoordinated authorities, and residentdriven substitutive infrastructure. Each of these frameworks presumes, reasonably, that correcting the underlying material or institutional deficit would remove, or at least substantially weaken, the corresponding urban imbalance. This article argues that such a presumption, however sound as a first approximation, cannot be sustained once one takes seriously a further dimension of peripheral urban disadvantage that operates independently of measurable material conditions: the symbolic reputation of the city itself. Drawing on Loïc Wacquant's account of territorial stigmatization, Pierre Bourdieu's theory of symbolic capital and symbolic violence, Henri Lefebvre's tripartite conception of social space, and the broader logic of othering associated with postcolonial theory, this article develops the concept of Territorial Stigmatization and Symbolic Disinvestment (TSSD): the proposition that a dependent peripheral city can accumulate a durable negative reputational identity-codified in media discourse, institutional planning language, and popular perception-that independently depresses public and private investment decisions, and that persists even after the objective material and institutional conditions that originally gave rise to it have measurably improved. Three testable hypotheses are advanced, together with a mixed-methods pathway combining discourse analysis, investment-gap econometrics, and perception surveys, for empirically evaluating TSSD in the case of Témara. The article closes by arguing that TSSD supplies the seventh and, in a specific sense, the most stubborn layer of the theoretical architecture developed in this research programme: a layer capable of obstructing recovery even after every other identified imbalance has been substantially resolved.

title: The Art of Strategic Noise: When to Poison a Data Science Contest?
affiliations: Fudan, Fudan University - School of Management, School of Economics, Peking Univeristy and Fudan University

detail.title: The Art of Strategic Noise: When to Poison a Data Science Contest?
detail.abstract: Data science contests enable seekers to crowdsource predictive and algorithmic solutions from heterogeneous solvers, but releasing training data often raises the need to protect sensitive information, such as user-side privacy and firm-side proprietary business information. A common response is to poison the released data by injecting noise. Prior work predominantly treats such poisoning as a data-protection necessity that inherently degrades data utility. We reconceptualize data poisoning as a strategic contest-design lever to manage solvers' incentives. We develop a model wherein a seeker chooses the noise scale and two heterogeneous solvers choose their effort. Data poisoning generates a fundamental tradeoff: it worsens data quality but levels the playing field and stimulates effort. We establish a moderate-asymmetry principle: poisoning is optimal only when solvers' expertise asymmetry is moderate-large enough to warrant leveling the playing field, but not so large that the requisite noise destroys the data's intrinsic value. Furthermore, we identify a complementarity between data poisoning and prize design. Strategically injecting noise restores competitive pressure, optimally inducing the seeker to augment the prize purse and potentially achieving a Pareto improvement that strictly benefits all parties. Finally, extending the analysis to a multi-solver environment reveals that optimal poisoning depends crucially on expertise skewness in addition to the dispersion. Overall, our results recast data poisoning from a defensive data-protection instrument into a proactive economic design choice.

title: The Federal Reserve Balance Sheet and the Direction of US Sectoral Equity Connectedness: A Quantile and Frequency Analysis
affiliations: University of Thessaly - Department of Economics and Dublin City University

detail.title: The Federal Reserve Balance Sheet and the Direction of US Sectoral Equity Connectedness: A Quantile and Frequency Analysis
detail.abstract: We study the connectedness of the Federal Reserve balance sheet with three pillars of the US equity market: the banking, technology, and pharmaceutical sectors. A quantile vector autoregression estimated on weekly returns measures directional connectedness in the lower tail, at the median, and in the upper tail; a frequency decomposition separates short-run from long-run linkage; and a determinants model relates the time-varying connectedness to the financial and policy environment. Including the balance-sheet quantity destabilises the system in the upper tail, so the directional core is identified on the eighteen-equity system, on which total connectedness is stable at roughly three-quarters of forecast-error variance across market states, while its direction and horizon are not. The banking sector is the persistent net transmitter of return shocks, most forcefully in bear markets and in the long-run band, while technology and pharmaceutical equities are net receivers. The balance sheet is peripheral as a node in a weekly-return network, yet it is a reliable driver of connectedness: its expansion lowers aggregate comovement and rotates transmission towards banks, equity volatility is the dominant correlate of the level of connectedness, and a money-market funding measure acts specifically on cross-sector integration. The relation between balance-sheet policy and systemic comovement is state-dependent, calming in normal conditions and coincident with stress in fragile ones. The evidence locates systemic propagation in a banking core whose centrality migrates with the volatility and policy environment.

title: Silicon vs. Satoshi: Tactical Asset Rotation Between NASDAQ-100 and Bitcoin
affiliations: Quantpedia and

detail.title: Silicon vs. Satoshi: Tactical Asset Rotation Between NASDAQ-100 and Bitcoin

declarations.declarationOfInterest: ☒ The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract:
We investigate a Donchian breakout rotation strategy between QQQ (NASDAQ-100) and Bitcoin (BTC), with a cash fallback during consolidation, and test it across eight lookback horizons (5–50 trading days) and two priority variants over a seven-year sample spanning 2019–2026. The strategy consistently outperforms passive benchmarks on a risk-adjusted basis, achieving Sharpe ratios up to 1.69, Calmar ratios exceeding 2.2, and maximum drawdowns compressed by 50–79% relative to buy-and-hold allocations. Results are robust across the 5–30 day lookback range, demonstrating that retail attention dynamics between technology stocks and cryptocurrency represent exploitable structure amenable to systematic harvesting.

In the modern retail attention economy, Bitcoin and the NASDAQ-100 are not merely separate assets; they are competing narratives. Both appeal to the same pool of speculative capital, the same appetite for asymmetric upside, and the same behavioral forces of FOMO, herding, and recency bias. When technology stocks dominate the imagination, capital clusters around QQQ and the artificial intelligence trade. When Bitcoin breaks out, the crowd’s attention pivots toward crypto’s promise of explosive upside.

This paper tests whether that rotation in attention leaves a systematic footprint. Using Donchian breakout signals across QQQ and Bitcoin, with cash as a fallback during periods of consolidation, we examine whether investors can harvest momentum without remaining permanently exposed to either asset’s full drawdown profile. The results suggest that the answer is yes: retail attention does not move randomly. It rotates, it concentrates, and—when measured through price breakouts—it can be systematically exploited.

title: Show Your Work: Paystub Requirements and Wage Theft
affiliations: University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business and University of Washington

detail.title: Show Your Work: Paystub Requirements and Wage Theft
detail.abstract: Wage theft costs workers in the U.S. billions of dollars annually. Paystubs include information critical for identifying and investigating wage theft, yet many states do not require firms to provide them. We ask whether requiring firms to disclose paystubs to employees deters wage theft. Using state-level variation in paystub disclosure requirements and geographic variation of firms' establishments across states, we find that when establishments are required to provide paystubs, they are less likely to underpay their workers for overtime hours. This relation exists whether the requirement comes directly from the establishment's state or indirectly via the firm's headquarter state. Further, the relation is stronger when enforcement is more robust, labor market competition is lower, and wage information is more complex. Our findings suggest a gap in federal labor regulations and support the value of disclosure to employees for disciplining managers.

title: Risk and Return in Government Bonds
affiliations: Boston College, National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), University of Chicago - Harris School of Public Policy and Harvard University - Business School (HBS)

detail.title: Risk and Return in Government Bonds
detail.abstract: As the risks of government bonds vary over time, does the compensation that investors require for holding them change? While realized excess returns show little relation to bond risk, we find that subjective expected excess returns constructed from professional forecasts of future long-term yields are tightly linked to bonds' stock market betas, consistent with a CAPM-style relation. In a U.S. month-by-maturity panel from 1988-2024, the correlation of subjective excess returns with rolling bond-stock betas is 66%. The estimated market price of risk is comparable to the equity premium and stable when controlling for time and maturity fixed effects. Realized excess returns are predicted by subjective excess returns, but this predictability is driven by higher-frequency variation and not by betas. Similar results hold in an international panel of developed countries from 1989-2024. The change in betas from positive to negative accounts for half of the decline in long-term U.S. Treasury yields from the 1980s to the 2010s and implies a negative term premium as early as 2001. During quantitative easing episodes, the price of bond risk declines, suggesting an increased investor willingness to bear risk.

title: Capability Compression and Combinatorial Creativity: How Software-Defined Manufacturing Bypasses the Network Dependence of Complex Innovation

detail.title: Capability Compression and Combinatorial Creativity: How Software-Defined Manufacturing Bypasses the Network Dependence of Complex Innovation
detail.abstract:
Complex innovation concentrates in large, well-connected cities because the

non-fungible capabilities it requires are geographically distributed and costly to access [1,

2]. Regions that lack these specific capabilities must either accumulate them locally over

long periods or rely on intercity network links — creating a connectivity dependence that

constrains where complex goods can be produced [3, 4]. We argue that general-purpose

manufacturing platforms disrupt this connectivity dependence through capability

compression — embedding multiple, previously distributed non-fungible capabilities into a

single, small-footprint tool. Specifically, we examine a digitally programmable pulsed-laser

nanomanufacturing system that synthesizes functional materials directly from molecular

precursors at ambient conditions. One desktop-scale platform produces nonequilibrium

metals, photonic structures, micro-batteries, and catalyst nanoparticles — products whose

conventional fabrication requires separate cleanrooms, foundries, and specialized facilities

concentrated in a handful of global hubs. An integrated uncertainty-aware machine

learning framework predicts material outcomes from precursor-pulse inputs, compressing

not only physical infrastructure but also the tacit process knowledge normally locked

within networks of specialized engineers — adding a software complexity dimension that

makes the compressed capabilities transmissible and updatable [5]. This dual compression

— of physical infrastructure and non-fungible know-how into software — lowers the

activation cost of recombinant search in the product space, yielding combinatorial

creativity: the number of novel capability-product experiments a local actor can execute

per unit time and capital. By expanding combinatorial creativity, capability compression

enables deep-tech startups and university laboratories in emerging innovation ecosystems

to explore complex product categories without legacy infrastructure or sequential 

capability accumulation. We derive three testable predictions: (i) adopting regions will

exhibit positive innovation scaling residuals unexplained by population or connectivity,

entering complex technology classes faster than relatedness density predicts; (ii) the

product space will develop new short-range links between previously distant technological

clusters; (iii) a region’s entry rate into novel patent subclasses will scale with the platform’s

ML-navigable chemical programmability. We discuss implications for distributed

manufacturing policy and non-sequential industrialization pathways.

title: Digital Work, Earnings Premiums, and the Gender Gap: Evidence from Pakistan's Labour Force Survey 2024–25
affiliations: and Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS)
