detail.title: Digital Work, Earnings Premiums, and the Gender Gap: Evidence from Pakistan's Labour Force Survey 2024–25
detail.abstract: Digital labor platforms and online work are rapidly growing in Pakistan, yet rigorous empirical evidence on the effect of this growth on Wages is very scarce. This paper uses the recent Labor Force Survey 2024- 2025, the first national dataset to separately identify online and digital workers, to examine three related questions: whether digital work generates a wage premium over traditional employment, whether this premium differs by gender, and the characteristics of individuals to predict entry into digital work. Using Mincer's equation, OLS regression on a restricted sample of 24406 workers, this research estimates a premium for digital work while controlling for age, gender, education, and job characteristics. The findings reveal that the conditional earnings premium is a 6.97%. Heterogeneity analysis across gender shows that digital work does not bridge the gender wage gap, as women face 22.5% earning penalty in both digital and physical work. Platform analysis shows differences in premiums for different kinds of online jobs. The probit model shows that people with higher education, especially those with higher computer qualifications and living in urban areas, have a significant increase in probability of entering and participating in the digital labor market. Overall, the findings suggest that while digital work is associated with higher earnings, its benefits are uneven across workers and types of online employment.

title: The Human Victim Defense Framework: Legal Architecture for Autonomous AI Harm

detail.title: The Human Victim Defense Framework: Legal Architecture for Autonomous AI Harm

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper. The author holds a full-time position at a technology company in Bahrain unrelated to the subject matter of this paper, and this paper was prepared independently, outside that role and without its involvement, review, or endorsement. XWHYZ Solutions FZC LLC and its WHYLD Research Division, under which this paper is published, are independent of and have no financial relationship with the author's employer.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper presents a legal and policy analysis and does not involve human subjects, human data, animal subjects, or the collection of primary empirical data of any kind. No ethics committee or institutional review board approval was required or sought, as none of the conditions triggering such review (human participants, identifiable personal data, clinical or behavioral experimentation) apply to this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding from any funding agency, commercial entity, or not-for-profit organization. The work was conducted independently and self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract:
No existing legal, institutional, technical, or evidentiary framework — in any jurisdiction, patent database, academic record, or standards body — addresses the defense of human victims against autonomous AI harm across five required dimensions simultaneously: pre-crystallization victim standing, behavioral identity continuity, longitudinal trajectory evidence, refusal-capable institutional design, and surrogate drift liability attribution. Each dimension was confirmed absent through systematic research conducted across SSRN, Google Scholar, WIPO PatentScope, USPTO, and legislative trackers spanning EU, US, UK, Singapore, UAE, and GCC jurisdictions through May 2026.

This paper presents the Human Victim Defense Framework — the first complete architecture addressing all five dimensions. The framework encodes ten hypotheses, nine operational mechanisms, ten coined terms, and one new professional archetype across a closed-loop interdependent architecture in which every mechanism feeds every other. No mechanism creates new enforcement authority. Every mechanism activates, anchors to, or routes through existing legal infrastructure. The framework is model law ready and technology-agnostic by constitutional design.

The framework is grounded in two published foundational works. The ASI Governance Canon provides the governing design principles: non-dominance as first-order invariant, constraint-before-capability, and refusal-to-act as a safety primitive. The Temporal Stewardship Synthetic Integrity framework provides the temporal architecture: longitudinal behavioral drift as the central failure mode, witness-not-authority as the correct stewardship posture, and monitor-only as the safe operating mode. The Universal Cognitive Schema provides the live technical substrate for behavioral identity continuity at protocol level.

The framework requires one legislative action to begin operationalization: a jurisdiction willing to pilot the Mandatory Behavioral Baseline Declaration registry. Everything else follows from that single founding decision.

title: The Case for Globally Beneficial Technology
affiliations: and Carnegie Mellon University

detail.title: The Case for Globally Beneficial Technology

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I.G. and A.K. are both employees of Google DeepMind.

detail.abstract: To whom do the fruits of advanced technological innovation belong? To their inventors, to the organizations and individuals involved in making such discoveries possible, or to still larger groups of people, potentially encompassing all of humanity? This question sits at the heart of the present investigation. The arguments developed here focus on an expansive reading of the entitlement to benefit from technological breakthroughs: we argue that they should be designed, developed, and distributed in ways that benefit everyone. This central claim, which encompasses technologies such as advanced forms of artificial intelligence, is grounded in an exploration of five moral arguments that involve human rights, beneficence, contingencies of birth, the global tree of knowledge, and global economic justice. Taken together, they underpin the argument for globally beneficial technologies.

title: From Ruin to Renewal: Turning Floods into Engines of Transformation

detail.title: From Ruin to Renewal: Turning Floods into Engines of Transformation
detail.abstract: This study extends the classic Solow-Swan growth model to explore how the reconstruction of capital after major floods shapes Pakistan's long-term economic growth. The model divides total capital into three key components-traditional, modern, and human capital-to reflect the structural diversity of Pakistan's economy. Floods are introduced as sudden external shocks that damage these forms of capital differently, disrupting the pace of recovery and future growth. The analysis shows that when post-flood rebuilding focuses mainly on traditional capital, such as housing and basic infrastructure, short-term recovery occurs but long-run growth remains limited due to low technological progress. In contrast, reconstruction that also strengthens modern and human capital-through investment in technology, industry, and education-leads to higher productivity and long-run economic growth. The findings suggest that Pakistan's recovery from floods is not just about rebuilding what was lost, but about investing smarter in what can sustain future development. The study concludes by emphasizing the importance of balanced and forward-looking reconstruction policies, such as the Twin Capital Reconstruction (TCR) Program, whereby budget allocation towards rebuilding capital in a flood-affected economy should have a fixed proportion diverted towards investments in modern and human capital, alongside traditional capital, so as to ensure long-term growth.

title:
When the Scaffold Stays On:
 AI, Practice Style, and Screening in Elite Skill Formation

detail.title:
When the Scaffold Stays On:
 AI, Practice Style, and Screening in Elite Skill Formation
detail.abstract: Generative AI raises short-term productivity by completing tasks that learners would otherwise practice on their own. Whether this exchange erodes frontier skill depends on the mode of use: substitute-users let AI stand in for deliberate practice and fail to develop skill, while complement-users use it to accelerate skill development. For institutions that train and certify talent, the design question is not whether to allow AI but how to govern the mode of its use. We ask whether AI-prohibited evaluation gates can separate the two modes. In elite competitive programming, the International Collegiate Programming Contest (ICPC) and the International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI) prohibit AI under in-person proctoring, with qualification-round entry, whereas Codeforces (CF) practice is unproctored and open to all. From CF submission histories we build an AI-prompt signature, more first-attempt acceptances, fewer attempts, fewer debugging retries, consistent with AI-assisted practice. CF practice has shifted toward this signature across entry cohorts spanning two AI rollouts. In CF contests, a stronger signature predicts smaller rating gains for users with no ICPC-IOI affiliation, but not for those who qualified. Inside the AI-prohibited ICPC environment, a shift toward AI-style practice predicts higher non-AI-aided scores for AI-era entrants. The same signature carries opposite signs across the two environments, exactly the pattern a type-separating gate predicts. The message is constructive: AI-style practice is compatible with frontier skill; the erosion risk links to the substitute mode; and that mode is separable by gates standard at credential boundaries, from medical and legal boards to professional certification.

title: Reconciling Health Care Split-Payment Frictions: Extending Longitudinal Capitation to Fee-for-Service Markets for Optimal Social Efficiency

detail.title: Reconciling Health Care Split-Payment Frictions: Extending Longitudinal Capitation to Fee-for-Service Markets for Optimal Social Efficiency

declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: A growing number of states are adopting the AHEAD framework to address the healthcare spending crisis. This framework combines hospital global budgets and capitation with a largely unmitigated fee-for-service (FFS) sector across disparate payment architectures. While this design provides direct institutional cost savings, it induces strategic stinting of care and asymmetric spillovers between the capitated and FFS frameworks, culminating in substantial social welfare losses. This paper develops an institutional mechanism design framework to reconcile the systemic inefficiencies of these split-payment frictions, eliminating these welfare losses to recover the socially optimal frontier. We prove that the structural principles of Longitudinal Capitation can be extended directly to an open FFS payment architecture to regain volume control and establish optimal social efficiency. Although Maryland currently faces split-payment alignment inefficiencies, as the pioneer of this system, it possesses the turn-key infrastructure required to adopt the longitudinal framework developed herein and finally achieve its long-sought health efficiency gains. Ultimately, Maryland's regulatory infrastructure provides a scalable blueprint for other Reconciling Split-Payment Frictions 2 states, particularly those participating in the AHEAD demonstration, to actualize the optimal social efficiency of healthcare provision.

title: The Silver Economy and Regional Transformation: Population Ageing as a Driver of China's Regional Coordinated Development

detail.title: The Silver Economy and Regional Transformation: Population Ageing as a Driver of China's Regional Coordinated Development
detail.abstract: Population ageing is conventionally framed as a fiscal and social burden, yet its spatial economic implications for regional development remain underexplored. This paper proposes a conceptual framework that reconceptualizes the ageing transition as a potential catalyst for regional economic restructuring and convergence. Drawing on theories of the demographic transition, consumption-based growth, and industrial upgrading, the analysis identifies four mechanisms through which the silver economy can contribute to regional coordinated development: the spatial redistribution of care and health industries toward lower-cost regions, the revitalization of rural and peripheral areas through age-friendly migration and retirement settlements, the upgrading of traditional manufacturing toward gerontechnology and assistive devices, and the creation of new interregional fiscal and service-sharing arrangements. The paper situates these mechanisms within China's evolving regional policy landscape, examining how provinces and cities are developing silver economy clusters, cross-regional elderly care collaborations, and age-friendly urban and rural environments. It further discusses the institutional preconditions for leveraging ageing as a development opportunity, including portable social security, the integration of health and care systems, and the cultivation of a skilled care workforce. The study concludes that harnessing the silver economy represents a shift in regional policy thinking from viewing demographic change as an external shock to be absorbed toward recognizing it as an endogenous force that can be shaped and channeled for spatial equity.

title: Institutional Trust and Willingness to Pay for Environmental Protection
affiliations: , Ege University and Afyon Kocatepe University

detail.title: Institutional Trust and Willingness to Pay for Environmental Protection

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no conflict of interest in this research
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this paper

detail.abstract: Designing effective fiscal instruments for sustainability requires understanding the political drivers of public support. While environmental concern is vital, it is often insufficient to generate support for costly policies like taxation. Institutional trust serves as the critical bridge translating values into a willingness to pay (WTP). Drawing on cross-national data from the World Values Survey (Waves 5 and 6) and utilizing multilevel cumulative link mixed models, this study disaggregates institutional confidence into trust in parliament, government, corporations, and environmental organizations. We further assess how democratic quality proxied by parliamentary confidence and democratic orientation conditions these dynamics. Our findings reveal that confidence in democratic representative institutions, particularly parliament, is the most robust predictor of WTP for environmental protection. This factor consistently outperforms trust in government performance, corporate actors, and environmental groups. Interestingly, while trust in environmental organizations boosts concern, it does not increase fiscal support. This illustrates a conceptual gap between environmental awareness and financial commitment. Moreover, the influence of government trust diminishes over time which highlights the enduring importance of stable democratic legitimacy. This study clarifies how specific trust mechanisms shape preferences for collective action. The results underscore a clear policy imperative: building democratic legitimacy is foundational to securing public acceptance of the costly fiscal strategies necessary for sustainability. By providing robust empirical evidence, this study positions institutional trust as the cornerstone of sustainable environmental policy.

title: Bridging the Gap between Alleviation and Equity: An Evaluation of Kenya's Consolidated Social Protection Fund and the Limits of Cash Transfers
affiliations: Maseno University and Maseno University

detail.title: Bridging the Gap between Alleviation and Equity: An Evaluation of Kenya's Consolidated Social Protection Fund and the Limits of Cash Transfers
detail.abstract: This paper critically evaluates Kenya's Consolidated Social Protection Fund. Anchored by the Inua Jamii programme and the Cash Transfer for Orphans and Vulnerable Children (CT-OVC) as an instrument for addressing poverty and inequality. Drawing on theoretical contributions and empirical literature on social protection and inequality, alongside empirical evidence from Kenya's household surveys, Food and Agricultural Organization (FAO) Transfer Project evaluations, and comparative data from South Africa and Brazil, the paper argues that Kenya's fund is a necessary but structurally insufficient tool for achieving distributional equity. Micro-level evidence confirms meaningful gains in food security, consumption, and local economic activity among beneficiaries, yet Kenya's Gini coefficient has remained stubbornly elevated. Declining modestly from 0.470 in 2005/06 to 0.404 in 2015/16 before stagnating, while income-based estimates place it as high as 51.3 as of 2019 (Damiano et al., 2023; Mbara, 2024). The paper concludes that closing the gap between alleviation and equity requires systematic integration of social protection with progressive taxation, labour market reform, and institutional capacity investment.

title: FinGraph: A Free, Browser-Based Platform for Network Visualization and Econometric Analysis of Firm Financial-Statement Data

detail.title: FinGraph: A Free, Browser-Based Platform for Network Visualization and Econometric Analysis of Firm Financial-Statement Data

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a methodological software paper; no human or animal subjects were involved, and all computation runs client-side on the user's own data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. FinGraph was independently developed.

detail.abstract: Empirical research on firms increasingly draws on large financial-statement panels, yet the tooling remains fragmented: network exploration lives in one program, panel econometrics in another, forensic accounting diagnostics in a third, and most require programming skill, paid licences, or the upload of proprietary data to remote servers. This paper introduces FinGraph, a free, single-page web application that unifies exploratory network analysis and a broad suite of econometric and accounting-research methods for firm-year financial data, and that runs entirely in the user's browser so that data never leave the machine. From an uploaded panel FinGraph automatically recognises the column conventions of major data providers (Compustat/WRDS, CRSP, CSMAR, Refinitiv Worldscope/Datastream) and derives labels, financial ratios and distress scores. It then supports: correlation and partial-correlation (Gaussian graphical model) networks with false-discovery-rate and backbone filtering and community detection; firm peer networks; a descriptive dashboard; panel regression with pooled OLS, fixed effects, random effects, Fama-MacBeth estimation and cluster-robust standard errors; a regression-diagnostics suite and a robust fixed-versus-random-effects test; moderation and mediation; quasi-experimental designs (difference-indifferences and event study, instrumental variables, propensity-score matching, regression discontinuity, and the Callaway-Sant'Anna staggered-adoption estimator); bankruptcy and earnings-quality scores; discretionary-accruals earnings-management models and a Benford's-law screen; principal component analysis and firm clustering; quantile regression and specification-curve robustness analysis; and machine-learning prediction. Every estimator was validated against data generated from known processes and against standard reference formulae. FinGraph lowers the barrier to rigorous, reproducible financial-statement research while preserving data privacy, and is offered with a citable version and an open licence.

title: Demand for PCAOB Reports and Audit Firm Disclosures: Perspectives of Audit Committee Members
affiliations: Arizona State University, Arizona State University (ASU) - School of Accountancy, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and University of Oklahoma

detail.title: Demand for PCAOB Reports and Audit Firm Disclosures: Perspectives of Audit Committee Members
detail.abstract: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act charges audit committees (ACs) with overseeing external auditors on behalf of investors, yet little is known about how AC members (ACMs) use audit performance information or what additional information they demand. We survey 342 ACMs of U.S. publicly traded companies and conduct 35 semi-structured interviews with ACMs, audit partners, and investors. Interpreting results through agency theory, we find that ACMs overwhelmingly view PCAOB information as relevant to their oversight—yet passively rely on auditors to provide it rather than proactively seek it. ACMs prioritize audit partner responsiveness, expertise, and communication skills over all audit firm-level metrics when evaluating auditors. They express strong demand for engagement-level disclosures—including auditor feedback on management competence—that no regulation currently requires auditors to provide. ACMs view the PCAOB’s most important role as communicating directly to ACs, not investors. These findings inform the calibration of audit quality disclosure requirements and PCAOB communication strategy.

title: DisclosureBeta: LLM Risk Disclosures as Noisy Measurement Channels for Forward Betas

detail.title: DisclosureBeta: LLM Risk Disclosures as Noisy Measurement Channels for Forward Betas
detail.abstract: For a firm whose price history is too short to trust-about to list, a recent listing, or a name just past a regime break-the beta a desk needs cannot be estimated the usual way, and the state-of-the-art fallback is a comparable-firm peer beta with no error budget; the recent text-based competitor (Breitung, 2025) reports strong empirical IPO accuracy but no identification theory, error budget, or lower bound. We fill that gap. We show that a beta read from the firm's own risk disclosures beats the peer beta where it matters: on a frozen, balanced panel of 180 S-1/F-1-gated IPO and recent-listing events (2019-2024), the disclosure-read beta lowers average squared beta error against the desk-relevant peer beta (1.040 vs. 1.055; paired-bootstrap 95% CI [-0.026,-0.003] for text-minus-peer; one-sided p = 0.005), robust to median, trimmed, Vasicek-shrunk, peer-history-shrunk, and cheap-text controls. The effect is an average-error reduction, not event-by-event dominance (the sign test is weak, 95/180). We obtain the estimator by treating the language model not as a black-box feature extractor but as a noisy measurement channel on latent firm risk, and writing its channel noise into the asset-pricing error budget. The estimator conditions Fama-French five-factor loadings on an inferred market regime and on the read disclosures; theorems identify the regime-conditional beta function, bound its error by nonparametric sampling error, detector misclassification, and measured channel noise, and a variance-weighted blend collapses to the rolling beta for stable long-history firms while shifting to text exactly when price history is short or stale. The long-history control behaves as it should-on mature mega-caps, own price history remains the wall and text is a near-tie-and an ensemble-reader audit supplies the mechanism. We make no claim that "LLMs beat prices"; the contribution is an identified, auditable way to read disclosures as a forward-beta measurement channel, and the economic payoff is a market-calibrated discount rate for firms that today have only a peer beta.

reference: Umair Ahmad, Uzma Chaudhry & Maddy Nash, "Pakistan and the FATF Grey List – Part A," Harvard Law School Case Studies Program, No. CSP-073-A (September 2025)
title: Pakistan and the FATF Grey List – Part A
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and

detail.title: Pakistan and the FATF Grey List – Part A

publicationDetails.detailsText: Umair Ahmad, Uzma Chaudhry & Maddy Nash, "Pakistan and the FATF Grey List – Part A," Harvard Law School Case Studies Program, No. CSP-073-A (September 2025)

detail.abstract: This case study, prepared in the form of an internal government memorandum, examines Pakistan's engagement with the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) and its placement on FATF's "grey list" of jurisdictions under increased monitoring. Framed as a briefing memo dated April 2022 from Pakistan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the case asks readers to develop policy recommendations for a newly appointed Federal Cabinet on how Pakistan can achieve and sustain compliance with FATF's anti-money laundering (AML) and countering the financing of terrorism (CFT) standards. The case provides background on FATF's institutional structure, its evaluation methodology, and the process by which jurisdictions move on and off the grey list, before tracing Pakistan's specific regulatory history with FATF from 2008 to 2022 — including its removal from the list in 2015, its re-listing in 2018, and its subsequent progress toward compliance with a 27-point (later 34-point) action plan. It examines structural factors that have historically facilitated money laundering and terrorism financing in Pakistan, including regional instability, exploitation of the charitable/NGO sector, narcotics trafficking, exploitation of natural resources, kidnapping and human trafficking, and informal value transfer systems such as hawala/hundi. The case also surfaces the political dimensions of the FATF listing process, including allegations from Pakistani officials that the process has been politicized. Students are asked to grapple with the practical, political, and constitutional (Article 10A fair trial rights) challenges Pakistan faces in completing its remaining compliance obligations and to propose recommendations for exiting the grey list and avoiding future re-listing.

title: Terrain-Conditioned Diffusion for Law-Compatible Housing Siting: A Case Study in the Zurich Agglomeration

detail.title: Terrain-Conditioned Diffusion for Law-Compatible Housing Siting: A Case Study in the Zurich Agglomeration
detail.abstract: Zurich's housing market is among the tightest in Europe. The conventional supply response, outward extension of the building zone, is largely precluded by Swiss planning law, which mandates inward development on land that is already zoned and accessible by public transport. This paper examines whether a terrain-conditioned diffusion model, trained to extend small settlements in hilly terrain, can inform the siting of new housing under these constraints. The published model is executed in the browser on Uster, a municipality in the Zürcher Oberland, using elevation from AWS Terrain Tiles and building and road geometry from OpenStreetMap for a 1.9 km window. The model allocates approximately 1.4 km 2 of new development, concentrating low and medium density residential use on the southeastern terraces and assigning no growth to the western sector, where the town abuts Lake Greifensee. The allocation is consistent with the sectors available for expansion under cantonal land protection. We embed the model in a protected-land mask and a four-stage screening procedure that links its output to the cantonal structure plan, the value-capture levy, and the municipal non-profit housing target. The paper describes the procedure, reports the case result, extends the reading to adjacent municipalities, and discusses the limitations of using a generative model for planning support.

title: Order Flow and Cryptocurrency Returns: A Machine Learning Approach with Out-of-Sample Validation
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Maulana Azad National Institute of Technology, Bhopal

detail.title: Order Flow and Cryptocurrency Returns: A Machine Learning Approach with Out-of-Sample Validation
detail.abstract: The results indicate that overall order flow plays a significant role in explaining variations in cryptocurrency returns. Using machine learning for out-of-sample predictions, we demonstrate that order flow is an effective predictor of daily cryptocurrency returns. Portfolio strategies that rely on machine-learning forecasts based on daily order flow achieve an alpha of up to 0.86% per day and a Sharpe ratio of 3.97 annually. Order flow outperforms economic fundamentals in predicting returns, especially when nonlinear machine learning models conditioned on order flow are used, demonstrating strong out-of-sample predictive power beyond arbitrage limits. In addition to statistical analysis, we assess the economic value of conditioning on order flow through portfolio sorting. Overall, our findings suggest that order flow consistently influences cryptocurrency returns.

title: The Limitation of Language in Intimate Relation

detail.title: The Limitation of Language in Intimate Relation
detail.abstract: This paper proposes that language has a limit, and that the limit is generative. Across six dimensions of relational life, its existence, its maintenance, the value it generates, its ethics, its justice, and its evolution, there is in each case a core that language reaches toward and cannot reach. The paper sets out these six limits, each as a claim of its own, and then argues that what stands at the limit is drive in the psychoanalytic sense. Drive is not a content language omits and might recover; it is the phenomenology of manque, the gap between the symbolic and the Real that resists complete symbolization. This gap has two faces, a pre-symbolic remainder cut off when the subject enters language and a resulting impossibility of closure, and they are one. Around it drive circles and desire slides. By a thought experiment the paper shows that closing the gap would extinguish rather than fulfill them, so that the non-closure of language is the condition of their persistence. It then follows drive into the time of relation and draws out the generativity of the limit in the poem, in an ethics without possession, and in a justice that guards what it cannot settle, with a coalgebraic and reduction-theoretic counterpart offered as a heuristic. The paper offers no final synthesis; its form enacts its content.

title: Economic Impact of Domestic Natural Gas Market Regulation on Nigeria's Urea Fertilizer Industry and Global Industrial Competitiveness
affiliations: University of Port Harcourt

detail.title: Economic Impact of Domestic Natural Gas Market Regulation on Nigeria's Urea Fertilizer Industry and Global Industrial Competitiveness
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the economic impact of domestic natural gas market regulation on Nigeria's urea fertilizer industry and its implications for global industrial competitiveness. Natural gas constitutes 70 to 90 percent of urea production costs, rendering gas pricing policy a determinative variable in the competitiveness of nitrogen fertilizer producers. Nigeria, endowed with approximately 209 trillion cubic feet of proven gas reserves, the largest in Africa, has implemented a tiered domestic pricing framework under the Petroleum Industry Act (PIA) 2021 and the Gas Pricing and Domestic Demand Regulations (GPDDR) 2023, prescribing a subsidised feedstock price band of USD 0.90 to USD 2.42 per MMBTU for gas-based industrial users. Through regulatory analysis, cost-structure analysis, and comparative industry benchmarking, this study evaluates whether Nigeria's gas pricing regime translates into sustained cost competitiveness for its principal urea producers: Dangote Fertiliser Limited, Indorama Eleme Fertilizer and Chemicals Limited (IEFCL), and Notore Chemical Industries. Key findings reveal a structurally contradictory regulatory landscape: while the regulated feedstock price represents one of the most competitive globally, persistent gas supply unreliability, evidenced by Dangote Fertiliser's capacity utilisation declining to 32 percent in 2022 (Agusto & Co., 2024), effectively negates the cost advantage embedded in the pricing framework. The paper identifies rent asymmetry between gas producers and downstream fertilizer manufacturers, chronic infrastructure financing gaps, and the tension between domestic supply obligations and export parity pricing preferences as systemic impediments. Policy recommendations centre on supply reliability mechanisms, long-term indexed gas supply agreements, strategic industrial gas reserve policy, and a Gas-for-Equity arrangement under which upstream gas producers receive equity stakes in fertilizer enterprises in exchange for long-term supply commitments.

title:
Buddhist Philosophy in Dialogue with Western Thought: 
Core Concepts and Comparative Perspectives
affiliations: Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology

detail.title:
Buddhist Philosophy in Dialogue with Western Thought: 
Core Concepts and Comparative Perspectives
detail.abstract: This paper examines the encounter between Buddhist and Western philosophical traditions across ontology, epistemology, causation, ethics, philosophy of mind, and soteriology. Adopting Matilal's principle of "double vision", fidelity to each tradition's internal logic while allowing cross-traditional interrogation, it treats Buddhist philosophy, drawn from Abhidharma, Madhyamaka, Yogācāra, and Pramāṇa traditions, as a living interlocutor rather than an exotic relic or mere religious mysticism. The analysis demonstrates that core Buddhist doctrines such as anattā (non-self), śūnyatā (emptiness), and patītyasamutpāda (dependent origination) provide rigorous, argument-driven alternatives to the substance-based and essentialist frameworks that have dominated large swaths of the Western canon. Comparative engagements with figures including Hume, Kant, Heidegger, Schopenhauer, and contemporary analytic philosophers reveal both striking structural convergences and irreducible philosophical divergences. Crucially, the paper argues that Buddhist philosophy's defining and distinctive feature is its thoroughgoing embeddedness within a soteriological project (salvation, liberation, or ultimate freedom from dissatisfaction), the diagnosis and cessation of unsatisfactory (dukkha), which consistently orients its metaphysical, epistemological, and ethical analyses toward practical liberation rather than purely theoretical self-clarification. While Western traditions have independently arrived at analogous critiques of substantial selfhood and static essences, they seldom embed these within a comprehensive therapeutic framework. The paper concludes that comparative philosophy, properly practiced, is neither assimilation into foreign categories nor uncritical syncretism, but a sustained, mutually transformative conversation that clarifies the distinctive contributions of each tradition while generating genuinely new philosophical problems.

title: Optimization Theory and Rationality in Intimate Relations

detail.title: Optimization Theory and Rationality in Intimate Relations
detail.abstract:
This paper argues that optimization is not a law of the universe, and that morality and the manner of being of intimate relation are not, in their structure, optimization problems. It proceeds in two movements that it is careful to keep apart. The first is a formal proof, carrying no value judgment, that intimate relation furnishes no well-defined optimization problem: the value at stake is in part non-structurable, since the drive, which any complete objective must include, resists representation as a term; it is relational, generated within the relation and existing only there, so that no external standpoint could fix the objective; it is incommensurable, so that to price certain goods is to betray rather than mismeasure them; and the subject is constituted within the relation rather than given before it, so that the optimizer the model presupposes is a product of the process it is meant to stand outside of. Each failure strikes a distinct precondition, and any one leaves the operation of maximization undefined.

The second movement takes that result as given and criticizes the imposition of the frame regardless. To optimize where no optimization problem exists converts a value that should circulate into one that can be settled and drawn off, in the manner the theory of generative justice names as extractive computation; it is a symptom of the crisis of the symbolic and of a life-world habituated to the logic of capital, under which a local, historical operation is projected onto the cosmos as its law; and it mistakes the kind of thing morality is, since an optimizing practice, even a successful one, may fail as an ethics, the optimal and the good being orthogonal. The paper then recovers a rationality that responds rather than maximizes, described through response, attunement, and the sustaining of generation, and it closes in polyphony, refusing to name a new master objective, since to do so would reinstate the frame. That refusal is the paper's positive claim, enacted in its form.

title: The Dual Conscience Greenium in Green Sukuk: First Global Empirical Evidence on Shariah-ESG Dual Screening Pricing

detail.title: The Dual Conscience Greenium in Green Sukuk: First Global Empirical Evidence on Shariah-ESG Dual Screening Pricing
detail.abstract: This thesis examines whether the simultaneous satisfaction of Islamic law and international environmental standards makes a bond cheaper or more expensive to issue. The study compares green sukuk to conventional sukuk and conventional green bonds within a three-quadrant framework using 5,938 bond observations from 2015 to 2026 across eleven currency markets drawn from LSEG Workspace. The comparison reflects the coupon rate at issuance as the primary outcome. The findings are conditional on time and context. Before 2021, green sukuk carried a small premium reflecting market immaturity. However, after 2021, that reversed into a discount of approximately 21 basis points as dualmandate institutional demand reached a critical threshold. The anticipated Shariah compliance penalty does not survive controlled comparison. Green sukuk price approximately 103 basis points more favorably than conventional green bonds in the full sample and 174 basis points more favorably within key Islamic markets where investors have no substitute instrument. Climate Bonds Initiative certification associated with higher rather than lower coupons. It points to unresolved structural complexity costs. The study contributes to the first simultaneous global estimation of both compliance pricing effects. The study documents a 2021 market development threshold and provides direct counterevidence to the Shariah liquidity penalty hypothesis.

reference: Published for Jean Monnet Centre of Excellence Digi-U
title: A New Way to Look at EU Copyright Law: Regulating Digital Platforms to Promote Education

detail.title: A New Way to Look at EU Copyright Law: Regulating Digital Platforms to Promote Education

publicationDetails.detailsText: Published for Jean Monnet Centre of Excellence Digi-U

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a new way of looking at EU copyright law, shifting the analytical focus from the traditional binary of infringements and exceptions toward the regulation of digital platforms as a means of promoting education. It begins by examining the misalignments that characterise the EU's regulation of digital copyrights, particularly as they affect the public interest in education, access to knowledge, and the safeguarding of the public domain. It then reviews the leading doctrinal proposals advanced to remedy these shortcomings, before introducing its central contribution: a lens that treats specific market actors-notably digital platforms and educational institutions-as strategic regulatory addressees, and even as "regulatory sandboxes", within the EU legal framework. Drawing on the legislative experience of the Copyright in the Digital Single Market Directive, and in particular Articles 5 and 17, the author shows how the EU has assigned tailored obligations, liability schemes, and conditions to online content-sharing platforms and educational institutions. The paper argues that such interventions are not merely redistributive-shifting entitlements between rightholders and users-but jus-generative, establishing new legal relationships, balances, and practices. It concludes that recognising platforms as enablers of copyright rules on educational uses opens a more imaginative and effective avenue for calibrating EU copyright law to contemporary digital realities.

title: Perpetual Futures: Mechanics, History and Purpose
affiliations: Elm Partners and Elm Partners

detail.title: Perpetual Futures: Mechanics, History and Purpose
detail.abstract:
Following the US CFTC's approval of perpetual futures for U.S. markets in mid-2026, this paper explains how these increasingly important derivatives work and traces their origins. Unlike a traditional futures contract, which rolls toward a fixed expiration date and converges to spot price through ordinary arbitrage, a perpetual future never expires. In its place, exchanges rely on a periodic "funding rate" paid directly between long and short position holders to keep the contract's price tethered to the underlying spot price. We walk through the mechanics of this funding rate in detail using Binance's BTC perpetual —  the largest venue for the instrument — including its premium-index calculation, its built-in interest-rate baseline, and the hard caps that bound how far the rate can move in a single settlement window.

We connect our discussion to the academic literature, including He, Manela, Ross, and von Wachter's (2023) "random-maturity arbitrage" framework, which extends standard no-arbitrage pricing to instruments with no fixed maturity, and to Gehr's (1988) and Shiller's (1993) earlier work on undated and perpetual-style contracts. We also place the modern crypto perpetual in a longer historical lineage, tracing a structural precedent back to the Chinese Gold and Silver Exchange Society's century-old undated gold contract in Hong Kong.

Finally, we assess the perpetual structure critically against its alternatives — traditional futures contracts, margin lending, and contracts for difference — and argue that its persistently elevated and highly variable funding costs are not fully explained by conventional risk-based arbitrage limits alone. We offer a speculative account of why the perpetual structure may have been favored over more transparent alternatives, touching on thin early-market liquidity, weak oversight of self-dealing on offshore platforms, and the incentives facing the arbitrage capital that supplies leverage to retail longs on unregulated, offshore platforms.

title: The Extraction of Relational Value in the Cultural Domain: A Lacanian-Psychoanalytic Deconstruction of Political Economy

detail.title: The Extraction of Relational Value in the Cultural Domain: A Lacanian-Psychoanalytic Deconstruction of Political Economy

keywords: Alienation of the Structure of Desire

detail.abstract: Under the symbolic crisis, as the reproduction of signifiers cheapens the sign, value migrates toward relation, which the sign cannot reproduce. A prior work stated the general theory of this migration and of capital's capture of relational value. This paper addresses that capture in the cultural domain, and advances six contributions beyond the prior account. It distinguishes the symbolically guaranteed domain, whose value rests on the scarcity of a sign, from the relational domain, whose value is relational at its root and whose sign is an outer shell, and it argues that the cultural domain, as a relational domain, is reached by the crisis through the stripping of the shell and the exposure of the relational core. It develops the guarantee mechanism, and divinity as the site to which what exceeds the individual is attributed, at the level of a general definition distinguished from its Lacanian and other realizations. As its theoretical center it states the alienation of the structure of desire: capital, unable to reach the drive that circles das Ding, seizes the mediation through which drive is structured, which is culture, and reroutes that structuring toward a commodified object, so that drive is demoted to desire, a movement that is at once, in the register drawn from Marx, alienation. It follows the exclusion this works from an economic into an ontological register, draws out the dialectical point that capital profits because the relation is real, and reaches the ontological claim that capital, having arisen from relation, cannot become a relational subject and can only hold relation as an owner. The paper advances no proposal, and leaves to the reader the recognition of where a given cultural circuit stands and to whom its value returns.

title: Socialism in One Country: Structural Defects and the Break-up of the USSR

detail.title: Socialism in One Country: Structural Defects and the Break-up of the USSR

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. The study is non-institutional and conducted in a personal capacity. Drafts, source verification, literature search, computations on the primary data, and the preparation of code and figures were carried out with the assistance of AI tools (including Claude, Anthropic), under the author's direction and review. All ideas, theses, interpretations, and conclusions are the author's own; AI was not used to generate insights, interpret data, or draw conclusions. Responsibility for every claim, figure, and conclusion rests entirely with the author.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable — the study uses only published aggregate statistical data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: The USSR did not collapse from any single trigger but from the interaction of two structural defects rooted in its founding choice — building socialism in one country by command rather than market. First, administrative pricing left the economy unable to measure its own internal flows: the question of who subsidized whom has no ruler-independent answer and flips sign between domestic and world prices. Second, the ethno-territorial design — fixed by the 1922 Union Treaty and the 1924 Constitution — embedded nations in bordered republics with the right to exit. Drawing on three independent transfer computations (world-price recalculation, budget transfers, long-run capital flows) and the recovered primary Goskomstat 1988 world-price recalculation, the paper shows the RSFSR was the net donor in world prices and in the budget yet roughly balanced in raw domestic prices — its apparent domestic deficit is entirely a foreign-trade artifact of underpriced energy exports that reverses sign under world pricing. The donor direction is robust; its magnitude is an artifact of non-market pricing, and the same measurement defect extends beyond Soviet borders. The dissolution is presented as a structural consequence of the founding choice — an explanatory model, not a theorem. Data and code are open.

title: When the Scaffold Stays On: AI, Practice Style, and Screening in Elite Skill Formation

detail.title: When the Scaffold Stays On: AI, Practice Style, and Screening in Elite Skill Formation
detail.abstract: Generative AI raises short-term productivity by completing tasks that learners would otherwise practice on their own. Whether this exchange erodes frontier skill, the capability required for top-tail performance without AI, depends on the mode of use: substitute-users let AI stand in for deliberate practice and fail to develop skill, while complement-users use it to accelerate skill development. For institutions that train and certify talent, the design question is therefore not whether to allow AI but how to govern the mode of its use. We study one governance mechanism, the AI-prohibited evaluation gate, and ask whether it can separate the two modes. Elite competitive programming provides a test case. The International Collegiate Programming Contest (ICPC) and the International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI) prohibit AI under in-person proctoring and admit entrants through qualification rounds, whereas online Codeforces (CF) practice is unproctored and open to all. From CF submission histories we build an AI-prompt signature, marked by more first-attempt acceptances and fewer attempts and debugging retries, consistent with AI-assisted practice. Three findings follow. CF practice has shifted toward this signature across entry cohorts spanning two AI rollouts. In open CF contests, a stronger signature predicts smaller rating gains for users with no ICPC or IOI affiliation, but not for users who qualified for the AI-prohibited contests. Inside the AI-prohibited ICPC environment, a shift toward AI-style practice predicts higher non-AI-aided scores for AI-era entrants. The same AI-prompt signature carries opposite signs depending on whether the contest screens its entrants through an AI-prohibited qualification gate, exactly the pattern a type-separating gate predicts. The message is constructive: AI-style practice is compatible with frontier skill; the skill erosion risk links to the substitute mode of use; and that mode is separable by the kind of gates already standard at credential boundaries, from medical and legal boards to professional certification.

title: Bayesian Stories: Persuasion, Suggestion, and Mantra
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Bayesian Stories: Persuasion, Suggestion, and Mantra
detail.abstract: We give a predictive-processing account of three phenomena usually treated apart: a rhetorical device from the smoking-cessation literature, the rebound produced by negated instructions, and the contemplative use of mantra. Belief is a precision-weighted posterior. The claim is negative: persuasion and suggestion rarely supply better evidence, and so rarely move a posterior mean. They act instead on the support of a distribution, collapsing it or filling it, or on the precision that weights prior against likelihood. Working in an exponential family, we isolate four generators of belief change, show that translate and reweight move the natural parameter while collapse changes the base measure that carries the support, and prove that bounded evidence can only translate and reweight, never delete. Carr's blank page is the information projection onto the beliefs that vanish on the deleted set, with a Pythagorean cost identity and an irreversibility property. The "no rush" rebound is ironic instantiation, with intrusion increasing in prohibition precision; an appendix derives the monotonicity from precision as gain, and it is the non-commutativity of collapse and fill. Self-hypnosis is offline editing under lowered precision; future pacing is a contraction with a computable stationary law and an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck limit. Mantra realises all three: as iterated pseudo-observation it concentrates a posterior at an explicit rate; as channel occupation it empties one; as serial negation it is a martingale whose limit sits on a non-predicable residual. We give three designs with estimands and a power calculation, and state the limits.

title: More Information, Less PowerField Experimental Evidence on the Effect of InformationProvision on Residential Electricity Consumption
affiliations: Energieinstitut at the Johannes Kepler Universität Linz, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: More Information, Less PowerField Experimental Evidence on the Effect of InformationProvision on Residential Electricity Consumption
detail.abstract: We study the causal effect of digital information provision on household electricityconsumption using a randomized field experiment with a staggered rollout.Households were randomly assigned to an information condition (N = 449), receivingaccess to a smartphone application with feedback on electricity use, costs,emissions, social comparisons, and gamified learning features, or to a controlcondition (N = 443) without app access. We measure electricity consumption usinghigh-frequency smart-meter data for up to 70 weeks after treatment. App accessreduces daily electricity consumption by approximately 4.5–4.7%, with reductionsconcentrated in daytime hours (07:00–22:00), when households have greater scopeto adjust consumption. Point estimates remain negative throughout the observationperiod, but statistical significance is concentrated in the first six months afterrollout. App engagement declines sharply after rollout, and higher engagementis associated with larger and more persistent reductions in consumption. Thefindings suggest that digital feedback can reduce residential electricity demand,but that persistence depends on sustained user attention

title: Pair Trading in Leveraged ETFs: Analysis of a Cross-Jurisdictional Strategy Profitability

detail.title: Pair Trading in Leveraged ETFs: Analysis of a Cross-Jurisdictional Strategy Profitability
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the empirical profitability of a cross-border pairs trading strategy utilizing leveraged Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs) listed in the US and UK that track identical underlying indices and specifically focuses on the pair of TQQQ and LQQ3. Despite the theoretical Law of One Price, we identify persistent short-term price divergences driven by jurisdictional liquidity shifts and time-zone imbalances. Utilizing a Z-score-based mean-reversion model, we demonstrate that these discrepancies offer significant market-neutral alpha, performing consistently in both bullish and bearish regimes. However, we also conduct an analysis of the impacts of transaction costs and bid-ask spreads, which we find can greatly erode profits for retail investors who do not have access to an institutional grade set up with advantage of scale.

title: Treated Records: Policy Reforms and the Administrative Data That Evaluate Them

detail.title: Treated Records: Policy Reforms and the Administrative Data That Evaluate Them
detail.abstract: Empirical economics often evaluates reforms using the programs' own administrative records. When a reform resets the categories, dates, or identifiers those records use, the records become treated: measurement error becomes endogenous to treatment. I develop a treated-records audit and apply it to Risk Rating 2.0, the U.S. flood-insurance repricing. The raw records imply excess exit by legacyflagged policies and excess continuation within cohorts; the audit rejects both. The legacy flag broke: broad incumbent differentials are near zero, the real response sits in pre-reform subsidy classes, and new-entrant selection is a separate margin. Measurement parameters, like behavioral ones, are not policy-invariant.

title: Extended Dividend, Payout, and Return Patterns

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: A modified Campbell-Shiller identity decomposes dividend-price ratios exactly into future stock returns, dividend growth rates, and an adjusted dividend-price ratio. Unfortunately, we have only one history for the US stock market, where dividend-price ratios were limited in range from 1.1% to 8% (with a geometric mean of 3.3%). This paper explores portfolios (and stocks) with much higher dividendprice ratios from about 5% to 77% (geometric mean of 14%). At these much higher yields, portfolio dividend-price ratios predicted future dividend reductions rather than future stock returns. Broader payout ratios-dividends plus share repurchases-behaved similarly.

title: Curriculum-Guided Physics-Informed Neural Networks via Gaussian Mixture Models
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Inner Mongolia University of Science and Technology, Academy of Military Medical Sciences and Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU) - School of Mathematics and Statistics

detail.title: Curriculum-Guided Physics-Informed Neural Networks via Gaussian Mixture Models
detail.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a mesh-free framework for solving partial differential equations (PDEs), yet their training is often plagued by gradient pathologies, spectral bias, and slow convergence on PDEs with strong nonlinearity, sharp gradients, or multiscale features. To address these issues, we propose the curriculum-guided Gaussian mixture PINN (CGMPINN), which couples a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) with dynamic curriculum learning. A GMM is periodically fitted to the PDE residuals to quantify spatiallyvarying learning difficulty; a smooth curriculum then progressively shifts training focus from easy to hard regions, while a precision-based variance modulation suppresses unreliable clusters during early optimization. The dual curriculum is governed by a single shared parameter and can be combined with self-adaptive loss balancing. We further establish three theoretical guarantees for the framework: uniform equivalence between the curriculum-weighted and standard PDE losses, sublinear convergence of the gradient norm undersummable objective drift, and a Rademacher-complexity generalization bound with an explicit weighting-induced bias. Numerical experiments on six benchmark PDEs spanning elliptic, parabolic, hyperbolic, advection-dominated, and nonlinear reaction-diffusion regimes show that CGMPINN consistently attains the lowest relative L2 and maximum absolute errors among all compared methods, reducing the relative L2 error by up to 97.8% over the standard PINN at comparable computational cost.

title: Evaluating Economic Impact of Industrial Parks Development Projects in Ethiopia
affiliations: , Rift Valley University and Industrial Parks Development Corporation

detail.title: Evaluating Economic Impact of Industrial Parks Development Projects in Ethiopia
detail.abstract:
Industrial parks development projects are widely adopted as key instruments for economic transformation in developing countries. In Ethiopia, 32 industrial parks have been established across various zones, special zones, and city administrations, reflecting the government’s strategy to promote industrialization and structural change. This study assesses the factors influencing the economic impact of industrial parks and evaluates their micro- and macroeconomic effects in Ethiopia. Zones and city administrations hosting industrial parks are classified as treated areas, while those without industrial parks are considered control areas.

The study employs both primary and secondary data sources and applies Ordered Probit and Difference-in-Differences (DID) estimation techniques to address the research objectives. The findings indicate that high community commitment, abundant non-financial resources, strong government support, and social capital significantly enhance the economic impact of industrial park development. Conversely, limited skilled labor supply, concentration of industrial parks in urban areas, and outdated technology reduce their effectiveness.

The results further reveal that industrial parks have significantly improved most macroeconomic indicators, except domestic capital formation. Survey responses also indicate strong perceived contributions of industrial parks to employment generation, infrastructure development, environmental protection, and technology transfer. Based on these findings, the study recommends that the government design targeted policy and incentive frameworks to attract domestic investment and enhance the overall developmental impact of industrial parks in Ethiopia.

title: International Banking Flows and Financial Crises

detail.title: International Banking Flows and Financial Crises
detail.abstract: This paper studies the dynamics of capital flows disaggregated by instrument and sector during episodes of different financial crises. We construct a novel indicator of bank inflows and find that they generally contract during twin crises, the simultaneous occurrence of banking and currency crises. This is not observed for other types of capital inflows and other types of crises. We propose a model with financial intermediaries facing financial frictions to rationalize this finding, providing a new explanation based on a feedback loop between bank inflows, bank leverage, and nominal exchange rates that can account for twin crises, and we study how different macroprudential policies can reduce their likelihood. We test sufficient statistics of the model in a discrete choice model of early warning indicators that confirms the theoretical predictions.
