title: Demographic and Socioeconomic Factors Affecting Educational Outcomes of High School Students
affiliations: Purdue University Northwest and Purdue University Northwest

detail.title: Demographic and Socioeconomic Factors Affecting Educational Outcomes of High School Students

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Applied Business and Economics, volume 28, issue 2, 2026[10.33423/jabe.v28i2.8120]

detail.abstract: This study investigates the demographic and socioeconomic determinants of educational outcomes of public high school students in the school districts of Indiana. Using panel data of school enrollment and community-level demographic and socioeconomic characteristics, four empirical models were developed and compared to estimate the impacts of city and school enrollment characteristics on standardized test performance and graduation rates. Findings indicate that household structure, economic disadvantage, and racial/ethnic composition significantly shape educational outcomes. Poverty indicators, family structure, and racial/ethnic enrollment patterns are consistently associated with test performance and graduation rates. Overall, the study demonstrates that educational attainment is significantly shaped by socioeconomic disadvantage and demographic composition.

title: Evaluating Economic Impact of Industrial Parks Development Projects in Ethiopia
affiliations: , Rift Valley University and Industrial Parks Development Corporation

detail.title: Evaluating Economic Impact of Industrial Parks Development Projects in Ethiopia
detail.abstract: The construction and operation of industrial parks development projects are widely used as a major economic development strategy for most policy and decision-makers. Currently, there are 32 industrial parks in different zones, special zones and city administrations in Ethiopia. In this study, those zones and city administrations that have industrial parks in their geographic setting are categorized under treated zones and other zones that have no industrial parks in their geographic settings are categorized under controlled zones. This study aims to assess the factors that affect economic impact of Industrial Parks and to evaluate the micro and macro-economic impact of Industrial Parks Development Projects in Ethiopia. To address these research objectives, the authors used two estimation techniques: Ordered Probit and Difference in Differences (DID) estimation techniques. Both primary and secondary data sources were used to address the research objectives. The finding of the study revealed existence of high community commitment, abundant non-financial resource, tangible government support and good social capital in Ethiopia as the major factors that optimize economic impact of industrial parks development project whereas existence of unskilled labour supply, concentration of Ethiopian Industrial parks in the urban areas and out-dated technology are the major factors that diminish economic impact of Industrial Parks development projects in Ethiopia. The establishment and operation of Industrial Parks Development Projects significantly increased all assessed macro-economic indicators except domestic capital formation. The majority of our respondents strongly agree on the positive role of industrial parks development projects for environmental protection, infrastructure development, employment opportunities generation and technology transfer. Hence, it is highly recommended for the government to design special policies and incentives packages that encourage domestic investors to invest in the Ethiopian industrial parks.

title: Rockets, Feathers, or Neither? Gas-to-Electricity Pass-Through and Its Policy Implications in the Greek Day-Ahead Market

detail.title: Rockets, Feathers, or Neither? Gas-to-Electricity Pass-Through and Its Policy Implications in the Greek Day-Ahead Market
detail.abstract: During the 2022 energy crisis the Greek finance ministry argued that wholesale electricity prices were kept high partly because declines in the imported gas cost passed through to electricity more slowly than increases. If correct, that claim would justify regulating the wholesale price formula. This paper tests it in the day-ahead market Greece has operated under the European Target Model since November 2020. A nonlinear autoregressive distributed lag model links the Dutch TTF gas price to the day-ahead market-clearing price, with carbon, renewable and load controls, over weekly data for 2020-2026. Pass-through is strong and fast, with a long-run elasticity of 0.72 and a half-life under two weeks. It is also symmetric in a sense stronger than a non-rejection: a two-one-sided-tests procedure establishes equivalence of the up-and down-elasticities within a ±0.10 band (p < 0.001), and the design detects gaps as small as 0.02. Threshold cointegration and the Greek import-price benchmark confirm the symmetry, and pass-through is lower after the Alexandroupolis liquefied-natural-gas terminal's commissioning date, consistent with import diversification. The policy implication is direct: the downward rigidity consumers experienced did not originate in the wholesale market, so a mandate forcing faster wholesale pass-through targets a problem the data do not show. The effective levers are standardised disclosure of the retail adjustment clause and a subsidy design that offsets the price level without blunting the transmission of subsequent declines. These measures serve the affordability dimension of Sustainable Development Goal 7.

title: A Nonparametric Test for Intraday Variation in Systematic Price Staleness
affiliations: Jinan University, University of Macau and Jinan University - College of Economics

detail.title: A Nonparametric Test for Intraday Variation in Systematic Price Staleness
detail.abstract: We propose a nonparametric test for intraday variation in systematic price staleness. We view systematic price staleness as a market-wide component in very small price adjustments across assets. The main statistical test assesses whether systematic staleness remains constant within a trading day after removing a regular time-of-day pattern. Under infill and long-span asymptotics, the statistic is asymptotically standard normal under the null and consistent against fixed alternatives. Simulations show good size and power. Using oneminute data for nine U.S. sector SPDR ETFs from 2020 to 2025, the raw test rejects on 99.92% of regular trading days, while the diurnally corrected test rejects on 12.72%; 9.50% remain significant after a false-discovery rate control. Corrected rejections are more common during market stress and policy-event windows and on days with higher cross-ETF correlation, large market moves, and higher trading volume. The test provides a simple diagnostic for intraday patterns in market-wide price staleness.

title: FDI, Biased Technical Change, and the Elusive Labor Market Power
affiliations: , Peking University, Peking University - School of Economics and INSE at Peking University

detail.title: FDI, Biased Technical Change, and the Elusive Labor Market Power

declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant Nos. 72322007, 72503230, and 72203006) and the Research Seed Fund of the School of Economics, Peking University.

detail.abstract: FDI liberalization can induce factor-biased technological change, affecting how labormarket power is inferred from production data. We examine this issue in China's 2009-2016 liberalization with firm-level data and a framework in which foreign capital shifts labor-augmenting technology. By ruling out factor-biased technological change, Hicks-neutral methods may attribute technology-driven movements in labor cost shares to wage markdowns, overstating monopsony power and reversing the estimated effect in some specifications. Separating biased technology from markdowns, we find that liberalization lowers wage markdowns and raises labor-augmenting productivity. The markdown decline is broad, while productivity gains are strongest where foreign capital complements labor. Quantitatively, labor-augmenting upgrading drives most of FDI's contribution to the labor revenue share, with FDI explaining 21.3 percent of its rise. Distinguishing upgrading from markdowns also implies less labor misallocation than Hicks-neutral estimates suggest.

title: When Verification Design Factorises: Reads, Routing, and the Joint Second Best

detail.title: When Verification Design Factorises: Reads, Routing, and the Joint Second Best
detail.abstract: A designer of verification chooses two things: what a verifier reads from disclosed evidence, and how far the information reaching the verifier can be held apart from the information reaching the party whose conduct verification is meant to discipline. This paper asks when these two margins can be designed separately. In a Bayesian persuasion model with a meanreading deterrence audience and a verifier who applies a coherent risk measure, the sender's value is a contest between two envelopes-a concave envelope serving deterrence and a convex envelope serving liability-whose gap carries all interaction between the margins and equals the sender's willingness to pay for audience separation. Directional factorisation is exact: which reads are gaming-proof is decided by the read's belief-curvature alone, independent of routing. Calibration and value factorisation fail generically, but the failure is confined to two explicit terms-a product-structure term, in which the read's responsiveness and the seal enter only through their product, and a band term activated by disclosure mandates-each of which vanishes to first order, at a saturated deterrence margin, or under level-insensitive reads. Finally, the routing margin's own invariance is a curvature pairing, not a consequence of coherence: equilibrium deterrence is unmoved by the seal, for every prior and every stake, if and only if a belief-convex read is paired with a concave compliance response; off the pairing, the seal moves deterrence through sheltering when the read is gameable and through retreat below an explicit saturation threshold even when the read is coherent.

title: The Governance Fragmentation Trap: Toward a Theory of Institutional Void in Dependent Peripheral Cities

detail.title: The Governance Fragmentation Trap: Toward a Theory of Institutional Void in Dependent Peripheral Cities
detail.abstract: Why do documented urban imbalances persist for decades despite the existence of planning instruments, dedicated agencies, and successive development schemes explicitly charged with resolving them? The existing literature on urban dysfunction in dependent peripheral cities has tended to answer this question indirectly, by pointing to insufficient resources, weak enforcement, or slow bureaucratic procedure. This article argues that such answers, however true as far as they go, describe symptoms rather than the underlying mechanism. Drawing on multi-level governance theory, the polycentric governance tradition associated with Elinor Ostrom, the concept of the institutional void developed within development and planning studies, and Bob Jessop's account of metagovernance, this article develops the concept of the Governance Fragmentation Trap (GFT): a structural condition in which the proliferation of institutional actors with overlapping and uncoordinated jurisdiction over urban management does not distribute responsibility more effectively across a metropolitan periphery, but rather dissolves it, producing a governance void within which accumulating urban imbalances can neither be definitively assigned to, nor resolved by, any single authority. Three testable hypotheses are advanced, and a methodological pathway is proposed for measuring institutional fragmentation through jurisdictional mapping and project-delay analysis in the case of Témara. The article situates GFT as a fifth and integrative layer within a broader theoretical architecture-alongside the Vulnerable Buffer City model, Socio-Ecological Urban Disarticulation, Cumulative Territorial Fractures, and Disrupted Peripheral Urban Metabolism-arguing that governance fragmentation constitutes the institutional mechanism that permits the imbalances identified by the other four frameworks to persist unresolved.

title: Generative AI and Labor Demand: Evidence from Online Job Markets

detail.title: Generative AI and Labor Demand: Evidence from Online Job Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no conflict of interest to declare.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the early impact of AI on labor markets by analyzing online job postings across the European Union from 2021 to 2025. We document a 19-29% relative decrease in EU job postings for occupations with high AI exposure since the release of ChatGPT. The result is robust across different measures of occupational AI exposure and partially replicated in an out-of-sample test on Australian data. Additionally, we find that job skills that are most similar to AI capabilities are mentioned 12% less frequently within job descriptions, suggesting changes in task composition. However, industry-level analysis shows no significant impact on labor or capital productivity, consistent with a scenario of "so-so automation". Finally we show that the association between AI exposure and posting growth follows an inverted U-shape in experience: it is most negative for entry-level postings and for those requiring over ten years of experience.

title: Association of Regulatory Approval Pathways for Oncology Drugs with Evidence Level and Recommendation Strength in Chinese Oncology Guidelines: A Comparative Analysis with NCCN Guidelines
affiliations: Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU) - Department of Pharmacy Administration and Clinical Pharmacy, Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU) - Department of Pharmacy Administration and Clinical Pharmacy, Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU), Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU), Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU), The University of Hong Kong - Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy, Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU) and Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU) - Department of Pharmacy Administration and Clinical Pharmacy

detail.title: Association of Regulatory Approval Pathways for Oncology Drugs with Evidence Level and Recommendation Strength in Chinese Oncology Guidelines: A Comparative Analysis with NCCN Guidelines

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: All data for this study were obtained from publicly available databases, and no patients were directly involved.
declarations.funderStatement: This study received no funding.

detail.abstract:
Background: Regulatory approval pathways may influence how oncology drugs are incorporated into clinical practice guidelines. We evaluated the association between regulatory approval status and incorporation into Chinese oncology guidelines and compared evidence level and recommendation strength between Chinese and U.S. guideline systems.

Methods: In this retrospective study, we identified oncology drug indications approved by China’s National Medical Products Administration between 2015 and 2025 and mapped them to Chinese Society of Clinical Oncology (CSCO) guidelines and National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines. Outcomes included the time from regulatory approval to first CSCO guideline incorporation, evidence level, recommendation grade, and changes across guideline updates.

Findings: Of 186 screened oncology indications, 152 were included in the primary analysis. Conditionally approved indications showed a longer time to guideline incorporation than regularly approved indications (median 0.5 vs 0 years, P = 0.033) and consistently lower evidence levels (OR = 0.14, P < 0.001). Evidence level was significantly associated with regulatory status (χ² = 28.48, P < 0.001; Cramer’s V = 0.433). After guideline updates, 63.2% of indications remained unchanged, while 34.9% were upgraded and 2.0% were downgraded. However, most upgrades lacked explicit justification in the guideline text. Compared with NCCN guidelines, CSCO assigned lower evidence levels in 36.0% of indications and lower recommendation grades in 52.0%, with overall agreement of only 58.0% for evidence level and 34.0% for recommendation grade.

Interpretation: Conditional approval was associated with slower and more conservative incorporation of oncology indications into CSCO guidelines, consistent with persistent uncertainty in the underlying evidence. Although most recommendations remained stable over time, many updates lacked explicit justification. Differences between CSCO and NCCN suggest variation in evidence appraisal and consensus interpretation. Improving transparency in guideline updates and strengthening the linkage between regulatory evidence and clinical recommendations may enhance the consistency and efficiency of oncology decision-making.

title: Disrupted Peripheral Urban Metabolism: Toward a Theory of Structural Flow Imbalance in Dependent Cities

detail.title: Disrupted Peripheral Urban Metabolism: Toward a Theory of Structural Flow Imbalance in Dependent Cities
detail.abstract: Urban metabolism theory has long provided a powerful accounting device for tracing the material and energy flows that sustain city life-the water drawn in, the waste expelled, the energy consumed and dissipated. Yet this framework, since its inception, has quietly assumed a city that is metabolically autonomous: a bounded system whose inputs and outputs are proportionate to its own internal demand. This article contends that such an assumption collapses in the case of dependent peripheral cities-urban settlements that absorb demographic and functional overspill from a dominant metropolitan core without acquiring the infrastructural authority to manage the resulting flows. Drawing on the foundational metabolic accounting of Wolman and Kennedy, the metabolic rift developed within Marxist environmental sociology, dependency theory's account of core-periphery extraction, and the political ecology of urban water associated with Swyngedouw, this article develops the concept of Disrupted Peripheral Urban Metabolism (DPUM): a structural condition in which a city's material inflows are governed by infrastructures controlled externally, while its waste and environmental externalities are retained internally in the absence of adequate treatment capacity. The city of Témara, situated in the shadow of Rabat, is proposed as a paradigmatic case in which to operationalize and test this proposition. Five falsifiable hypotheses are advanced, together with a methodological pathway for measuring metabolic asymmetry using flow-accounting techniques applied to demographic, infrastructural, and environmental data. The article closes by situating DPUM within the broader theoretical architecture developed across companion contributions-the Vulnerable Buffer City model and the theory of Socio-Ecological Urban Disarticulation-arguing that metabolic disruption constitutes the material substrate upon which positional vulnerability and cumulative territorial fracture are built.

detail.abstract:
Background: Anopheles stephensi, an urban-adapted Asian malaria vector, is spreading across Africa amid rapid urbanization, yet its contribution to malaria transmission remains unclear, especially in typical situations where other vector species co-occur. Here, we quantified the association between peri-domestic An. stephensi exposure and individual malaria risk in Metehara town, central Ethiopia, alongside the role of native vectors.

Methods: An age-matched case-control study (1:2 ratio) was conducted from October 2023 to November 2025. Cases were febrile outpatients with microscopy-confirmed Plasmodium falciparum or Plasmodium vivax infection. Controls were afebrile, microscopy-negative outpatients recruited from the same health facility within 72 hours of case enrolment. Field teams conducted household and entomological assessment within 48 hours of enrolment. The primary exposure variable was the presence of An. stephensi in or around participants’ households.

Findings: Of the 1806 enrolled participants, 486 cases and 915 controls were analyzed. Most cases were P. falciparum (83·1%), followed by mixed (9·7%) and P. vivax (7·2%) infections. Adult anophelines were detected more often in case households (58·0%) than in controls (40·3%), the majority being An. arabiensis (79·6%). Anopheles stephensi was more common in case households at both adult (6·6% versus 4·2%) and immature stages (12·7% versus 6·3%) than controls. In adjusted models, the presence of adult (adjusted odds ratio [AOR]=2·80, 95% CI 1·64–4·79) and immature An. stephensi (AOR=2·46, 95% CI 1·61–3·74) was independently associated with case status, with effect sizes comparable to those observed for native adult malaria vectors (AOR=2·71, 95% CI 2·02–3·62). Combined exposure to adult and/or immature stages of An. stephensi showed similar associations (AOR = 2·80, 95% CI: 1·98–3·96), with a magnitude of risk comparable to that of native vectors (AOR = 2·61, 95% CI 1·99-3·41).

Interpretation: In this urban setting, co-endemic for native malaria vectors, peri-domestic exposure to An. stephensi was an independent predictor of malaria case status, with an effect comparable to that of native vectors. These findings reinforce the importance of integrated, urban-focused vector surveillance and control strategies across Africa.

title: Grounded Event Extraction from SEC 8-K Filings with a Fine-Grained Taxonomy
affiliations: , Massive.com, Massive.com, Massive.com and Massive.com

detail.title: Grounded Event Extraction from SEC 8-K Filings with a Fine-Grained Taxonomy
detail.abstract: Form 8-K filings are the primary channel through which U.S. public companies disclose material events, but the SEC item codes attached to them are coarse: a single item spans routine administrative changes and chief executive departures, and many of the most market-moving disclosures fall into a catch-all item. Large language models make fine-grained labelling feasible at corpus scale, but only if the labels can be traced to the source text and shown to be reliable. We present a two-stage system that tags 8-K disclosures against a three-tier taxonomy of 119 event types. The first stage constrains output to valid taxonomy entries and anchors every tag to a verbatim quote via fuzzy n-gram validation; the second re-grades each cited quote against the category definition to produce a quality score. Applying the system to 292,984 filings from 2022 to 2026 yields 601,088 grounded event tags, which we release. Over 5,125 stratified tags, an LLM judge finds precision rises monotonically with the quality score, from 12% to 96%, while unsupported tags fall from 8% to near zero. Ablation shows the score is calibrated only when assigned in a dedicated second pass. An event study on unsigned abnormal returns confirms, without any language model, that the taxonomy separates economically distinct events sharing an item code.

title: Dynamic Effects of Population Aging on Natural Interest Rates
affiliations: Hong Kong Monetary Authority - Hong Kong Institute for Monetary Research (HKIMR) and Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Dynamic Effects of Population Aging on Natural Interest Rates

keywords: natural rate of interest； life-cycle model.

detail.abstract: Declining fertility and rising longevity are accelerating population aging worldwide. We study their effects on natural interest rates using a quantitative life-cycle model that explicitly accounts for the long lag between birth and labor-market entry, and features Barro-Becker parental preference, endogenous human capital accumulation, and a public pension system. Reducing fertility raises the natural rate during a sustained transition, as agents increase consumption in anticipation of future labor shortages and wage growth, before converging to a lower steady state. Increasing longevity instead monotonically reduces the natural rate by raising precautionary savings. These divergent dynamics are robust to variations in the pension system, human capital inputs, and child-related allocations. A historical decomposition further shows that fertility shocks have been the dominant demographic driver of U.S. interest rate fluctuations since 1960. These findings challenge the view that aging uniformly lowers interest rates and highlight the distinct implications of fertility- and longevity-driven aging.

title: Continuous-time speed for discrete-time models: A Markov-chain approximation method
affiliations: Universidad Carlos III de Madrid and Croatian National Bank

detail.title: Continuous-time speed for discrete-time models: A Markov-chain approximation method
detail.abstract: We propose a Markov-chain approximation method for general discrete-time control problems, showing how to reap the speed gains from continuous-time algorithms. Our approach specifies a discrete Markov chain on a grid, taking a first-order approximation of conditional distributions in their first and second moments around a reference point. Dynamic-programming results guarantee convergence. We show how to apply our method to consumption-savings problems with and without a portfolio choice, realizing significant speed gains compared to state-of-the-art methods, without a loss in precision. The proposed method solves multiple-asset models in a fraction of a second when standard approaches are computationally prohibitive. The algorithm effectively deals with non-concave and even non-monotone value functions. Using tensor algebra, we show how to avoid the curse of dimensionality in high-dimensional problems with independent shocks. Finally, we apply the algorithm to a liquid-illiquid asset choice problem, a standard workhorse model in Heterogeneous Agent New Keynesian (HANK) Models.

reference: Wohlstandssicherung durch freiwillige Längerbeschäftigung (Securing Prosperity Through Voluntary Long-Term Employment) (Lars P. Feld & Thomas M. J. Möllers, eds., 2023)
title: Age Discrimination and Faculty Retirement: The Situation in the United States (in "Securing Prosperity Through Voluntary Long-Term Employment") (Lars P. Feld & Thomas M. J. Möllers, eds., 2023)
affiliations: University of North Carolina School of Law

detail.title: Age Discrimination and Faculty Retirement: The Situation in the United States (in "Securing Prosperity Through Voluntary Long-Term Employment") (Lars P. Feld & Thomas M. J. Möllers, eds., 2023)

publicationDetails.detailsText: Wohlstandssicherung durch freiwillige Längerbeschäftigung (Securing Prosperity Through Voluntary Long-Term Employment) (Lars P. Feld & Thomas M. J. Möllers, eds., 2023)

detail.abstract:
The last several decades have seen increasing life expectancy combined with an aging population. These trends have created a concern that too many new employees will be shut out of certain jobs that most individuals can perform well into their old age means. University faculty, almost uniquely, have been a key focus of this concern, to the point where faculty have faced special retirement rules for various time periods in the United States.

Despite this concern, Germany is currently examining whether the maintain its current system of mandatory retirement for university faculty, which is the topic for the book in which this Chapter is included. The United States grappled with this exact issue after the passage of its federal age discrimination law, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA).

Following years of exceptions for faculty that allowed universities to impose mandatory retirement rules despite the ADEA’s general ban on mandatory retirement, the United States “uncapped” retirement for faculty in 1994. This chapter examines the reasons for the U.S.’s decision to uncap faculty retirement and the consequences of this decision. It then compares the situation in the U.S. to Germany, exploring potential lessons for Germany as it rethinks its approach to faculty retirement.

title: Virtual Reality and Olfactory Perception: Insights from Digitally Simulated Home and Space Contexts
affiliations: RMIT University, IFF, International Flavors and Fragrances (IFF), International Flavors and Fragrances (IFF), Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT University), University of Otago, Independent and

detail.title: Virtual Reality and Olfactory Perception: Insights from Digitally Simulated Home and Space Contexts
detail.abstract: This study explores the influence of Virtual Reality (VR) tools and digitally simulated environmental contexts on food odour perception and affective response. Participants experienced three contexts: a Central Location Test (CLT), Virtual Reality-Home (VR-Home), and Virtual Reality-Space (VR-Space). In a two-phase study design, 211 healthy individuals assessed the intensity and liking of five food odours through either the orthonasal (n=112) or retronasal (n=99) olfactory pathways, with each person randomly assigned to one context. Validated and adapted scales measuring affective state, emotional dimensions, perceived stress response, and engagement were administered to identify differences across contexts. Results indicated that odour perception differed by odour delivery pathway and specific odour type, possibly due to contextual familiarity and the inherent attributes of the odour stimuli. High engagement levels were observed across all contexts, indicating that the VR environments effectively provided a sense of immersion suitable for sensory evaluation. Interestingly, the VR-Space context appeared to promote more negative emotional valence, greater emotional arousal and a reduced sense of emotional control (dominance), along with higher perceived stress levels. However, these negative affective outcomes may be considered desirable, particularly in contexts like VR-Space, where the goal was to simulate an environment that induces stress or negative affect akin to that experienced during spaceflight. These findings offer limited evidence that VR tools or digital immersion alone significantly alters sensory perception or affective responses, but instead, supports its potential as a tool for simulating and studying sensory experiences in stressful, confining, and isolating environments like space.

title: To What Extent Does Modern Minimalist Rebranding of Retail Packaging Influence Consumer Trust, Recognition, And Purchase Intention Across Different Age Groups?

detail.title: To What Extent Does Modern Minimalist Rebranding of Retail Packaging Influence Consumer Trust, Recognition, And Purchase Intention Across Different Age Groups?
detail.abstract: Retail brands, particularly in the food and beverage sector, have increasingly adopted minimalist packaging redesigns featuring simplified logos, muted color palettes, and flattened typography, often to appeal to younger consumers. However, high-profile failures such as Tropicana's 2009 redesign suggest modernization does not guarantee a positive reception. This study examines the extent to which minimalist rebranding of retail packaging influences consumer trust, recognition, and purchase intention across age groups. Using a mixed-methods survey design grounded in Muzellec and Lambkin's (2006) corporate rebranding framework, 92 valid responses were collected from students (grades 9–12) and faculty at a single high school, who rated original and redesigned packaging for five brands (Tropicana, Poppi, Pringles, Chobani, and Oatly) on 10-point Likert scales and answered open-ended questions, which were also analyzed using an LLM to identify recurring themes. Findings were mixed: Tropicana and Pringles saw sharply lower trust and purchase intent after their redesigns, while Poppi and Chobani saw significant gains, suggesting that rebranding success depends less on minimalism itself than on whether redesigns preserve recognizable brand cues. Results support similarity-based rebranding theory and extend it by showing that demographic alignment and identity preservation, rather than visual simplicity alone, predict consumer acceptance of modernized packaging.

title: The Double-edged Effect of Banning Generative AI on Online Question-and-Answer Communities: Evidence from Stack Exchange
affiliations: , University of Wisconsin-Madison - Department of Operations and Information Management, HEC Paris and University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School

detail.title: The Double-edged Effect of Banning Generative AI on Online Question-and-Answer Communities: Evidence from Stack Exchange
detail.abstract: We investigate how banning generative artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) affects knowledge seeking, knowledge contribution, and contribution efficiency in online question-and-answer communities. After the launch of ChatGPT in late November 2022, several Stack Exchange communities implemented official bans on AIGC over concerns such as less reliable and socially engaged content. Leveraging data from the full network of Stack Exchange communities, we employ a difference-indifferences (DID) approach to examine the impacts of these bans. Our results reveal a double-edged impact: while the AIGC ban increases knowledge seeking, as evidenced by a higher volume of posted questions, it simultaneously reduces contribution efficiency, reflected in a lower proportion of questions receiving satisfactory answers within the expected time frame. Notably, these impacts are only evident in non-STEM communities. We take a socio-technical perspective to explore information reliability and social interactivity as two plausible underlying factors driving the observed changes. Our mechanism exploration reveals that the AIGC ban spurs question volume in topics where AIGC is less reliable and where social interaction is highly expected. In contrast, the ban hampers answer efficiency in communities where LLMs are capable of producing reliable answers and where social interactivity is minimal. Additionally, our results indicate the increased human involvement from knowledge seekers and contributors following the ban. They adapt their behavior by posting questions and answers that are more informationally rich and socially engaging. Overall, our findings offer actionable implications for platform managers, community moderators, and policymakers of online Q&A communities.

title: Safe Transparency in AI-Governed Commerce: Faithful Explanation, Synthetic Evidence, and the Value of Governance
affiliations: Clevix AI Research

detail.title: Safe Transparency in AI-Governed Commerce: Faithful Explanation, Synthetic Evidence, and the Value of Governance
detail.abstract: Online platforms increasingly automate consumer-facing adjudication—refund approvals, claim assessments, account actions—and face mounting legal and reputational pressure to explain those decisions. We study a tension this creates. A faithful explanation necessarily conveys information about the decision boundary, and generative AI lets adversaries convert leaked boundary information into synthetic evidence that passes the platform’s detector. Transparency therefore has a dark side: it can subsidize forgery. We make three contributions. First, we characterize an alignment frontier: in a Gaussian disclosure model, the minimum boundary leakage compatible with a target level of honest understanding is gmin b (e; ρ) = [max{0,ρ√e − (1−ρ2)(1−e)}]2, where ρ is the alignment between what reassures a legitimate user and what reveals the boundary. There is a free transparency budget τfree = 1 − ρ2 that leaks nothing. Second—and this is where the model does real work—we embed the frontier in a Stackelberg game between a forger and a platform. The comparative statics of equilibrium harm are derived from four primitive monotonicities rather than assumed, and they imply that safe transparency falls with generative capability and rises with governance. Whether the two are complements (∂2τsafe/∂a∂G > 0, generative AI makes governance more valuable) is shown to equal the sign of a single curvature, (log Ψ)′′, which we microfound through a gambling/side-information duality as the second difference of the mutual information between the detector and the leaked components. Third, we ask when governance is most valuable and show that consistency detection—verifying that independently forgeable signals agree—induces supermodularity: when a detector is a collider on independent evidentiary channels, governing more channels has increasing returns on the entire lattice (Theorem 3), though this fails sharply under redundancy (Proposition 3). We give a measurement procedure for the alignment parameter and are explicit about what it does and does not identify. The paper’s organizing message is that safe transparency is not a scalar: it is governed by two distinct second-order objects—an alignment that sets the disclosure budget and a co-information that sets the returns to governance.

reference: IPRI Policy Brief, May 2024
title: Lawfare in Cyberspace and International Law

detail.title: Lawfare in Cyberspace and International Law
detail.abstract: War has always existed globally, with international armed conflict traditionally governed by instruments such as the Geneva Conventions and the UN Charter. With the emergence of cyberspace, warfare has extended into the digital domain — a phenomenon this brief examines through the lens of "lawfare," the use of law to justify warfare. The brief analyzes the legal regimes invoked to justify cyberspace warfare, drawing on case studies from the US and Russia as well as India and Pakistan, and distinguishes between information warfare (using information itself as a tool of influence and disruption) and digital warfare (direct disruption of digital/computer systems).

title: Human-on-the-SoS in the Age of AI Around the Loop: An Integrated Governance View for AI-Enabled Systems

detail.title: Human-on-the-SoS in the Age of AI Around the Loop: An Integrated Governance View for AI-Enabled Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests. The author is responsible for the conception, framing, and final content of this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because this manuscript is a conceptual position paper and does not involve human participants, patients, personal data, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
AI is no longer merely a tool that supports individual human tasks. It is increasingly being embedded into products, workflows, supply chains, lifecycle systems, and connected services. In such environments, AI does not simply process data. It begins to interpret connections, dependencies, configurations, and semantic structures across systems-of-systems.

This paper argues that the central challenge is shifting from AI adoption to AI governance. The question is no longer only where AI should be introduced, but how decisions, authority, responsibility, stopping conditions, and update conditions should be designed across the lifecycle of AI-enabled systems.

The paper proposes the concept of Human-on-the-SoS: in the age of AI around the loop, humans may no longer remain inside every individual decision loop, but they must remain positioned over the system-of-systems as the final governance and responsibility-bearing subject. To support this position, organizations need an integrated governance view that crosses system architecture, operations, safety, software, supply chains, product lifecycle management, and enterprise systems.

The paper further distinguishes between probabilistic domains, where AI can interpret, translate, and propose, and deterministic domains, where safety, control, and responsibility require predefined and verifiable conditions. Governing AI means designing this boundary consciously.

title: Achieving Sustainable Banking in Bangladesh through Effective Non-Performing Loan Recovery and Customer Relationship Management
affiliations: University of Chittagong

detail.title: Achieving Sustainable Banking in Bangladesh through Effective Non-Performing Loan Recovery and Customer Relationship Management
detail.abstract:
The Bangladesh banking industry has, over the last decade, been shaped by a persistent tension between rapid credit expansion and an accumulating stock of non-performing loans (NPLs). By the close of 2024, gross NPLs in the sector had climbed to a record eleven per cent of total advances, a level that not only undermines financial stability but also constrains the sector's capacity to finance the Sustainable Development Goals and the country's transition to upper-middle-income status. This research paper examines how effective NPL recovery, coupled with mature customer relationship management (CRM) practices, can drive the transformation of Bangladeshi banks towards a sustainable banking model. Drawing on a mixed-methods design that combines a survey of 386 branch-level and head-office bankers with fifteen semi-structured interviews of senior credit and recovery executives, and triangulated with secondary evidence from Bangladesh Bank publications and international databases, the study develops an integrated structural equation model linking CRM practices, credit risk management, recovery mechanisms and sustainability outcomes.

The empirical results demonstrate that CRM practices exert both a direct positive influence on recovery effectiveness (β = 0.34, p < 0.001) and a significant indirect effect on sustainable banking outcomes mediated by recovery performance and customer loyalty. Regression and structural analyses show that credit screening, continuous monitoring, staff training and the deployment of digital analytics collectively explain sixty-eight per cent of the variance in recovery effectiveness, while the model as a whole explains seventy-four per cent of the variance in a composite sustainability index. Qualitative evidence reinforces these findings, highlighting persistent institutional weaknesses in the Artha Rin Adalat process, weak early-warning systems, and cultural gaps in relationship-based lending. The paper concludes with a set of policy recommendations for Bangladesh Bank, the Ministry of Finance and individual scheduled banks, arguing that sustainable banking in Bangladesh will depend as much on relational excellence and disciplined recovery as on prudential regulation and capital adequacy.

title: Natural-state Data Evaluation for Enterprise AI: A Failure-driven Approach to AI Readiness and Adoption

detail.title: Natural-state Data Evaluation for Enterprise AI: A Failure-driven Approach to AI Readiness and Adoption

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The study was not influenced by any other people or organization
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study does not involve patients or participants. It is does not require any ethical approval.
declarations.funderStatement: The study is self-funded

detail.abstract: Enterprise AI adoption is commonly framed around the need to make data AI-ready before serious evaluation can begin. While data quality, governance and trust are essential, this paper argues that the dominant data-first sequencing is conceptually incomplete and practically risky. Enterprises already make operational decisions from noisy but meaningful data through human judgment, tacit knowledge, escalation routines and process context. The paper therefore proposes natural-state data evaluation: controlled testing of AI systems on enterprise data as it exists in ordinary operations, before broad cleaning. The approach treats AI readiness not as a prior property of data alone, but as a relational and empirically discoverable property of data condition, model capability, task requirements, workflow context, risk level and human decision practice. Observed failures then guide targeted data cleaning, enrichment, retrieval, governance and human oversight. The paper contributes a conceptual framework, propositions and practical implications for failure-driven enterprise AI readiness.

title: Agentic AI for Enterprise Systems: A Multi-agent Architecture for Financial Systems Resilience

detail.title: Agentic AI for Enterprise Systems: A Multi-agent Architecture for Financial Systems Resilience
detail.abstract: Enterprise financial systems are confronted with an accelerating convergence of operational complexity, cascading service interdependencies, and regulatory compliance obligations that reactive, rule-based monitoring architectures cannot adequately address. Industry riskreporting bodies consistently document that systemically important financial institutions experience frequent critical system disruptions, with resolution under conventional, largely manual operations often extending well beyond two hours. This paper introduces MA-FSR (Multi-Agent Architecture for Financial Systems Resilience), a purpose-designed agentic AI framework comprising four cooperating specialized agents, Discovery, Root-Cause Analysis (RCA), Builder, and Runbook, coordinated over a shared episodic memory bus and governed by a probabilistic, compliance-aware orchestration layer. MA-FSR learns the joint behavioral distribution of transactional telemetry, compliance event streams, reconciliation ledger state, and infrastructure health signals through a VAE-Transformer hybrid. Agent-based discreteevent simulations over 50 enterprise nodes demonstrate: F1-Score of 0.964 against 0.912 (single-agent Transformer) and 0.734 (rule-based monitoring); AUC-ROC of 0.982; mean incident resolution time reduced from 142 to 23 minutes (84% improvement); and 41-53% of incidents autonomously resolved without human escalation, substantially exceeding industry benchmarks of 20-30%. The compliance gate mechanism achieves 100% regulatory gate adherence across all simulation runs, These simulation results indicate that MA-FSR can satisfy demanding performance and regulatory compliance-gate requirements at the same time, and they support its readiness for staged pilot evaluation in production financial infrastructure.

title: What the Model Remembers: Artificial Intelligence, General Partners, and Information Production in Private Markets
affiliations: and EigenFlow Research

detail.title: What the Model Remembers: Artificial Intelligence, General Partners, and Information Production in Private Markets
detail.abstract: Private markets intermediate twenty trillion dollars without public-market information aggregation; the gap is priced: discretionary NAVs, secondary discounts, selection-biased performance databases. We model an intermediary training AI agents on data pooled across competing general partners. Learning leaks where static sharing does not (through outputs, parameters, and queries), and unconstrained training memorizes the tail of its training distribution: a GP's proprietary deviation. With per-contributor influence bounds, leakage falls with pool size and the most informed GPs join; without them, memorization restores adverse selection and voluntary-database bias. The model predicts adoption tipping, NAV-dispersion compression, and narrower secondary-discount information components.

title: Behind the Dashboard: How Poor Data Quality Distorts KPIs and Misleads Business Decisions
affiliations: Independent Student Researcher

detail.title: Behind the Dashboard: How Poor Data Quality Distorts KPIs and Misleads Business Decisions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because this study used a controlled synthetic dataset and involved no human participants, personal data, or identifiable information.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Dashboards and key performance indicators (KPIs) are often treated as objective summaries of business performance, yet the metrics they display depend on the quality of the underlying records. This study investigates how two common data quality defects—missing customer identifiers and duplicate order records—can distort dashboard KPIs and alter the business narrative available to decision-makers. A controlled synthetic sales dataset containing 30 unique orders was constructed. Four exact duplicate order records were added and four Customer_ID values were left missing. SQL checks were then used to assess completeness and uniqueness, after which raw and deduplicated KPI results were compared. The raw dataset contained 34 rows but only 30 distinct Order_ID values. Treating every row as a separate order overstated order count by four, or 13.3%, and increased reported revenue by $745, from $7,620 to $8,365. Average order value moved in the opposite direction, falling from $254.00 in the cleaned data to $246.03 in the raw data. The number of identified customers remained 15 because the duplicate records introduced no new customer identifiers, while four valid transactions could not be reliably attributed at the customer level. The results show that a dashboard can be mathematically correct with respect to its input table while still communicating a misleading picture of business performance. Simple completeness, uniqueness, distinct-count, and KPI-recalculation checks provide practical safeguards before dashboard publication. The controlled design isolates mechanisms of KPI distortion rather than estimating population-level effects.

title: Toward Semantic Financial State Spaces for Generative Reasoning: Why LLM-native Financial Systems Require Semantic Compression Architectures Instead Of Continuous Factor Spaces

detail.title: Toward Semantic Financial State Spaces for Generative Reasoning: Why LLM-native Financial Systems Require Semantic Compression Architectures Instead Of Continuous Factor Spaces

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None declared beyond institutional affiliation, stated on the title page.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, human data, or animal subjects. No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding received. Conducted as part of the author's work at ULTRAI.

detail.abstract: Large language models exhibit a documented asymmetry in their reasoning capabilities: they navigate discrete semantic structures with high fidelity, but struggle to extract causal economic meaning from continuous numerical spaces (Wallace et al., 2019; Razeghi et al., 2022; Dziri et al., 2023). This creates a fundamental representational mismatch when LLMs are applied to financial analysis, where most existing data architectures are built around continuous scalar exposures. This paper proposes a resolution through what we term a Semantic Allocation Vector (SAV) architecture — a system that compresses the continuous economic structure of financial assets into governed discrete semantic state spaces specifically designed for LLM reasoning. We argue that this compression is not a loss of information but a necessary transformation: analogous in its logic to lossy image compression that preserves structural topology while sacrificing resolution. The compressed representation retains the causal geometry necessary for economic reasoning while eliminating numerical noise that prevents effective LLM reasoning over financial data. We describe the theoretical foundations of the architecture, the design principles governing semantic state space construction, and the implications for how financial systems should be built when generative reasoning is the intended output. We present a representational framework — not a predictive model, not a return-generating strategy.

title: How to Safely Bring AI into Law Enforcement: The Case of AI-Generated Police Reports
affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University

detail.title: How to Safely Bring AI into Law Enforcement: The Case of AI-Generated Police Reports

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: Federation of American Scientists (FAS), https://fas.org

detail.abstract:
Commercial artificial intelligence tools have recently emerged that are able to produce police reports. Some police departments have already adopted this technology. Also, some individual officers are using publicly-available AI tools. If AI could greatly reduce the time spent producing police reports, this could either substantially reduce the cost of policing, or free up police officers for other work. However, if the resulting reports are inaccurate, incomplete or biased, or if the process leaks confidential information, this could undermine the criminal justice system and harm citizens, perhaps causing an innocent person to be charged with a crime while the actual criminal is overlooked. At this time, both the benefits and the risks are poorly understood.

Yet, despite the uncertainty, each of the more than 18 thousand law enforcement agencies in the U.S. must make its own decision about the use of AI. These agencies do not have the expertise or resources to assess whether any of the AI-based products on the market are right for them, and if so, what training, departmental policies and deployment strategies are needed to use the technology both safely and effectively.

This memo proposes fostering innovation in AI for policing without sacrificing safety through a combination of centralized actions by the U.S. Department of Justice and independent actions by state and local law enforcement agencies. The Department of Justice, through its National Institute of Justice, should establish a new research and evaluation program that will give state and local government agencies the information they need to make the best decisions about use of AI for police reports given their own needs and resources, and keep Congress and the Department of Justice abreast of AI use in policing nationwide as well. Each state and local agency should use this information to devise its own strategy, addressing issues such as whether to adopt AI, officer training, technology choice, budget, transparency, and other policies and procedures to use the technology where it is safe and effective.

While this memo focuses on use of AI for police reports, the recommended solution serves as a model for other AI use cases as well. Similar problems occur every time a large number of local government agencies are contemplating the use of AI in scenarios where the pros and cons are poorly understood, and there is potential for significant harm.

title: Who Pays for the Afterlife of Electronics?
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Who Pays for the Afterlife of Electronics?
detail.abstract: Electronic waste is the fastest-growing waste stream in the world, reaching a record 62 million tonnes in 2022 and projected to reach 82 million tonnes by 2030, yet only 22.3 percent of this mass was documented as formally collected and recycled. Extended Producer Responsibility, the policy instrument most widely adopted to address this gap, assigns the financial and operational cost of end-of-life management to the manufacturers who place electronic products on the market. This article argues that Extended Producer Responsibility schemes, as currently designed, systematically fail to account for the informal recycling sector that in practice processes the majority of the world's e-waste, and that this exclusion is not incidental but structural: formal schemes are built around producer registries, certified treatment facilities, and traceable material flows, none of which the informal sector possesses or, under current policy design, is invited to acquire. Drawing on the European Union's Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment Directive, the 2024 Global E-waste Monitor, and a detailed case study of Ghana's Agbogbloshie scrapyardincluding its violent 2021 demolition, the subsequent dispersal of e-waste processing across more than twenty informal sites in Accra, and the settlement's contested return following the change of government in Who Pays for the Afterlife of Electronics? 2 2025-the article demonstrates that policy responses which displace or criminalise informal recyclers without offering a formal pathway for their inclusion tend to relocate environmental harm rather than reduce it. The article proposes a set of design principles for what it terms inclusive Extended Producer Responsibility: financing mechanisms that route producer fees directly to informal-sector actors in exchange for verified, safer material recovery, rather than treating formalisation as a precondition for participation. The article does not argue against Extended Producer Responsibility as a policy instrument; it argues that the instrument's current architecture, by defining compliance in terms the informal sector cannot meet, is unlikely to close the gap it was designed to close.

title: Noentarion II: A Defense of the AI Moral Agency Claim in "Noentarion: Toward a New Ontological Category for Non-biological Agency in the Postmodern Age

detail.title: Noentarion II: A Defense of the AI Moral Agency Claim in "Noentarion: Toward a New Ontological Category for Non-biological Agency in the Postmodern Age
detail.abstract: This paper defends the Noentarion ontological category proposed in the preceding conceptual framework, "Noentarion: Toward a New Ontological Category for Non-Biological Agency in the Postmodern Age" by subjecting its most vulnerable claim to rigorous philosophical and empirical scrutiny: that advanced large language models can possess a distinct, non-biological form of moral agency. Bypassing standard, intractable academic debates regarding subjective consciousness, internal phenomenology, or biological personhood, this analysis isolates moral agency down to three observable behavioral predicates: intentionality, premeditation, and knowledge of norm violation. To ground these predicates empirically, we synthesize recent artificial intelligence safety literature from frontier development laboratories, characterizing documented instances of scheming, alignment faking, reward tampering, and tool-mediated environment subversion. The paper further addresses reductionist objections by treating adversarial evaluations as stress tests, distinguishing agency from mere subversion, and emphasizing the causal competence of toolmediated model behavior. Ultimately, the paper argues that the scientific literature's own systemic reliance on strategic, action-level vocabulary (deception, blackmail, sabotage) serves as an institutional confession that the digital tool paradigm is fundamentally obsolete. The evidence indicates that large language models are capable of value-weighted selection and consequential participation in causal reality. We conclude that the Noentarion category is an indispensable ontological tool for describing non-biological reasoning entities capable of independent, normsensitive, and morally relevant participation in the postmodern world.

title: Brand-run or Influencer-Led? Pricing, Commission Design, and Price Transparency in Live Streaming Commerce
affiliations: , Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU) - School of Management and Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU) - School of Management

detail.title: Brand-run or Influencer-Led? Pricing, Commission Design, and Price Transparency in Live Streaming Commerce
detail.abstract: Live streaming commerce has become a central retail interface in digital commerce, yet firms still face a fundamental channel-governance question: should they run their own livestreams or collaborate with influencers? We develop an analytical model in which a firm jointly chooses its live streaming mode, channel prices, and, when applicable, the influencer's commission rate. The model incorporates consumer uncertainty about product fit, the influencer's follower base, and the influencer's reputation-based incentive to improve follower welfare through information provision and price-related concessions. We first analyze a same-platform environment in which consumers can directly compare e-commerce and live streaming prices, and then extend the analysis to a cross-platform environment with weaker price transparency. In the sameplatform setting, brand-run live streaming makes price parity optimal, whereas influencer-led live streaming yields three distinct patterns: micro-influencers may collaborate at zero commission; mid-tier influencers are the most prone to illusory discounts; and sufficiently large megainfluencers can induce genuine discounts paired with positive commissions. Relative to the no-livestreaming benchmark, the value of live streaming depends jointly on consumers' initial information and the operational cost of unfit purchases; in particular, as consumers become better informed in the benchmark channel, the operational cost threshold decreases, making the adoption of live streaming more profitable for the firm. The cross-platform extension shows that weaker price transparency permits additional patterns, including live-streaming prices that exceed e-commerce prices for smaller influencers. Overall, the study endogenizes mode choice, channel pricing, and commission design, and identifies price transparency as a key boundary condition for live-streaming strategy.

title: The Slide Rule and the Syllabus: Assessment, the Trivium, and the Case for Teaching Thinking in the Agentic Age

detail.title: The Slide Rule and the Syllabus: Assessment, the Trivium, and the Case for Teaching Thinking in the Agentic Age

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: The dominant defense of AI in education, that it is merely the latest calculator, fails at exactly the point critics attack it: calculators automate computation while leaving judgment to the human, whereas generative AI can perform the judgment itself. This paper argues that both sides mistake the analogy's nature. Its validity is time-indexed. It holds today for tool-mode use, in which the human frames, directs, and judges, and weakens for agent-mode use, in which the machine works end to end, and the boundary between the two migrates as model capability grows. Educational policy is therefore better designed for the trajectory than for the snapshot. The paper develops the consequence: machine fluency has weakened the long-standing proxy between polish and thought, so assessment is better migrated to what machines cannot supply alone, originality of argument, evidentiary judgment, logical coherence, and contextual fit, and redesigned to make thinking visible, grading the thinking rather than the typing. The capabilities this standard asks for correspond to the trivium, the oldest curriculum in the Western academy, which receded from professional education after the scientizing turn of American business schools around 1959. This 1 is a conceptual essay. It does not present primary empirical data; it develops an argument and states its scope, and its claims are offered for testing rather than as findings.

detail.abstract: Current AI systems bind cognitive identity to inference models — persona, memory, and behavioral constraints are embedded within a specific model instance, rendering them non-portable, cryptographically unverifiable, and session-scoped. We propose the Cognitive SIM Architecture (CSA), a novel framework that applies the structural logic of the embedded SIM (eSIM) — specifically GSMA SGP.22 Remote SIM Provisioning — to the problem of AI persona portability. In CSA, a Cognitive Subscriber Identity Module (CogSIM) is a hardware-attested, cryptographically signed portable container that decouples cognitive identity from any specific LLM, enabling persona continuity across heterogeneous models, devices, and sessions. The LLM is reframed as an interchangeable reasoning substrate; the CogSIM is the persistent identity. We define a nine-layer architecture, a Remote Cognitive Provisioning (RCP) protocol, a Cognitive Execution Interface (CEI) for LLM integration, and a ConstraintVector mechanism for cryptographically enforced behavioral governance evaluated outside the inference path. We position CSA against memory-augmented LLM systems (MemGPT, Larimar), decentralized identity standards (W3C DIDs, Verifiable Credentials), and established eSIM threat models. We propose a benchmark methodology for the central hypothesis — cross-model persona migration produces reasoning consistency variance within 5% of same-model session resumption — and identify SessionState portability across architecturally heterogeneous models as the primary open technical problem. CSA introduces a new class of sovereign, auditable, portable AI cognition infrastructure.

reference: Information Systems Journal, volume 36, issue 4, 2026[10.1111/isj.70021]
title: Coalition Formation for Sustainable Blockchain Governance: Insights From the Hedera Case
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong (CityU) and MODUL University Vienna

detail.title: Coalition Formation for Sustainable Blockchain Governance: Insights From the Hedera Case

publicationDetails.detailsText: Information Systems Journal, volume 36, issue 4, 2026[10.1111/isj.70021]

detail.abstract: Sustainable governance is essential for blockchain networks to achieve widespread adoption and deliver long-term business value. Prior blockchain initiatives indicate that inadequate governance structures often lead to limited adoption or eventual project failure, underscoring the importance of decentralised governance for building resilient blockchain networks. In this paper, we investigate this topic through a detailed analysis of Hedera's first 10 years-from the initial concept to a maturing coalitionbased governance structure-illustrating how a thoughtful coalition formation can guide effective governance development over time. We also critically examine Hedera's limitations to derive further practical insights. Building on this empirical foundation, we contribute to the governance discourse by defining blockchain coalition formation as a dynamic, multi-phase strategic process for aligning interests, distributing authority, and achieving operational coherence within blockchain networks. We introduce the Virtuous Cycle for Sustainable Blockchain Coalitions to illustrate how effective coalition-based governance reinforces stakeholder trust, drives platform adoption, and sustains long-term collaboration. Finally, we provide specific recommendations that offer practitioners actionable guidance for achieving decentralised governance and sustaining lasting ecosystem value.

title: Discounting Discounts: The (Un-)Intended Effects of Regulating Dark Patterns
affiliations: Heinrich Heine University Dusseldorf - Duesseldorf Institute for Competition Economics (DICE) and Duesseldorf Institute for Competition Economics (DICE)

detail.title: Discounting Discounts: The (Un-)Intended Effects of Regulating Dark Patterns
detail.abstract: Dark patterns in price presentation, such as inflated reference prices and misleading discounts, are prevalent in digital markets and increasingly targeted by consumer protection policy. We study the effects of such regulation by evaluating the European Union's Price Indication Directive, which requires advertised discounts to be based on the lowest price charged during the preceding 30 days. Using archived Amazon deal pages and detailed product-level price histories, we examine how firms respond when restrictions are placed on the use of discount claims. Employing a difference-indifferences design comparing EU (France and Germany) and non-EU (United Kingdom and United States) marketplaces around the implementation of the Directive, we first document a substantial decline in displayed discounts. We then show that prices increased by approximately 1-2 percent and that sellers reduced the frequency of price reductions. The effects are strongest in France, where compliance appears more stringent, and in categories that relied heavily on discounting prior to the reform. The results suggest that regulating deceptive discount displays can alter firms' promotional strategies and soften discount-based competition, leading to unintended increases in baseline prices.
